name: Que of Li Ye
sub: Zitong · Eastern Han single stone que
lede: A plain stone shaft with no bracketed upper storey, its cap a later replacement, and yet regarded as the earliest surviving Han que gate-pillar in China. The shaft is a single stone 2.45 m high; only its south face carries two lines of clerical script reading 'Que of Master Li, Attendant Censor of the Han', apparently recut in a later age. Li Ye was a scholar of Zitong who refused office under Wang Mang and Gongsun Shu; after the Eastern Han destroyed Shu in 36 CE (Jianwu 12) his gate was honoured, and the que is accordingly dated to the early Eastern Han. The Southern Song gazetteer Yudi jisheng already records that it was broken by the Red Eyebrows. The plate shows the south face of the single surviving pillar.
facts: Form: a single que of which only the base stone and shaft remain. The base is 0.25 m high, 1.57 m long and 0.8 m wide; the shaft is one stone 2.45 m high, 0.97 by 0.69 m at the foot, tapering to 0.68 by 0.49 m at the top. Of the four faces only the south bears a border line and inscription, the other three being plain; the cap is a later addition.

Dating: traditionally placed around 36 CE (Jianwu 12) on the strength of the biography of Li Ye in the Hou Hanshu, making it the earliest of the Sichuan que; the earliest record is Wang Xiangzhi's Southern Song Yudi jisheng, which says 'the Red Eyebrows broke its two que'. A shrine to Li Ye was built beside it in the Jiajing reign of the Ming; in 1845 (Daoguang 25) the magistrate Zhou Shutang found the broken shaft, moved it into the Li Jieshi shrine and cut a 'Record of Moving the Que' on it.

Significance: because shaft and cap are undecorated and the structure so simple, it has even been argued that 'the Li Ye que is not a que'; yet precisely because only the shaft survives it shows the basic mass of a Han que before any upper storey was added. A shelter pavilion was built over it after the 1950s, and inspection after the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake found it undamaged. The cap drawn in the plate is a later replacement and is not counted as original Han fabric.

name: Taishi Que of Dengfeng
sub: West que · Spirit-way que of Zhongyue Temple
lede: China's oldest surviving ritual structures are not halls but a pair of stone que gate-towers. In 118 CE (Yuanchu 5 of the Eastern Han), Lü Chang, magistrate of Yangcheng, raised these spirit-way towers before the temple of Mount Taishi, copying the timber gate-towers of his day into stone: a lower 'child' tower leans against each 'mother' tower, and the roofs are carved with ridges, tile rows and rafters. The plate shows the west tower, slightly taller than the east one at 3.96 m, with the seal-script title 'Zhongyue Taishi Yangcheng' still on its south face.
facts: Form: The two towers face each other 6.75 m apart; each joins a mother tower to a lower child tower on its outer side, built up from base, shaft and roof. The west tower stands 3.96 m, its shaft laid in eight courses of stone, its roof imitating a hip roof with main ridge, hip ridges, tile rows and rafters.

Dating: A clerical-script inscription under the eave of the west tower's child tower, on the north face—27 lines of 7 characters—records why Lü Chang and others built the que in 118 CE; the six-character seal-script title 'Zhongyue Taishi Yangcheng' is cut in relief on the south face. In 1971 the east tower's roof was restored from scattered fragments.

Significance: With the Shaoshi and Qimu que (118–123) it forms the 'Three Han Que of Zhongyue', the only Han temple que surviving in China. The shafts carry low-relief scenes of carriage processions, horse acrobatics, cockfights, jugglers, pavilions and the Azure Dragon and White Tiger; in 2010 the site was inscribed as part of the UNESCO World Heritage 'Centre of Heaven and Earth' monuments of Dengfeng.

name: Shaoshi Que of Dengfeng
sub: West que · Spirit-way que of Mount Shaoshi
era: Reign of Emperor An of Han
lede: The most densely carved of the three que. The Shaoshi Que was the spirit-way gate of the temple of Mount Shaoshi, a double mother-and-child tower like the Taishi Que, but its four faces are packed with more than seventy scenes: horse races, kickball (cuju), elephant training, cockfights, dogs chasing hares, the dark bird of the Shang legend—the whole bustle of a Han mountain-god festival cut into stone. The inscriptions carry no exact date; because the names match those on the Taishi and Qimu que, it is placed between 118 and 123, while the Zhengzhou Cultural Heritage Bureau gives 123 (Yanguang 2). The plate shows the west tower.
facts: Form: The east and west towers stand 7.60 m apart, both double mother-and-child que built of grey-blue stone blocks in three parts—base, shaft and roof. The west tower is 3.75 m high, the east 3.37 m; the roofs are badly damaged. The towers were restored to their original state in 1972.

Dating: Most of the inscriptions have weathered away; only the six-character seal-script title 'Shaoshi shendao zhi que' on the north face of the west tower and a few clerical-script phrases under the child tower's eave remain legible. Since the names match those on the Taishi and Qimu que, construction is placed in 118–123; the Zhengzhou bureau gives 123.

Imagery: The four faces preserve more than seventy scenes—carriage processions, banquets, winged immortals, the Four Spirits, animal combats, swordplay, hunting, elephant training, cockfights, kickball, the moon palace—of which the horse-acrobatics and hunting scenes are the finest. It holds the richest imagery of the three que, which together are China's only surviving Han temple gate-towers.

name: Qimu Que of Dengfeng
sub: West que · Spirit-way que of Qimu Temple
lede: The legend of Yu the Great's wife turning to stone and giving birth to Qi was given a temple in Han times; the temple is long gone, but the spirit-way gate-towers before it still stand. The Qimu Que was built in 123 CE (Yanguang 2) by Zhu Chong, governor of Yingchuan. Its shafts show Yu transformed into a bear, Guo Ju burying his son, elephant training, conjuring and a scene of women playing kickball, and the surviving tile rows and tile-ends of the roof are a direct sample of a Han roof. The plate shows the south face of the west tower; the two inscriptions on its back, about flood control and prayers for rain, are not in the picture.
facts: Form: The two towers stand 6.8 m apart, the west 3.17 m and the east 3.18 m high. The west tower rests on a two-layer stone base; its shaft is seven courses of stone stacked vertically, 2.75 m in all, topped by a bucket-shaped block and the roof. The roof is badly damaged; what survives shows a hip roof with tile rows, hip ridges, persimmon-calyx tile-ends and flat tiles, the main ridge lost.

Dating: Two inscriptions survive on the north face of the west tower. The seal-script 'Qimu Que Inscription' records that Zhu Chong, governor of Yingchuan, built the que in 123 CE and praises Yu's taming of the floods; below it the clerical-script 'Prayer for Rain', composed by Tangxi Dian, had 18 lines of 5 characters, of which 11 remain. In Han times the name was changed to Kaimu to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Jing (Liu Qi).

Imagery: The shafts carry horse acrobatics, mounted processions, jugglers, conjurers, elephant training, Guo Ju burying his son, Yu turning into a bear, pony riding, hunting, a tiger chasing a deer, twin dragons and the moon palace; the scene of women playing kickball is often cited as physical evidence of the game's popularity in the Han. About 190 m north stands the 'Qimu Stone', said to be the petrified wife of Yu.

name: Que of Gao Yi
lede: A timber-frame tower built up in red sandstone: the blocks rise in tiers as base, shaft, storey and cap, and in the storey the cap-blocks, the one-block-two-bearer bracket sets and the crossed layers of beams are each carved out; the rafters and tile-rows of the double-eaved hip roof are all there, with eaves projecting more than 0.6 m. The main pillar stands 5.9 m high with a 2.94 m ear-pillar attached, the best-preserved mother-and-child que in Sichuan. The tomb owner Gao Yi, governor of Yizhou, died in 209 CE (Jian'an 14), and the que was raised soon after. The plate shows the front of the western (right-hand) que.
facts: Form: a mother-and-child que in red sandstone imitating timber construction; the main pillar is in four parts, base, shaft, storey and cap, 5.9 m high in all. The shaft is four courses of solid stone 2.64 m high, with six columns carved on the north and south faces and a procession of carriages and riders on the lintel; the storey has four tiers, the first with six cap-blocks on its four faces, the second carried on one-block-two-bearer bracket sets; the cap is a double-eaved hip roof whose 24 beam-ends each bear a clerical-script character.

Dating: the inscription names the owner as 'the late Gao, Governor of Yizhou, Commandant of Yinping, Magistrate of Wuyang, Assistant of the Northern Office, Filial and Incorrupt'; Gao Yi died in office in 209 (Jian'an 14) and the que followed. In the Song the tomb was repaired and a Jingxian Hall built to house the Gao Jun eulogy stele; it was repaired in 1983 and 2012, badly damaged in the Lushan earthquake of 2013, and a conservation project was approved in 2015.

Significance: about thirty Han que survive in China, and this is counted one of the two most valuable in Sichuan; Liang Sicheng surveyed it and wrote it into his History of Chinese Architecture. The reliefs on the storey, the nine-tailed fox, the three-legged crow, Ji Zha hanging up his sword, all belong to the Han pictorial tradition. The left-hand que to the east keeps only its base and shaft, with a cap added later, and is not drawn in the plate.

lede: Huge stones are stacked into seven square tiers, with buttress stones leaning against the steps at the base and the entrance to the burial chamber opening in the upper part. name: Yungang Grottoes
era: Northern Wei · Period of the Five Caves of Tanyao
yearNote: Placed by the c. 460–470 construction phase of the Five Caves of Tanyao, to which Cave 20 belongs; 465 is used only for ordering.
lede: Yungang's most famous face is the product of a collapse: the front wall of Cave 20 fell away long ago, leaving the 13.7-metre seated Shakyamuni in the open air, where it became the emblem of the whole site. It belongs to the five colossal-image caves begun under the monk Tanyao in the early Heping years (c. 460): broad shoulders, deep chest and a robe baring the right shoulder fuse Gandharan exoticism with the physique of the Tuoba Xianbei. The plate shows this main image.
facts: Form: the main image sits cross-legged, about 13.7 m high, with a tall ushnisha, a squarish round face and ears reaching the shoulders; the heavy robe bares the right shoulder, yet a slanting fold covers the shoulder tip, read as a Chinese adaptation of the Western style. The standing Buddha on the east survives; the western Buddha and bodhisattva are mere traces.

Date: the Weishu records that in the early Heping years (460) the monk-superintendent Tanyao petitioned for five caves, today's Caves 16–20; all are colossal-image caves with domed ceilings and horseshoe plans, Cave 20 forming an earlier group with Caves 18 and 19. Excavation in front of the cave in 1992 recovered more than 130 drapery fragments of the lost western Buddha.

Significance: the five colossi stood for five Northern Wei emperors, 'made in the likeness of the emperor', and mark the beginning of imperial cave-building; Yungang preserves 252 caves and niches with some 51,000 images, inscribed as World Heritage in 2001, and the Cave 20 Buddha is its most widely reproduced image.

name: Songyue Temple Pagoda, Dengfeng
lede: China's earliest surviving brick pagoda, and its only twelve-sided pagoda with dense eaves. Fifteen tiers of brick eaves draw in tier by tier into a parabola—Liang Sicheng called it 'uncommonly graceful'. The upper shaft opens four arched doors, with a pagoda-shaped niche on each of the other eight faces; the lotus-petal door lintels and flame-jewel capitals carry echoes of Indian and Central Asian forms. The pagoda belongs to the late Northern Wei: tradition gives the Zhengguang era (520–525), while the Zhengzhou Cultural Heritage Bureau records a start in 509 (Yongping 2), and a statue dated Zhengguang 4 came out of the crypt beneath the tower.
facts: Form: A twelve-sided dense-eave pagoda of grey brick laid in clay, about 37–40 m high (37.045 m per the Zhengzhou bureau; 39.8 m in a 1980s survey), with a ground-floor diameter of 10.6 m. The upper shaft has arched doors on four faces and pagoda-shaped niches on eight, with octagonal engaged columns at the corners; above rise fifteen tiers of corbelled eaves, drawing inward to a brick finial.

Dating: Completed in the late Northern Wei—traditionally the Zhengguang era (520–525), while the Zhengzhou bureau records a start in 509 (Yongping 2). In 1986 the crypt yielded a Shakyamuni image with a dedication dated Zhengguang 4 (523). Exposed bricks had been reheated in a fire, so thermoluminescence dating returned Tang values, prompting a 1996 claim of a Tang construction that was later rejected.

Legacy: No earlier dense-eave pagoda is known, so the Songyue Pagoda is regarded as the prototype of the type; two 'heavenly chambers' inside the finial held reliquary jars and a silver stupa. It was listed among the first national key heritage sites in 1961 and inscribed as part of the Dengfeng World Heritage property in 2010.

name: Gongxian Grottoes
yearNote: 520 is only an approximate ordering point for the late Northern Wei sculptural phase and is not taken as an exact inscribed date for any cave or niche.
place: Henan · Gongyi · Siwan Village, Heluo Town
lede: Besides Longmen, the Northern Wei court cut one more imperial cave temple after moving its capital to Luoyang. Four of the five caves at Gongxian are built around a central pillar that worshippers circled—a cave type Longmen never used. Cave 1 is 6 m high; its square pillar, 2.8 m on a side, opens a niche on each face holding a Buddha, two bodhisattvas and two disciples, with lions crouching beside the throne. The three-tier processions of emperor and empress on the walls inside the door are among the most complete in any Chinese cave temple. The plate shows the main image and attendants on one face of the pillar, without the adjoining wall reliefs.
facts: Cave 1: Square in plan and 6 m high. The central pillar, 2.8 m on a side, carries a niche on each face with one Buddha, two bodhisattvas and two disciples, a lion carved on either side of the throne and strongmen and spirit kings on the pedestal. The east, west and north walls each hold four large niches; below the thousand-Buddha panels flanking the door are three-tier processions—the emperor on the east, the empress on the west.

Dating: A stele of 662 records that Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei founded Xixuan Temple here; a stele of 1494 records cave-cutting under Emperor Xuanwu in the Jingming era (500–503), continued under the Eastern Wei, Northern Qi, Tang and Song. Édouard Chavannes photographed the caves in 1907; several were later looted and the silt was cleared in 1954.

Scale: Five caves, one thousand-Buddha niche, three cliff images, 328 cliff niches and 7,743 Buddha figures survive. The square-pillar caves resemble Dunhuang rather than the stupa-pillars of Yungang and influenced the slightly later Xiangtangshan and Xumishan caves; the imperial processions in Caves 1, 3 and 4 are rare complete examples of the genre.

name: Great Buddha Temple, Xinchang
yearNote: 516 is the 15th year of Tianjian in the Liang, when the image was completed; 486 is the date of origin linked to Senghu's vow, and another account places the start of carving in the Jianwu era of the Qi. The temple's founding in the Eastern Jin is kept distinct from later restorations.
lede: Broad knees support a calm body as the stone Maitreya sits cross-legged in a rock chamber on Mount Shicheng. Carved by successive generations of monks during the Qi and Liang of the Southern Dynasties, it is a valuable surviving example of early large-scale Buddhist sculpture in Jiangnan.
facts: Qi–Liang creation: After Senghu made his vow, Sengshu and Sengyou continued the work, completing it in the 15th year of Tianjian in the Liang (516); it was formerly called the Stone Buddha of Three Generations.
Cliff-cut image: The Maitreya is carved from the rock face of Mount Shicheng, seated in full lotus with both hands resting between the knees; the knees are about 10.6 m apart.

Later care: The image has been redecorated and repaired over many periods and conserved several times in the modern era. The plate shows the historical stone image as it is today and excludes the modern reclining Buddha of the scenic area.

name: Xiaonanhai Grottoes
yearNote: The Palace Museum records excavation from the 1st to the 6th year of Tianbao in the Northern Qi; 553 is only an approximate ordering point within this range and does not mark the exact completion year of any one cave.
lede: All three caves are barely taller than a person—the middle cave is 1.78 m high and 1.19 m wide—yet this is the earliest place in China where long passages of Buddhist scripture were carved onto a cliff. In 550 (Tianbao 1 of the Northern Qi), Master Fang of Lingshan Monastery and others opened the caves on the south slope of Guigai Hill to commemorate the meditation master Sengchou, and the work continued for several years; each cave has a Buddha on three walls under a truncated-pyramid ceiling. The plate shows part of the cliff face around a cave door: the carvings beside the door are damaged, their outlines traceable only between the cracks.
facts: Form: The east, middle and west caves are all small meditation caves, square in plan with a truncated-pyramid ceiling and one niche on each of three walls. The middle cave faces south and measures 1.78 m high, 1.19 m wide and 1.36 m deep; a timber porch in front has been lost. The east cave, originally about 500 m east of the middle cave, was moved in 1999 to a spot 8 m east of it.

Dating: An inscription on the middle cave is dated Tianbao 1 of the Northern Qi (550) and records that Master Fang of Lingshan Monastery, Zilin, Duke of Yunyang, and others opened the cave in memory of the 'State Preceptor' Sengchou; scholars place the three caves between 550 and 560. The site was surveyed in 1983 and published in Wenwu in 1988.

Significance: Long scripture passages are carved on the cliff outside the caves, the earliest such engraved texts at any Chinese cave site; the imagery and style are close to the Xiangtangshan caves at Handan, Hebei, and the group is regarded as representative of Northern Qi meditation caves. Of the three, the middle cave is the richest and best preserved.

name: Xiangtangshan Grottoes
lede: A broad, round Buddha face, heavy shoulders and fine drapery folds are enclosed by a flame-shaped mandorla. The Great Buddha Cave of North Xiangtang preserves the serene mass of Northern Qi sculpture in the rock walls of Mount Gu, and its losses also bear the marks of a long history.
facts: Early Northern Qi: The Great Buddha Cave is one of the earlier large caves at North Xiangtang. Research usually places it in the reign of Emperor Wenxuan of the Northern Qi, about the 550s; the exact founding inscription has been lost.

Central-pillar cave: Cave 9 is a stupa-pillar cave with a central square pillar, the Buddhas of the Three Ages carved on three of its faces; the plate shows the principal figure on the front face, about 3.5 m tall.

Present condition: The principal figure's hands and part of its drapery are lost, but the round head halo and flame mandorla remain recognizable; the carvings of the cave group have suffered weathering, looting and later repairs.

name: Great Cliff Buddha of Mount Dapi
sub: The Great Stone Buddha of Xun County, seated against the cliff
yearLabel: Later Zhao, Northern Qi or other views
yearNote: Proposed dates include the Later Zhao and the Northern Qi. Here 560 serves only as an ordering point based on the Northern Qi start-of-carving view recorded in 2004 material from Cultural Relics Press and does not indicate a confirmed start date; a 2026 Henan Daily on-site conservation report adopts the Later Zhao view. The disagreement is retained and should not be read as a settled Northern Qi date.
lede: The Buddha sits inside the cliff, and the hall built over it reaches only his shoulders—locals in Junxian say 'an eight-zhang Buddha in a seven-zhang hall'. This Maitreya, seated with legs pendant, is 22.29 m tall; his right hand is raised palm-outward in the gesture of fearlessness, his left rests on his knee, and his feet stand on lotus pedestals. When it was carved remains unsettled—Later Zhao and Northern Qi have both been proposed—and the surface carries layers of later repair and paint. The plate shows the visible part from the head to the knees; the protective Great Buddha Hall and the feet buried below ground are not drawn.
facts: Form: A Maitreya seated in the 'pendant-leg' posture carved from the cliff on the east slope of Mount Dapi, 22.29 m tall (another record gives 21.33 m); a snail-curl coiffure, a thick neck with three incised folds, left hand on the knee, right forearm extended with the palm turned outward, legs hanging down onto a double lotus. About 3 m above the feet is now below ground level.

Dating: The Junxian heritage authority holds that carving began under the Later Zhao of the Sixteen Kingdoms; a 2004 Cultural Relics Press reference records a Northern Qi start and completion in the early Tang—both views stand. The 29 m Great Buddha Hall sheltering the statue was rebuilt in 1445 (Zhengtong 10 of the Ming); the monastery was founded in the Taihe era of the Northern Wei and renamed Tianning Temple in the Ming.

Conservation: Locally it is called 'the earliest in China and the largest in the north', standing over 5 m taller than the Vairocana at Longmen. Because of severe surface powdering, cracking, seepage and salt damage, a restoration with the Chinese Academy of Cultural Heritage began in March 2025 and is due to finish in March 2028, after which the site will reopen.

name: Tianlongshan Grottoes
yearNote: The front portico of Cave 16 shown here belongs to the Northern Qi (550–577); 560 is an approximate ordering point. Sui and Tang dates of other caves are not applied.
lede: At Tianlongshan, the builders of the Northern Qi carved the facade of a timber Buddha hall into the living rock. The porch of Cave 16 is three bays wide: two octagonal stone columns stand on lotus bases, the capital blocks carry an architrave, and above it 'one-block-three-arms' brackets alternate with inverted-V struts beneath a bearing block and eave purlin. Not a single Northern Dynasties timber building survives, so this carved porch is one of the few witnesses to the eaves of that age. The plate shows this porch.
facts: Form: a three-bay porch; two octagonal stone columns taper upward and rest on square plinths with inverted-lotus bases. Capital blocks support the architrave, which carries two inverted-V struts with 'one-block-three-arms' brackets between them, topped by a bearing block, an eave purlin and a projecting roof. The east column is well preserved; the surface of the west column has flaked away.

Date: the Tianlongshan caves were begun under the Eastern Wei, and scholars agree that Caves 1, 10 and 16 were cut in the Northern Qi (550–577). A donor stele on the right wall of the porch has weathered so badly that its date can no longer be read, so no exact year is known. The guardians flanking the door and most of the heads inside were looted in the 1920s.

Significance: of the 25 surviving caves at Tianlongshan, researchers consider Cave 16 the most important Northern Qi cave. Its interior, with three niches on three walls each holding a Buddha, two disciples and two bodhisattvas, survives together with the porch, a rare sample of a Northern Dynasties hall-type cave and of timber-style exteriors; digital reconstruction since 2014 has rejoined seven lost sculptures to the cave.

name: Yicihui Stone Pillar
sub: Northern Qi stone pillar with a three-bay stone hall on top
yearNote: Its present location is Shizhu Village, Gaoli Township, Dingxing County; Yi County, given as the location in the old national listing, is an outdated administrative attribution. The Northern Wei wooden predecessor is kept separate from the Northern Qi stone structure.
lede: The pillar is not the surprise; the surprise is the little stone hall on top, three bays wide and two deep: rafters, hip rafters, bracket sets, lintels, columns and window frames are all carved in stone, in effect a model of timber architecture left by Northern Qi craftsmen. The Yicihui Stone Pillar (Yicihui Shizhu) stands about 7 m tall; its octagonal shaft carries more than 4,000 characters recounting how, after the failed uprisings of Du Luozhou and Ge Rong at the end of the Northern Wei, local people gathered and buried the dead and raised a pillar to mark their righteousness. An inscription at the top dates it to the 2nd year of Daning of the Great Qi (562).
facts: Form: limestone, about 7 m tall overall. A square base stone carries a lotus-petal plinth and an octagonal shaft 4.5 m high with a slight taper; the capping slab supports a small stone hall, three bays by two, with a single-eave hip roof and a carved Buddha image at the centre of its front and back.

Inscription: the shaft bears the nine large characters 'Biao yi xiang Yicihui shizhu song', a eulogy of more than 3,000 characters and nearly 1,000 characters of names, including the date 'Great Qi, Daning 2, 4th month, 17th day'. Weathering and cracks were repaired in 1990, and the protective pavilion was reinforced and renovated in 2011.

Origin: after the uprisings of Du Luozhou and Ge Rong (Northern Wei, 525-528) were crushed, villagers buried the insurgents' remains and set up a wooden pillar as a marker; the Northern Qi replaced it with this stone pillar and carved the eulogy. The earlier Northern Wei wooden pillar and the surviving Northern Qi stonework should be kept distinct.

name: Lingquan Temple Grottoes
sub: Armored guardians flanking a Sui cave doorway
yearNote: Uses the excavation date of the Dazhusheng Cave, not a single date for all the Lingquan Temple caves.
place: Henan · Shanying Town, Long'an District, Anyang
lede: A guardian king stands on either side of the cave door, armoured and armed, trampling an ox and a sheep—this is the façade of the Dazhusheng Cave at Lingquan Temple. In 589 (Kaihuang 9 of the Sui) the eminent monk Lingyu opened the cave on the south slope of Baoshan; it is small, 2.6 m high and 3.4 m wide and deep, yet filled with carved scriptures and Buddha names. The plate shows the shallow reliefs of the guardian kings Kapila and Narayana in the two niches outside the door; the doorway itself and the images on the three inner walls are not drawn.
facts: Form: The door faces south with a round arch and a pointed lintel. East and west of it a shallow arched niche holds a guardian king in relief about 1.8 m tall—Narayana on the east, Kapila on the west—gripping sword and trident and treading on an ox and a sheep. Both figures derive from the Candragarbha section of the Mahasamnipata Sutra.

Dating: An inscription above the Narayana figure records the excavation in Kaihuang 9 (589), the labour expended and the images inside. Within, Vairocana occupies the north wall, Amitabha the west and Maitreya the east, and twenty-four patriarchs of the Dharma transmission are carved beside the entrance; the heads and hands of the three main Buddhas have been hacked off.

Significance: The temple's predecessor, Baoshan Monastery, was founded in 546 (Wuding 4 of the Eastern Wei); more than two hundred Sui-to-Song cliff-carved pagoda niches survive around it, the largest and earliest cliff pagoda 'forest' in China. The cave's form continues the Northern Qi Xiangtangshan tradition, and its patriarch images in turn influenced those of the Leigutai Middle Cave at Longmen under Wu Zetian.

name: Zhaozhou Bridge (Anji Bridge)
sub: Side elevation of an open-spandrel stone arch bridge
yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau's description gives 605–616, and another account gives 595–605; 610 is only an approximate ordering point within the Sui and does not indicate an exact completion year.
lede: Two small arches open in each shoulder of the great arch, an 'open-spandrel' device that Europe did not arrive at until the late nineteenth century; Zhaozhou Bridge (Anji Bridge) had it in the Sui dynasty. A single, shallow segmental arch with a clear span of 37.02 m and a rise of only 7.23 m makes the deck as gentle as a slope. Zhang Jiazhen's Tang-dynasty inscription calls it 'the work of the Sui craftsman Li Chun'. A major repair in the 1950s replaced most of the stone, leaving the bright, new-looking surface seen today, which Liang Sicheng regretted for years.
facts: Form: a single-span open-spandrel segmental stone arch bridge, 50.82 m long and about 9 m wide; the main arch consists of 28 parallel rings of voussoirs with a clear span of 37.02 m and a rise of 7.23 m, and each shoulder carries two small arches to pass floodwater and reduce weight, the earliest known example of the open-spandrel arch.

Date: Zhang Jiazhen's 'Inscription for Zhaozhou Bridge' (Kaiyuan era, Tang) calls it 'the work of the Sui craftsman Li Chun'; Liang Sicheng surveyed it in 1933 and published 'The Great Stone Bridge of Zhaoxian, i.e. Anji Bridge'. Sources disagree on the exact year of completion within the Sui, so this entry is placed only approximately in that dynasty.

Repairs: in 1952-1956 the bridge was dismantled and rebuilt with cement grout, with about 87 percent of the stone newly bought; in 1963 Liang Sicheng wrote regretting that it had been made 'brand new'. In 1991 the American Society of Civil Engineers designated it an International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark.

name: Kaiyuan Temple, Zhengding
era: Founded in the 10th year of Zhenguan
lede: Pagoda and bell tower face each other in front of the main hall, with the hall behind them, the transitional layout of a Tang monastery moving from a pagoda-centred to a hall-centred plan, and the only surviving example in China. On the west, the Xumi Pagoda (Xumi Ta), begun in 636, is a plain, unornamented square pagoda of nine close-set eaves, a decade or so older than the Great Wild Goose Pagoda; on the east, the lower storey of the bell tower is still Tang work, making it the only surviving Tang bell tower in China. Liang Sicheng recognised it here in 1933.
facts: Form: the Xumi Pagoda is a square brick pagoda of nine dense eaves, plain-faced, 42.5 m tall; the bell tower has two storeys on a square plan three bays by three, with a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, 14 m high, brick-walled below and timber-framed above, and still hangs a Tang bronze bell.

History: the monastery was founded in 540 (Eastern Wei) and took its present name in 738; a stele of 777 preserved in the temple records a three-bay gate tower, a 'wild goose' pagoda and the Fachuan main hall at that time, and the bell tower was added in the late Tang.

Dating: after his 1933 survey Liang Sicheng judged the lower storey of the bell tower to be Tang, noting in his History of Chinese Architecture that its outer eaves 'seem Jin-Yuan below and Qing repair above'; most other halls have perished, leaving only the site of the Fachuan Hall.

name: Longmen Grottoes
era: Fengxian Temple completed in the 2nd year of Shangyuan
lede: Carving began after the Northern Wei moved its capital to Luoyang in the 17th year of Taihe (493) and continued into the Tang. The great niche of Fengxian Temple was begun in the 3rd year of Xianheng (672) and completed in the 2nd year of Shangyuan (675), with Wu Zetian donating twenty thousand strings of cash from her cosmetics allowance. The 17-meter Vairocana sits at the center, and the nine figures, with disciples, bodhisattvas, heavenly kings and guardians, stand in a single row — of all the niches in the grottoes, the one most like a hall.
facts: The Vairocana is 17.14 m tall overall, with a head 4 m high and ears 1.9 m long; it sits in full lotus on a lotus throne, and its round head halo is carved with lotus-petal and flame patterns.

The niche is about 36 m wide, with nine figures arranged symmetrically: Kasyapa and Ananda stand in attendance, Manjushri and Samantabhadra are 13.25 m tall, the heavenly kings trample demons, and the guardians are 9.75 m tall.

The two hills of Longmen hold more than 2,300 surviving caves and niches and over 100,000 statues. The Northern Wei Guyang Cave (493) and Central Binyang Cave came first, and the Tang Ten-Thousand-Buddha Cave (680) later; the site was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2000.

name: Xiuding Temple Pagoda
era: Founded in the Northern Qi · Rebuilt in the Tang
lede: A single-story square brick pagoda is covered entirely with 3,775 molded decorative bricks, rhombuses, rectangles and triangles fitted together into a net of relief. Archaeologists have called it “the true first flower pagoda of China.”
facts: First built in the 1st year of Tianbao in the Northern Qi (550) and rebuilt in the Tang; the decorative bricks of the surviving body were all fired in the Tang, so it is called a Tang pagoda.
It is 20 m tall overall, with a body 9.3 m high and 8.3 m wide, close to a cube; it is capped by corbeled eaves and a four-sloped pyramidal roof, with an inverted-bowl finial on top.
The decorative bricks show guardians, apsaras, the Azure Dragon, the White Tiger, monks and scrolling vines in more than seventy designs, fitted together with tight joints.

sub: Da Ci'en Temple · Seven-story pavilion-style brick pagoda

lede: The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda stands in Da Ci'en Temple, a brick pagoda built by Xuanzang to house the Buddhist scriptures he brought back from India. First built in the 3rd year of Yonghui (652), it was rebuilt with seven stories in the Chang'an era of the Wu Zhou (701–704). Its pavilion-style body tapers story by story, and its present appearance also reflects later brick casing and repairs.
facts: A square seven-story pavilion-style brick pagoda about 64.5 m tall overall; the brick walls render the form of a timber pavilion with columns and architraves in low relief.

name: Fengxue Temple
sub: A High Tang pagoda beneath nine tiers of multi-eaves
yearNote: Entered by the date of the surviving Tang main structure of the Seventh Patriarch Pagoda, not mixed with the Song Hanging Bell Pavilion or the Jin Middle Buddha Hall.
lede: A Tang pagoda stands at the very centre of the monastery: square in plan, nine storeys of close-set eaves, 24.17 m tall, its outline swelling gently into a parabola, with bells hung at the four corners of every storey. In 738 (Kaiyuan 26 of the Tang) Emperor Xuanzong had this reliquary pagoda built for the Tiantai patriarch Zhen and named it 'Seventh Patriarch'. The finial—inverted bowl, rings and jewel—is still in place, which is rare among surviving Tang pagodas. The plate shows only this pagoda; the Song-period Bell Pavilion and the Jin-period Middle Buddha Hall are not drawn.
facts: Form: A square brick pagoda of nine storeys with dense eaves, 24.17 m tall; the first storey holds a chamber and the storeys above are solid. The outline is a spindle-shaped curve, and wind-bells hang at the four corners of each storey. The finial of inverted bowl, rings, canopy and flame survives complete together with the body.

Dating: Built in 738 (Kaiyuan 26) to hold the relics of Chan master Zhen, and named 'Seventh Patriarch' by Emperor Xuanzong. In 859 (Dazhong 13) the abbot Daoyuan, while restoring the monastery, installed a Shakyamuni image inside the pagoda with relics sealed in its chest, hence its other name, Seventh Patriarch Relic Pagoda.

Significance: The monastery was founded under the Northern Wei as Xiangji Temple, renamed Qianfeng Temple in the Sui and Baiyun Temple in the Tang; more than 140 bays of buildings from Tang to Qing survive, and the Seventh Patriarch Pagoda, the Song Bell Pavilion and the Jin Middle Buddha Hall are called its 'three national treasures'. The surrounding pagoda forest keeps 83 Yuan, Ming and Qing brick and stone pagodas, the third largest group in China.

name: Daodejing Pillar of Longxing Daoist Temple
sub: Detail of the shaft and lotus base
yearNote: Uses the date of the subject drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
lede: In 733 Emperor Xuanzong ordered every prefecture to set up a stone-carved Daodejing in a major Daoist abbey; the pillar at Yixian is the only reasonably complete surviving example in China. Its octagonal white-marble shaft, 4.29 m high, carries all eighty-one chapters of the emperor's annotated Daodejing and an imperial edict of some two hundred characters, signed 'erected by imperial order by Tian Renwan, prefect of Yizhou and commander of Gaoyang Army' in the tenth month of 738. The calligrapher is unsigned; since Qian Daxin it has usually been attributed to Su Lingzhi. The plate shows part of the shaft and the lotus base of the Longxing Guan Daodejing Pillar.
facts: Form: 6 m tall overall, in three parts, cap, shaft and base. The octagonal shaft is 4.29 m high and 90 cm across, assembled from two blocks; it rests on an upturned-lotus base 1.10 m in diameter, beneath which the original lotus-patterned Sumeru pedestal was rediscovered during the 2001 restoration.

Inscription: the upper shaft carries the eighteen-character title 'Daodejing of the Supreme Mysterious Primordial Emperor, annotated by the Kaiyuan Divine-Martial Emperor of Great Tang' and a 205-character edict; below is the full annotated text, dated at the end to the tenth month of 738, followed by later colophons including one by Weng Fanggang.

Vicissitudes: blown down in a storm in 1873, the shaft was reassembled facing the wrong way, so that the text began on the north-east face, an error not corrected until 2001. The attribution to Su Lingzhi rests on Qian Daxin's inference in his 'Jinshiwen bawei'; the pillar itself bears no signature.

name: Haichunxuan Pagoda, Dongtai
era: Built in the Tang, repaired in the Song · Founding year yet to be determined
yearNote: 750 is only an approximate mid-Tang placement on the timeline and does not represent an evidenced construction year; construction supervised by Yuchi Jingde is treated only as legendary history.
lede: Two pagodas nested one inside the other: the outer brick shell is Song, and it wraps an earlier tower, which locals call a 'pagoda hugging a pagoda'. It stands by the old salt-transport river at Xixi, seven storeys, octagonal, with closely stacked eaves tapering upward to 20.8 m. Local tradition says the sea once lapped nearby and the tower began as a lighthouse for salt boats, becoming the pagoda of Guangfu Temple only after the coast retreated. The heritage register dates it to the Tang; the story that General Yuchi Jingde supervised its building is legend, and the founding year remains uncertain.
facts: Form: a seven-storey octagonal brick pagoda with dense eaves, 20.8 m high and 7.2 m across at the base; the body consists of two nested brick shells, the outer one from Song repairs and the inner one earlier, with small niches opening in the upper storeys.

Dating: local tradition holds that Yuchi Jingde oversaw construction in the Zhenguan era of the Tang, hence the alternative name Yuchi Pagoda, but no document confirms it; the heritage register lists it as Tang, Song repairs are attested, and the founding can only be placed roughly in the Tang. It became a Jiangsu provincial protected site in 1982 and a national key protected site in 2013.

Function: the site was once on the shore; tradition says the tower began as a navigation beacon, and as the Yellow River shifted into the Huai and the coast moved east, now about 75 km away, it became the pagoda of Guangfu Temple. Local sources call it the oldest surviving brick pagoda in Jiangsu, a witness to the salt fields and shifting coastline of the Huai region.

name: Main Hall of Nanchan Temple
lede: The oldest surviving timber building in China. Ink on the underside of the west collar beam reads 'Jianzhong 3rd year of the Great Tang (782) ... hall rebuilt', seventy-five years before the East Hall of Foguang Temple. It is only a three-bay hall paid for by villagers, and its remoteness is what saved it from the Huichang suppression of Buddhism; its roof is the shallowest of any surviving Chinese building, twelve eave columns carry the bracket sets directly, and there is not a single column inside.
facts: Form: three bays wide and three deep, nearly square, about 11.6 by 9.9 m; a single-eave hip-and-gable roof. Twelve eave columns carry the bracket sets directly, the capitals have five-puzuo sets with two projecting arms and no intermediate sets; the interior has no columns and no ceiling, four-rafter beams span front to back, and the walls are partitions, not supports.

Date: the ink inscription under the west collar beam records a rebuilding in 782; it was identified during the heritage survey of the early 1950s. In 1974–75 Qi Yingtao and Chai Zejun directed a restoration that removed later alterations. The three square columns on the west side are more archaic and are thought to survive from the original building.

Significance: only three Tang timber buildings with dated evidence survive, this hall, the main hall of Guangrenwang Temple at Ruicheng and the East Hall of Foguang Temple at Wutai. Of the original seventeen Tang statues inside, three were stolen in 1999 and fourteen remain, the earliest set of hall sculpture in China outside the Mogao Caves.

name: Longshan Grottoes
sub: Cave of the Great Master of the Three Heavens · Principal figure
era: Tang niche figures · Later Yuan extensions
yearNote: The niche of the Great Master of the Three Heavens is dated to the Tang following on-site signage and Jinyuan culture and tourism materials, and 800 is only an approximate placement; the Yuan-dynasty main body of the grotto group is described separately.
lede: Longshan near Taiyuan is the largest surviving Daoist cave complex in China, cut mainly under the early-Yuan Quanzhen Daoist Song Defang (Piyunzi); but the two earliest niches on the hill, the Xuanzhen niche and the niche of the Three Heavens Great Masters, are dated to the Tang by the site signage and local heritage materials. The plate shows the central seated figure of the Three Heavens Great Masters niche: hair in a high topknot, a loose robe, a face worn smooth by weathering, with the plain reserve of a Daoist image, nothing like the colossal Buddhas of Buddhist caves.
facts: Form: the figure shown is the main image of the Three Heavens Great Masters niche, seated cross-legged, with a high topknot and a wide robe whose folds are cut as simple parallel lines; the face is weathered, the outline soft. The plate takes only the central figure, from topknot to knees, and does not stand for the whole niche.

Date: the complex has eight caves, the Xuhuang, Sanqing, Woru, Xuanzhen, Three Heavens Great Masters and Qizhen niches plus two 'debate' niches; the main body was cut in the early Yuan under Song Defang, a disciple of Qiu Chuji. The Xuanzhen and Three Heavens Great Masters niches are dated to the Tang by the site signage and Jinyuan district heritage materials, with Yuan enlargement beside them; this entry follows that dating.

Significance: the largest and best-preserved purely Daoist cave site in China, with some sixty-odd stone figures whose plain dress and grave bearing set them apart from Buddhist sculpture; the Yuan carving is tied directly to the spread of Quanzhen Daoism in Shanxi, and the caves include images of Quanzhen patriarchs such as Wang Chongyang.

name: Dragon and Tiger Pagoda of Shentong Temple, Jinan
sub: Tang carved body · Later replacement top
era: Tang body, top repaired in later periods
yearNote: The base and carved body are attributed to the Tang on the basis of form, and the exact founding year is unknown; 800 serves only as an approximate placement on the Tang timeline. The brick top is a later addition, so the whole pagoda cannot be called original fabric of one date.
lede: Dragons, tigers and apsaras climb the stone walls of the pagoda, the fine carving set off by a massive Sumeru plinth. The Tang stone body of the Dragon and Tiger Pagoda carries a later replacement top, so repairs of different periods are layered in a single pagoda.
facts: Dating: The base and body are usually attributed to the Tang on the basis of architectural and carving style; the exact founding year is unknown, and 800 is only an approximate placement on the timeline.
Surviving layers: The carved stone body and the later brick top should be considered separately; the whole pagoda cannot be treated as original fabric completed in one year.
Form: A square pagoda chamber with doorways on four sides and stacked Sumeru plinths. Its name is the Dragon and Tiger Pagoda; it is not the twin pagodas of Lotus Pond in Kaohsiung.

name: Temple of King Guangren, Ruicheng
lede: Of the three Tang timber buildings left in China, this is the only one that is not a Buddhist hall: it is the main hall of a dragon-king temple where villagers prayed for rain. It stands on a terrace beside the ruined walls of the ancient Wei city; five bays wide yet little more than eleven metres across and four rafters deep, with not a single column inside. The capital brackets project two arms without intermediate sets, and the architrave rests directly on the column tops with no plate above. A stele of 832, the sixth year of Dahe, records that rebuilding.
facts: Form: the hall is five bays wide and four rafters deep, only 11.47 m across and 4.92 m deep, the end bays less than half the width of the second bays; a single-eave hip-and-gable roof on sixteen eave columns, with no interior columns and four-rafter beams spanning front to back. Capital sets are five-puzuo with two projecting arms, no intermediate sets and no transverse arms; the architrave does not project at the corners and there is no plate above it.

Date: two Tang steles were once set into the walls: the Record of Guangrenwang's Dragon Spring of 808 tells how a magistrate channelled the spring to irrigate fields, and the Record of the Dragon Spring of 832 records the rebuilding of the temple; the surviving hall is dated Tang on this evidence and its structure. A 1958 repair shortened the front eave rafters and altered the walls; a full dismantling restoration followed in 2013–14.

Significance: the only Daoist hall among the three surviving Tang timber buildings, and the earliest Daoist temple building in China. In 1108 the Song court ennobled the five dragons as kings, the Azure Dragon as 'Guangren King', hence the temple's name; locals still call it the Five Dragons Temple, after the spring that once issued from the bank below.

name: Dharani Pillar of Longxing Temple, Hangzhou
sub: Tang stone pillar · Detail of the shaft
era: 2nd year of Kaicheng · Upper part repaired in the Qing
lede: Beside a busy street, an octagonal stone pillar still carries scriptures carved in the Tang. Cracks run across its faces, and characters and repair seams overlap, leaving more than a thousand years of preservation and repair on the same stone.
facts: Tang date: The pillar was erected in the 2nd year of Kaicheng (837) and also bears an inscription of the 5th year of Dazhong (851); there were originally two, and one survives.
Later repairs: The shaft, base and other parts retain Tang components, while the upper part is a Qing repair; the surviving whole cannot simply be regarded as its original form of 837.

Partial plate: The plate selects the octagonal shaft and its supporting stone, showing the visible cracks and damage; the scripture is suggested with sparse strokes and is not a readable transcription.

name: Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple, Dali
sub: Dali · Qianxun Pagoda and the north and south pagodas
lede: At the eastern foot of the Cang Mountains, the Qianxun Pagoda and two smaller pagodas to the north and south stand in a triangle. The central square pagoda rises tall and straight, while the octagonal pagodas on either side are somewhat shorter, preserving the different outlines of Nanzhao and Dali Kingdom pagodas.
facts: The Qianxun Pagoda is generally dated to the reign of Quanfengyou of Nanzhao (823–859); it is a square sixteen-tier brick pagoda 69.13 m tall, and the catalogue orders it by this approximate date.
The north and south pagodas are dated separately to the Dali Kingdom; each is octagonal with ten tiers and 42.19 m tall, and they are not recorded as built in the same year as the Qianxun Pagoda.

The plate groups the three pagodas as seen from the east, with the Qianxun Pagoda in the center, the south pagoda on the left and the north pagoda on the right; the finials, bodies and bases of all three are drawn in full.

name: East Hall of Foguang Temple
lede: In June 1937 Liang Sicheng, Lin Huiyin and their party read, on the underside of a beam, the words 'donor of the Buddha hall, the lay woman Ning Gongyu, bearer of offerings from the capital', and matched the name to the sutra pillar of 857 standing before the hall: the first time Chinese scholars had found a Tang timber building with their own hands. The seven-bay hall stands on a terrace more than ten metres high; its bracket sets rise to nearly half the column height beneath deep eaves, and inside more than thirty Tang statues share the hall with Tang murals and inscriptions, the 'four wonders' in Liang's phrase.
facts: Form: seven bays and 34 m wide, four bays or eight rafters and 17.66 m deep, under a single-eave hip roof; capital sets are seven-puzuo with two projecting arms and two downward cantilevers, intermediate sets five-puzuo with two arms, the brackets about half the column height. The plan is a 'hall-type' frame with inner and outer rings of columns of equal height, and under the ridge purlin only inclined struts are used, with no king post.

Date: the ink inscription under the north exposed beam and the sutra pillar of 857 before the hall both name 'the lay woman Ning Gongyu', the basis for dating; the temple was destroyed in the suppression of 845 and rebuilt after Xuanzong restored Buddhism. In June 1937 Liang Sicheng's team from the Society for Research in Chinese Architecture surveyed it, and Mo Zongjiang recalled that scholars had believed no Tang building survived in China.

Significance: the largest surviving Tang timber building and the earliest example of a hip roof; 33 Tang statues on the altar, a Tang 'Amitabha preaching' mural in the bracket-eye panels and Tang ink inscriptions survive together with the architecture, the 'four wonders' of Liang Sicheng's History of Chinese Architecture. Inscribed as World Heritage with Mount Wutai in 2009.
quote: “This is the only Tang timber building we have encountered in all our years of searching… the foremost treasure among China's ancient buildings.” — Liang Sicheng, Notes on the Architecture of Foguang Temple on Mount Wutai

name: Tang Dharani Pillar, Songjiang
sub: Dharani pillar of the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani Sutra
lede: Tier upon tier of stone pedestals raise a slender octagonal shaft, with carved scripture alternating with reliefs of lotus petals, coiled dragons and Buddhas. Erected in the 13th year of Dazhong in the Tang, this pillar still stands on a school campus in the old town of Songjiang.
facts: Built in the 13th year of Dazhong in the Tang (859), it is the oldest above-ground cultural relic surviving in Shanghai; it was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1988.
It is about 9.3 m tall overall, with 21 surviving stone sections; the octagonal shaft is engraved with the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani Sutra and donors' inscriptions.

Pedestals, waisted sections, canopies and waist eaves are stacked in alternation, carved with lotus flowers, coiled dragons and Buddhist figures. The plate simplifies the weathered reliefs and scripture and is not a facsimile of the inscription.

era: Balhae period · Date of construction unknown

place: Heilongjiang · Ning'an · Xinglong Temple, Bohai Town
lede: A lotus base, a long stone column, an octagonal lamp chamber and a pavilion-style cap make up a freestanding carved stone lantern for an ever-burning flame. It is catalogued as Balhae period; the later temple behind it does not become ancient original fabric along with the lantern.
facts: The stone lantern is a freestanding carving; the plate draws only this subject and excludes the modern railing and the temple background.

name: Gongchen Pagoda, Lin'an
lede: In the 1st year of Zhenming in the Later Liang (915), Qian Liu, King of Wuyue, built a pagoda on Mount Gongchen, where his rise had begun. Square and five stories high, of brick imitating timber, it is the earliest surviving square pagoda in Zhejiang, and it still looks Tang.
facts: It is 25.3 m tall overall, with a five-story body 22.06 m high; brick engaged columns, architraves and bracket sets imitate a timber pavilion-style structure.
Each story has cusped kunmen openings on all four sides and corbeled eaves; the finial is iron.
Qian Liu was born in Lin'an, and Mount Gongchen takes its name from him; only the site of Gongchen Temple beside the pagoda remains.

name: West Side Hall of Longmen Temple
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Yuantou Village
lede: Only six or seven Five Dynasties timber buildings survive in all China, and three of them crowd into the Zhuozhang valley; the west side hall of Longmen Temple is the earliest. A sutra pillar of 950 says the monastery 'began building in the yiyou year', that is 925, the third year of Tongguang of the Later Tang. A three-bay hall under a gable roof, with no columns inside: the four-rafter beams run straight out over the column tops to form the simplest brackets, the architrave does not project at the corners, and there is no plate above it. Tang practice survived in the side hall of a village temple.
facts: Form: three bays wide and four rafters deep under a single-eave gable roof; no interior columns, the four-rafter beams span front to back, meeting the capital blocks and projecting as bracket arms, so the sets are 'dougong tiao' with no intermediate sets; the column tops are gently rounded, there is no plate and the architrave does not project. On the collar beam a camel-hump block carries a short post topped by another block, the earliest known instance.

Date: a statue stele of 930 in the temple already uses the name 'Longmen Cloister', and the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani pillar of 950 records that building began in the yiyou year (925), the basis for dating the west hall; an inscription records that stone columns were replaced in 1543.

Significance: timber buildings of six dynasties stand in one temple: the main hall of 1098 (Northern Song), a Jin gate hall, a Yuan Dipankara hall and an east side hall rebuilt in the Hongzhi years of the Ming, earning it the name 'museum of ancient architecture'; with Tiantai Hermitage and Dayun Monastery it is one of the valley's Five Dynasties survivals.

name: Dacheng Hall of the Zhengding County Confucian Temple
yearNote: The subject drawn is dated to the late Tang–Five Dynasties; the numerical year is only an approximate ordering point.
lede: The main hall of a county-town Confucian temple, yet the oldest surviving Dacheng Hall of any Confucian temple in China. When Liang Sicheng saw it in 1933 he compared its exterior with the buildings in the Dunhuang murals and 'strongly suspected it to be a relic of the late Tang or Five Dynasties'. Five bays by three under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof of low pitch, with massive, plain bracket sets, double-arm column-top sets without intermediate sets, it predates the Dacheng Hall at Qufu by several centuries. The county gazetteer dates the temple to 1374, but that is the founding of the Confucian temple, not of this hall.
facts: Form: five bays wide and three deep, about 650 square metres, with a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; the column-top bracket sets have two projecting arms without cross-arms and there are no intermediate sets, the brackets sitting directly on the column heads in the early manner.

Dating: the gazetteer records the temple's founding in 1374 (Hongwu 7), but in 1933 Liang Sicheng judged the hall on its form to be late Tang or Five Dynasties; after a 1991 visit Luo Zhewen called it the earliest extant Dacheng Hall in China, and the national register lists it under the Five Dynasties.

Repairs: listed as a Hebei provincial protected site in 1956; in 1997 the government spent over 700,000 yuan on emergency reinforcement, and in 2015 the National Cultural Heritage Administration funded repairs to the platform, roof tiles and timber members. This is the county temple, distinct from the Zhengding prefectural Confucian temple.

name: Tiantai Hermitage
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Wangqu Village
lede: A little three-bay hall, counted for decades among the 'four Tang timber buildings', until the dismantling repair of 2014 turned up ink on the ridge purlin and flying rafters: 'founded in the fourth year of Tiancheng of the Great Tang' and 'ninth month, second day, fourth year of Changxing ...'. Tiancheng 4 (929) and Changxing 4 (933) are both Later Tang reign years; the Later Tang, who styled themselves 'Great Tang', still built the way Tang carpenters had. It is the smallest, and the most Tang-like, of the three Five Dynasties timber halls in the Zhuozhang valley.
facts: Form: three bays wide and four rafters deep, about 7.15 m east-west by 7.12 m north-south, nearly square; a single-eave hip-and-gable roof on twelve eave columns. Each capital block sends out one bracket arm that carries the eave purlin through a bearing block, with no intermediate sets, the simplest 'dougong tiao'; a short post on the four-rafter beam carries the collar beam. The glazed ridge ornaments were replaced in the Jin.

Date: during the dismantling repair in November 2014 Shuai Yinchuan found the inscription 'ninth month, second day, Changxing 4 (933)' between ridge purlin and bearing block, and on a flying rafter the ink text 'founded in Tiancheng 4 (929) of the Great Tang, repaired in the renwu year of the Great Jin ... repaired in Kangxi 9 of the Great Qing'; He Dalong dates the hall to the Later Tang on this basis, while Wang Chunbo holds that a Tang foundation repaired in the Five Dynasties cannot be excluded.

Significance: the Tang stele before the hall is illegible, but micro-trace imaging in 2024 recovered more than eight hundred characters, not yet published; a pair of small stone lions at the corners was stolen in recent years. Together with the west hall of Longmen Temple and the Amitabha Hall of Dayun Monastery it is one of the valley's Five Dynasties survivals, and in form the closest to Nanchan Temple and Guangrenwang Temple.

name: Amitabha Hall of Dayun Monastery
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Shihui Village
lede: The Amitabha Hall of 940, the fifth year of Tianfu of the Later Jin, still keeps Five Dynasties murals on its east wall and screen wall: among all surviving temple murals in China, these are the only ones of that era, with the debate between Vimalakirti and Manjusri spread over nearly thirty square metres. The hall is only three bays wide, yet it is the earliest surviving timber building to set a plate on top of the architrave, and one intermediate bracket set per bay adds a layer of order unknown in Tang halls.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; eighteen eave columns with rounded tops and a slight inward lean, capital and intermediate sets alike five-puzuo with two projecting arms, one intermediate set per bay; a plate beneath the capital blocks, the earliest instance in surviving timber architecture. Columns are omitted inside, leaving only two.

Date: the monastery was founded in 938 by Fengjing, a monk from Youzhou, as Xianyan Cloister; the Buddha hall and abbot's quarters were begun in 940, the Seven-Treasure Pagoda built in 954 under the Later Zhou, and the name changed to Dayun Chan Cloister in 983. In 2015 state funds repaired water damage to roof and floor.

Significance: the Vimalakirti sutra scene on the east wall and the painting behind the screen wall cover about 28.8 square metres, with another 11 square metres on the bracket-eye panels and beams, the only Five Dynasties temple murals in China; Japanese troops failed in an attempt to strip the west and north walls during the war, villagers plastered over the east wall to hide it, and the paintings were rediscovered in a survey of 1962.

name: Black Pagoda, Fuzhou
place: Fujian · Fuzhou · Gulou District · Eastern foot of Mount Wu
lede: Planned with nine storeys, it stopped at seven. In 941, the third year of Yonglong of the Min kingdom, Wang Yanxi proclaimed himself emperor and began a pagoda on the site of a Tang-era Wugou Jingguang Pagoda at the eastern foot of Wushan; three years later he was killed in a coup and work halted at the seventh storey. The whole body is granite, with corbelled eaves and a narrow walkable gallery on each level; the weathered stone has turned dark, so Fuzhou people call it the Black Pagoda (Wuta). The name tablet set into the east wall of the fourth storey still opens with Wang Xi's title.
facts: Form: an octagonal seven-storey pavilion-style granite pagoda, 34.74 m in total height, with the base buried nearly 2 m below ground, leaving 32.86 m above it; each storey has corbelled eaves and a balustraded gallery, a guardian Buddha sits at the end of each of the eight ridges (56 in all), and the top carries an iron gourd finial.

Inscriptions: a black-shale name tablet reading 'Chongmiao Baosheng Jianlao Pagoda' is set into the east wall of the fourth storey, with 42 characters naming the donor Wang Xi and 80 naming the supervising officials; a pagoda record is set in the south wall of the fifth storey and a prayer tablet naming Min royalty and officials in the seventh. Southeast of the pagoda stands the stele of the Tang Jingguang Pagoda, dated 799.

History: a major repair in 1621 added eight guardian figures at the corners of the ground storey; a 1696 repair recast the finial; in 1958 the tilting body was banded storey by storey with steel. It is one of China's few surviving Five Dynasties stone pagodas, and its images and inscriptions are first-hand material for the history of the Min kingdom.

name: Wenfeng Pagoda
lede: A pagoda that is wider at the top than at the bottom. From the first storey to the fifth each is slightly broader than the one below—about a metre's difference over five storeys—so the whole reads like an opened umbrella, almost without parallel among Chinese pagodas. Built in 952 (Guangshun 2 of the Later Zhou), it is octagonal, five storeys high, brick-bodied with timber eaves, 38.65 m tall; above the fifth storey sits a small stupa-shaped tower, a pagoda on a pagoda. Originally the Tianning Temple Pagoda, it took the name Wenfeng ('Literary Peak') after Huang Bangning, prefect of Zhangde under the Qianlong emperor, inscribed 'Wenfeng rises in beauty' over its door.
facts: Form: An octagonal five-storey brick-and-timber pagoda with dense eaves, 38.65 m tall, 40 m around the base, standing on a round lotus pedestal of seven tiers of petals; the first and fifth storeys differ in width by about 1 m. The eight faces of the first storey carry brick reliefs of the life of the Buddha and the eight round corner columns each bear two dragons; one door is real and three are blind, their lintels carved with twin dragons chasing a pearl. The finial is a Tibetan-style stupa added in the Qing.

Dating: Tianning Temple was founded in the Renshou era of the Sui; the pagoda was built in 952 (Guangshun 2 of the Later Zhou) and repaired under the Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing. In 1772 (Qianlong 37) prefect Huang Bangning of Zhangde enlarged the temple and inscribed 'Wenfeng rises in beauty' over the pagoda door, giving it its present name; the most recent restoration was in 2015.

Significance: The base and first storey weigh close to 3,000 tonnes, storeys two to five plus the finial about 2,500—heavy below, light above—so the 'upside-down' pagoda rode out the 1966 Xingtai earthquake undamaged. Liang Sicheng noted in his History of Chinese Architecture that its form 'has many unusual points', and Zhao Puchu, climbing it, wrote of 'a layered umbrella holding a stupa aloft'.

name: Iron Lion of Cangzhou
sub: Original iron lion surviving at the old city (damage retained)
yearNote: The enlarged replica made in 2011 for Lion City Park is not used; the real damage, the lotus basin on its back and the necessary supports follow photographs.
lede: Cast in 953 under the Later Zhou, 6.26 m long, 5.47 m tall and 32 tonnes, the Cangzhou Iron Lion (Cangzhou Tie Shizi) is the largest surviving ancient cast-iron object. Its body is inscribed 'made by Li Yun of Shandong', it carries a lotus basin on its back and seems to bear the Diamond Sutra inside its belly, which makes it look more like the mount of Manjusri in a temple than the legendary 'Sea-Quelling Roar'. Over a thousand years it has been blown over, hacked, filled with sulphur and had its legs packed; today its four feet bear no load and a steel frame holds it up. The plate follows the original, breaks and props included.
facts: Form: 6.264 m long, 2.981 m wide and 5.47 m tall, hollow-bellied, weighing 32 tonnes against an estimated original of over 40; cast in sections with stacked clay moulds, about 500 in all. Head raised and mouth open, with straps across chest and haunches and a huge iron lotus basin on its back.

Inscriptions: 'cast in the 3rd year of Guangshun of the Great Zhou' on the right of the neck and along the teeth, 'made by Li Yun of Shandong' on the left flank, 'Lion King' on the head and under the neck, and what appears to be the Diamond Sutra inside the belly. Three explanations of its purpose, town guardian, sea-quelling image or the mount of Manjusri in a temple, remain unsettled.

Repairs: blown over by a gale in 1803 and righted in 1893; moved 8 m north in 1983, then damaged further by a sulphur compound poured in 1987 and by leg fillings in 1994-1995, so that the legs no longer bear weight and the lion stands only on external steel supports.

name: Zhakou White Pagoda
era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Wuyue
lede: The Zhakou White Pagoda carves the columns, tie beams, bracket sets and tiered eaves of a timber pavilion-style pagoda in miniature in white stone. Its nine-story body tapers up from a Sumeru plinth, and weathered stone eaves and an iron finial together outline this Wuyue structure on the bank of the Qiantang River.
facts: Conservation sources date the pagoda to the late Wuyue of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; no specific year of construction is firmly assigned.
It is an eight-sided, nine-story stone pagoda imitating a timber pavilion, each story made up of a balcony platform, a body and eaves.

The base is carved with the Nine Mountains and Eight Seas and with Buddhist sutras, and the body with reliefs of Buddhas, bodhisattvas and other figures; the plate keeps the present damage and does not complete it as a new pagoda.

name: Yunyan Temple Pagoda, Tiger Hill
era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Wuyue
lede: Its top is more than two metres off the vertical and it leans nearly four degrees, yet it has stood for over a thousand years: the Yunyan Temple Pagoda on Tiger Hill is one of the most steeply leaning old pagodas in China. Begun in 959, the sixth year of Xiande of the Later Zhou, and completed in 961, the second year of Jianlong of the Northern Song, it has seven storeys and eight sides and rises 47.7 m, its brick body imitating a timber pavilion with engaged columns, lintels and bracket sets. The lean was already noticed when the seventh storey was rebuilt in the late Ming, and a dated stone casket was found inside during the foundation works of 1957.
facts: Form: a seven-storey octagonal brick pagoda in pavilion style imitating timber, surviving to 47.7 m; the brick body carries engaged columns, lintels, bracket sets and balconies, the timber eaves of each storey are long gone and only brick eaves remain. The foundation sits half on rock and half on fill, the root of the lean.

Dating: built from 959 to 961, from the sixth year of Xiande to the second year of Jianlong; during reinforcement in 1957 a stone casket was found between the first and second storeys holding a sutra chest inscribed with the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the second year of Jianlong (961), matching the completion date. A repair in 1638, the eleventh year of Chongzhen, already found the tower leaning northeast, and the seventh storey was rebuilt with its centre shifted south.

Lean: the top leans about 2.3 m to the north-northeast, with a maximum tilt of 3 degrees 59 minutes; the lean began in the Ming. In 1957 grout was pumped into the foundation and the movement has since been held. Finds from inside the tower, including a Yue-ware celadon lotus bowl of the Five Dynasties, are now in Suzhou Museum.

name: Relic Pagoda of Qixia Temple
era: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · Southern Tang
lede: Dense-eaved pagodas are rare in the Jiangnan region to begin with, and this one is carved entirely in stone. The Sarira Pagoda of Qixia Temple is octagonal and five-storeyed, about 15 m high: a band of the Eight Scenes of the Buddha's life wraps the waist of the Sumeru base, the tall first storey rises above it with Heavenly Kings and guardians flanking the doors, and five tiers of stone eaves press down in close succession, each face between them holding two niches with a seated Buddha. The wooden pagoda built in 601 to house relics distributed by the Sui emperor is long gone; the present tower is a Southern Tang rebuilding, restored in 1929 to a design by Liu Dunzhen.
facts: Form: an octagonal five-storey stone pagoda with dense eaves, about 15 m in total height; a Sumeru base and three tiers of upturned lotus petals support the body, whose eight corners are carved as engaged columns, with doors on the south and north and Heavenly Kings and guardians on the other faces; the five stone eaves project far, each face between them opens two niches with a seated Buddha, and apsaras and worshipping deities are carved beneath the eaves.

Dating: tradition holds that in 601, the first year of Renshou, Emperor Wen of Sui distributed relics to the prefectures for pagodas, and the wooden pagoda at Qixia was one of them, later destroyed; the present stone pagoda was built in the Southern Tang (937-975) by Gao Yue and Lin Renzhao. In 1929 it was restored with funds from Robert Ho Tung and his wife, designed by Liu Dunzhen and directed by Ye Gongchuo; the finial is also a modern replacement.

Carving: the eight faces of the base's waist show the Eight Scenes of Shakyamuni, running clockwise from the descent on an elephant to the cremation after nirvana, and a band of waves, fish and shrimp, the 'Ocean of the Huayan Treasury', runs below. It is the largest surviving stone sarira pagoda in China and is regarded as a representative work of Jiangnan stone carving between Tang and Song; in 1993 eight fallen stone pieces were set back in place.

name: Stone Pagodas and Dharani Pillars of Lingyin Temple, Hangzhou
lede: The stone pagodas freeze tiers of timber eaves in stone, while the dharani pillars stack scripture and Buddha images on tall columns. This group of Wuyue survivals at Lingyin Temple dates from across the founding of the Northern Song, yet still belongs to Jiangnan under the rule of the Qian family.
facts: The stone pagodas were built in 960; two survive, octagonal and nine stories high, rendering in stone the columns, tie beams, bracket sets and projecting eaves of a pavilion.

The dharani pillars were built in 969, and two also survive; their shafts are carved with scripture, and the pedestals and upper parts are stacked in tiers. They belong to a different construction date from the stone pagodas.

The plate selects one stone pagoda and one dharani pillar and sets them side by side for comparison from historical photographs; the timber halls of the present temple have their own history of later rebuilding.

name: Zhenguo Temple, Pingyao
yearNote: Dated to the 7th year of Tianhui of the Northern Han. Although 963 already falls within the Northern Song reckoning, this part of Shanxi still belonged to the Northern Han, so the hall is not reassigned as a Song structure.
lede: The Northern Han lasted only twenty-eight years, and this hall is the one building it left above ground. The Wanfo Hall of 963, the seventh year of Tianhui, is three bays square; its eave columns are only 3.4 m tall, yet the bracket sets on them rise 1.7 m, seven-puzuo clusters with two arms and two cantilevers that push the eaves out nearly two metres. The brackets take up almost sixty per cent of the column height, the last enlargement of the Tang manner of big brackets on a small hall. Eleven Five Dynasties statues inside are as old as the building.
facts: Form: three bays wide and three deep, nearly square at 11.58 by 10.78 m and 8.8 m high, under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; twelve eave columns 3.42 m tall, no plate, the architrave not projecting at the corners. Capital sets are seven-puzuo with two projecting arms and two downward cantilevers, intermediate sets five-puzuo with two arms; the brackets are 1.74 m high and the eaves project 1.94 m.

Date: an inscription under the ridge purlin records construction in 963, the seventh year of Tianhui of the Northern Han, a date confirmed by a stele of 1819; the temple, originally Jingcheng Temple, was renamed Zhenguo Temple in 1540, and steles record repairs in the Jin, Ming and Qing.

Significance: the only surviving building of the Northern Han and one of the earliest Five Dynasties to early Song timber structures; the eleven figures on the altar, a Buddha, two disciples, two bodhisattvas, two attendants, two heavenly kings and two offering boys, are original Five Dynasties work, the only hall sculpture of that era outside the Mogao Caves. Inscribed as World Heritage with the Ancient City of Pingyao and Shuanglin Temple in 1997.

name: Hualin Temple, Fuzhou
era: 2nd year of Qiande, Northern Song · Built under Wuyue
place: Fujian · Fuzhou · Gulou District · Southern foot of Mount Ping
lede: The oldest surviving timber building south of the Yangtze, and a small hall built with 'first-grade timber': only three bays wide, yet its brackets use the largest module that the Yingzao Fashi reserves for halls of nine to eleven bays; the cap-blocks are huge, and the roof is carried almost entirely by the bracket sets over the columns. In 964 Fuzhou still belonged to Wuyue, and the prefect Bao Xiurang built this Yueshan Jixiang Chan Cloister from the dismantled timbers of the Min kingdom's palaces, so the hall is at once early Northern Song and late Five Dynasties. During the 1980s dismantling repair the whole hall was also moved more than ten metres east.
facts: Form: three bays (15.84 m) wide and four bays (14.70 m) deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof; an eight-rafter frame with front and rear rufu beams on four columns. Only 18 columns in all (14 eave columns, 4 interior), column-top bracket sets of seven tiers with two huagong and three downward ang, very large timber module, and an open ceiling.

Dating: the Chunxi Sanshan Zhi records the founding in 964; samples taken during the 1980s repair were carbon-dated to generally over a thousand years old. Enlarged to seven bays with double eaves in the Jiaqing-Daoguang era, the hall was dismantled and rebuilt in 1984-1989 to its early three-bay single-eave form, on a site 14.6 m east of the original.

Comparison: by date it follows the Tang and Five Dynasties timber halls of Shanxi such as Nanchan and Foguang temples, making it the oldest timber building south of the Yangtze, about half a century earlier than the main hall of Baoguo Temple in Ningbo; Chinese and Japanese scholars widely see its entasis columns and oversized brackets as a source for Kamakura-period architecture in Japan.

name: Chongming Temple, Gaoping
place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Hexi Town · Guojiazhuang Village
lede: The Middle Buddha Hall at the eastern foot of Shengfo Mountain was finished in 971, the fourth year of Kaibao of the Northern Song, a hundred and thirty years before the Yingzao fashi was issued, yet it is still built the Tang way: seven-puzuo capital sets with two arms and two cantilevers match those of the East Hall of Foguang Temple almost exactly, the brackets stand nearly as tall as the columns, and there is no plate, the architrave not projecting at the corners. Not one interior column stands inside; look up and the main load-bearing beam turns out to be two short timbers butted end to end, held under the joint by a longitudinal tie, the so-called 'broken beam', a unique case of making big use of small timber.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafters deep under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with a shallow pitch and deep eaves; capital sets are seven-puzuo with two arms and two downward cantilevers, the bracket height close to the column height in a ratio near 1:1, column tops gently rounded, no plate, architrave not projecting. There are no interior columns, the roof load passes through the bracket layer to the eave columns, and the beams are comparatively slender.

Date: a stele of 991, the Record of the Founding of the Imperially Named Chongming Temple on Shengfo Mountain, says the temple was founded in the Kaibao years; in the Taiping Xingguo years the founding monk Xingyong went to the capital and Emperor Taizong bestowed the name. The Middle Hall is dated to 971; major repairs followed in 1591 and 1826. The temple was originally called Langgu Temple.

Significance: the main load-bearing beam of the double-beam system is made of two short timbers of equal diameter and length butted together, carried under the joint by a longitudinal tie and resting at both ends on the tails of the front and rear eave brackets, the 'broken beam', unique among surviving ancient buildings; its bracket sets are one of nine surviving examples of this type predating the Yingzao fashi, hence the phrase 'Song structure in Tang manner'.
