name: Fengguo Temple, Yi County
place: Liaoning · Jinzhou · Old town of Yi County
lede: In the old town of Yi County, the Mahavira Hall of Fengguo Temple spreads its nine-bay facade beneath a single expansive hipped roof. Seven Liao painted clay Buddha statues sit side by side inside, facing the flying apsaras painted on the beam frame; timber structure, sculpture and painting together preserve the building practice of the eleventh century.
facts: Fengguo Temple was founded in the 9th year of Kaitai in the Liao (1020); its main surviving structure, the Mahavira Hall, is a Liao building.
The Mahavira Hall is nine bays wide and five bays deep, with a single-eaved hipped roof; doors open in the central seven bays of the front.

It was listed in 1961 in the first batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level; the hall preserves seven Liao painted clay Buddha statues and Liao paintings on the beam frame.

name: Liao Twin Pagodas of Zhuozhou
sub: Yunju Temple Pagoda · Zhidu Temple Pagoda
lede: Two Liao pagodas face each other north and south, freezing the columns, windows and bracket sets of timber pavilions in brick. The north pagoda has six stories and the south five, and their differing silhouettes form the landmark of old Zhuozhou.
facts: To the north is the Yunju Temple Pagoda, of six stories; to the south the Zhidu Temple Pagoda, of five. Both are octagonal pavilion-style brick pagodas imitating timber construction.

The Zhidu Temple Pagoda was built in the 11th year of Taiping in the Liao (1031) and is 44 m tall; each cardinal face has an arched doorway, and each diagonal face a false window with vertical mullions.

Studies differ on the date of the Yunju Temple Pagoda, proposing the Chongxi era, the 8th year of Da'an and others; this entry keeps the general label of the 11th century and does not present a disputed year as settled.

name: Huayan Temple
sub: Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall · Mahavira Hall
lede: The Khitan worshipped the sun, so the whole monastery faces east. The Bhagavat Sutra Repository Hall of the lower temple is a library hall of 1038, the seventh year of Chongxi of the Liao; thirty-eight bays of two-storey pavilion-style sutra cabinets line its walls, and over the rear window an arched bridge carries the 'heavenly palace pavilions' that Liang Sicheng called unique in China. The Mahavira Hall of the upper temple burned in the Liao-Jin war of 1122 and was rebuilt in 1140, the third year of Tianjuan of the Jin, on its Liao platform, nine bays wide, the largest ancient Buddhist hall standing. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall.
facts: Form: the Mahavira Hall stands on a platform 4 m high under a single-eave hip roof, nine bays wide and ten rafters deep, 1,559 square metres in area, with eaves projecting 3.6 m at a height of 9.5 m; the glazed owl-tail ridge ornaments are 4.5 m tall, the largest on any surviving ancient building; brackets are five-puzuo with two arms, and twelve columns are omitted inside. The Bhagavat Hall has a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, five bays wide and eight rafters deep, on a platform 3 m high.

Date: an inscription on the underside of a rafter in the Bhagavat Hall reads 'built at noon on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the seventh year of Chongxi, the wuyin year', that is 1038; the Mahavira Hall was first built in 1062, destroyed in 1122 when Jin troops took the city, rebuilt in 1140 and restored in 1997–2000. Early in the Wanli years of the Ming the monastery was divided into upper and lower temples.

Significance: the 38 bays of wall cabinets, the heavenly palace pavilions and the 29 statues in the Bhagavat Hall are all original Liao work, the cabinets being the only Liao architectural model in China, and the attendant bodhisattva 'with joined palms and bared teeth' is especially famous; the east-facing orientation is linked to the Khitan custom of 'revering spirits and worshipping the sun'; the Mahavira Hall is the largest ancient Buddhist hall surviving in China.

lede: The White Pagoda of the Liao city of Qingzhou stands on the grassland, its seven-story body imitating timber in brick. Doors and windows, reliefs of heavenly kings and tier upon tier of bracket sets interweave, preserving the refined and ornate appearance of a Khitan Buddhist pagoda.
facts: Begun in the 16th year of Chongxi (1047) and completed in the 18th year of Chongxi (1049).
An octagonal seven-story pavilion-style pagoda; carved brick bracket sets support timber eave rafters.
It stands in the northwest of the site of the Liao city of Qingzhou and is also called the Sakyamuni Buddha Relic Pagoda.

name: Huanghuatan Pagoda
lede: Huanghuatan Pagoda stands on Xita Hill beside the Daling River, facing the site of the Liao city of Jianzhou across the fields. Its octagonal body carries thirteen tiers of close-set eaves, and the flower baskets and flying apsaras above the arched doorways still show the delicacy of Liao brick carving.
facts: The pagoda is in Dapingfang Town, Longcheng District, Chaoyang, Liaoning; its main body is Liao, and the exact year of construction is undetermined.
The octagonal brick pagoda consists of a high platform, a double Sumeru plinth, the shaft and thirteen tiers of close-set eaves.
Repairs were completed and the finial re-erected in 2012; this plate depicts the present, post-repair appearance from 2023 photographs of the site.

name: Yingxian Wooden Pagoda
lede: A sixty-seven-metre tower built entirely of wood, raised in 1056, the second year of Qingning of the Liao, and still standing after nine hundred and seventy years. Five storeys and six tiers of eaves show outside, but four hidden storeys lie within, nine in all; more than fifty kinds of bracket sets carry it tier upon tier, earning it the name 'museum of dougong', and not one iron nail is used. It has ridden out repeated earthquakes, took more than two hundred shells in the warlord fighting of 1926, and in 1974 yielded Liao printed sutras and relics of the Buddha's teeth from inside its statues: the tallest and oldest wooden pagoda in the world.
facts: Form: an octagonal storeyed timber pagoda 67.31 m high, 30.27 m across at the base and weighing about 7,400 tonnes; five storeys and six eaves outside, with a hidden storey between each of the first four, nine levels in all; a secondary eave surrounds the ground storey and balconies with railings ring each level; the main timber is North China larch, the brackets elm, more than fifty bracket types in all, and an iron finial crowns the top.

Date: Ming gazetteers record construction in 1056 and repairs in the Mingchang years of the Jin; inscriptions on the plaques record further repairs in 1194, 1436 and 1471. The pagoda took more than two hundred shells in 1926; the removal of infill walls and diagonal braces in 1935 left the structure twisted; a reinforcement scheme was fixed in 2013 and work began in 2014.

Significance: the seated Shakyamuni in the ground-floor inner bay is about 10 m high; in 1966 and 1974 Liao printed and handwritten sutras and two tooth relics of the Buddha were found inside the statues. Certified by Guinness World Records in 2016 as the world's tallest wooden pagoda; the plaques 'Divine Craft Reaching the Heights' by the Yongle emperor and 'Wonder of the World' by the Zhengde emperor still hang on it.

name: Nan'an Temple Pagoda
yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau presumes a Liao date from its form; 1100 serves only as an approximate Liao value for sorting. 1706 marks the Qing encasing of the base and repairs, and in 1986 eave corners partly damaged by shelling were repaired.

lede: Nan'an Temple Pagoda rises among the rooftops of the old town of Yuzhou. A tall first story stands on an upturned-lotus base, thirteen close-set eaves taper gently, and an iron finial extends the silhouette into the sky.
facts: Dating: The surviving octagonal multi-eaved brick pagoda is dated to the Liao by its form; the exact year of founding is unknown, and this guide uses an approximate value.

name: White Pagoda of Jixian, Tianjin
yearNote: The national listing dates it to the Liao through Qing. 1100 is only an approximate timeline placement for the Liao form and does not represent the exact year of founding, rebuilding or making of all surviving members; the plate shows the present appearance after repairs over the centuries.
lede: An octagonal lower section and three low tiers of eaves support a rounded inverted-bowl body, and a finial of tapering rings extends the silhouette above. Traces of pale plaster remain between the gray bricks, and this White Pagoda preserves a meeting of two forms, the pavilion and the stupa.
facts: The Tianjin register of national protected sites records the date of the Jixian White Pagoda as Liao to Qing; its present appearance includes later repairs, and no single early date sums up the whole pagoda.

The plate keeps the octagonal lower section, three low tiers of eaves, inverted-bowl body and ringed finial, distinguishing it from an ordinary multi-eaved pagoda or a purely Tibetan-style white stupa.

name: Tianning Temple Pagoda, Beijing
lede: Built in the 9th to 10th years of Tianqing in the Liao (1119–1120), octagonal with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves and 57.8 m tall overall, it is the oldest above-ground structure in Beijing. Above the Sumeru plinth, three tiers of upturned lotus petals support the tall shaft, and higher still thirteen eaves press one upon another, drawing ever tighter.
facts: The eight faces of the shaft: arched doorways on the four cardinal faces, flanked by brick-carved vajra guardians and bodhisattvas; windows with vertical mullions on the four diagonal faces.
All thirteen tiers of close-set eaves rest on brick bracket sets imitating timber, and the spacing between eaves shortens level by level; Liang Sicheng said it had “a rich musical rhythm.”
A solid brick pagoda that cannot be climbed; it is the only Liao building within the Liao Southern Capital to survive to the present.

name: Huilong Temple
sub: Main hall · South bank of the Zhuozhang River
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Houbi Village
lede: In Houbi Village on the south bank of the Zhuozhang River, all that remains of Huilong Temple is a three-bay main hall. Two octagonal stone columns stand in the front porch, and a low, gently pitched overhanging gable roof reaches out to either side; with no tall pagoda or multistory halls, the weight of early timber construction rests among the few bracket sets beneath the eaves.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and four rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; two octagonal stone columns stand in the central bay of the front eave, the supports at either side are enclosed in the walls, and behind are one door and two windows.
No plate beam (pupaifang) is laid over the column heads, and the architraves do not project beyond the corner columns, preserving archaic structural features.

The national listing gives the date as Jin; other accounts, citing form and scientific dating, give the late Northern Song to early Jin. There is as yet no exact construction date, and the timeline gives only an approximate placement at the Song–Jin transition.

name: Shanhua Temple
sub: Mahavira Hall · Hall of the Three Sages · Puxian Pavilion
lede: The Liao Mahavira Hall stands at the north, the Jin Three Sages Hall and gate line the axis, and the Puxian Pavilion rises on the west: the largest and most complete Liao-Jin monastery surviving. From 1128, the sixth year of Tianhui of the Jin, the monk Yuanman spent fourteen years rebuilding it, finishing in 1143. The Puxian Pavilion shown in the plate was built in 1154, the second year of Zhenyuan: two storeys outside with a hidden balcony storey between, a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, three bays square, one of the few surviving witnesses to Liao-Jin multi-storey halls.
facts: Form: the Puxian Pavilion is three bays wide and three deep under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, two storeys outside with a balcony mezzanine between the two main floors; in the side bays of the upper eave the capital, intermediate and corner sets are joined into one by shared arms, a rare device. The Mahavira Hall is seven bays and 41.8 m wide, five bays and 26.18 m deep under a single-eave hip roof; the Three Sages Hall is five bays and 32.5 m wide, its six-puzuo sets with diagonal arms stacked like opening flowers.

Date: founded in the Kaiyuan years of the Tang, destroyed by fire in 1122, the second year of Baoda of the Liao; rebuilt by the monk Yuanman from 1128 to 1143, with the Puxian Pavilion added in 1154; named Shanhua Temple by imperial decree in 1445. The Mahavira Hall is Liao, the gate, Three Sages Hall and Puxian Pavilion Jin. The Three Sages Hall underwent major repair in 2007.

Significance: the Mahavira Hall is the third-largest ancient Buddhist hall standing, with a complete set of thirty-four Jin statues, the Five Buddhas and the Twenty-four Devas; the stele of 1176 in the Three Sages Hall, with a text by Zhu Bian recording the rebuilding, is the basis of the temple's history; Liang Sicheng said of the Three Sages Hall brackets that they 'amply express the vigour of an age still on the rise'.

name: Erxian Temple of Xixi, Lingchuan
sub: Rear hall · Cult of the Two Immortals
yearNote: 1142 is the year a stele records for the start of rebuilding, not the precise completion year of the rear hall; the surviving main structure is dated by its Jin style.
place: Shanxi · Lingchuan · West of Lingchang Village, Chongwen Town
lede: The rear hall of the Xixi Erxian Temple carries its broad eaves on a three-bay front porch, with bracket sets running continuously beneath. The main hall and the dressing towers on either side retain Jin forms and also bear the architectural imprint of the cult of the Two Immortals in southeastern Shanxi.
facts: Jin rear hall: A stele records that rebuilding began in 1142; the surviving main hall and dressing towers retain a Jin style, while most of the temple's other buildings are Ming and Qing.
Three bays, six rafters: The rear hall sits on a stone platform, three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, and keeps a front porch before its doors.

Cult of the Two Immortals: The temple is dedicated to the Two Immortals, and two-story, triple-eaved dressing towers stand on either side of the main hall; this plate redraws only the front of the rear hall.

name: Macun Brick-Carved Tombs
sub: Tomb No. 1 · Woman opening the door
yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate sorting point for the early Jin, not the exact burial year of any tomb; the cemetery as a whole spans the late Northern Song to the Jin.
place: Shanxi · Jishan · Macun Village, Jifeng Town
lede: Inside brick-built tomb chambers, bracket sets, doors, windows and balustrades form an underground mansion. In Tomb No. 1 a young maid leans out from behind a half-closed door, and the narrative reliefs beside her preserve Song–Jin life on small brick surfaces.
facts: Underground mansion: The tomb chambers imitate a timber-framed residence in carved brick, with columns, bracket sets, doors, windows and platforms together forming an architectural space.
Woman opening the door: In Tomb No. 1 the central door leaf stands half open and a maid leans out from behind it; reliefs of narrative scenes with figures survive on both sides.
Song–Jin cemetery: The cemetery as a whole dates from the late Northern Song to the Jin; this plate shows a detail of the early Jin Tomb No. 1 and does not represent all the tomb chambers.

name: Yuanjue Temple, Hunyuan
place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan · Shiqiao North Lane
lede: In the old town of Hunyuan, Yuanjue Temple has left a Jin brick pagoda. A tall first story carries nine tiers of close-set eaves that taper step by step; carved brick imitates timber bracket sets, and a slender iron finial traces a distinctive outline at the top.
facts: According to the Hunyuan Prefecture Gazetteer, the surviving brick pagoda was built in the 3rd year of Zhenglong in the Jin (1158) and was repaired many times in the Ming and Qing.
The pagoda is an octagonal, nine-story multi-eaved pagoda about 30 m tall; its shaft and base use carved brick to represent imitation-timber bracket sets and ornament.
The pagoda of Yuanjue Temple in Hunyuan was listed in 2013 in the seventh batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level.

name: Chunhua Temple, Pingshun
era: Before the 9th year of Dading, Jin
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Yanggao Village
lede: Of this old temple founded in the Northern Qi, only a Jin main hall remains. Before the hall stand two stone dharani pillars of the 3rd year of Kaibao in the Northern Song (970), carved with the Usnisa Vijaya Dharani Sutra and the Diamond Sutra, two hundred years older than the hall itself.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and an exposed roof frame with no ceiling.
The bracket sets are four-puzuo with a single projecting arm, and the cantilevers are cut in the split-bamboo style, a practice of the Song–Jin transition.
According to a stele, it dates from before the 9th year of Dading in the Jin (1169).

name: Hua Pagoda of Guanghui Temple
era: Founded in the Tang · Restored in the Dading era, Jin
lede: The most ornate of China's surviving flower pagodas: the lower three stories form an octagonal pavilion, each of its four corners embracing a small hexagonal pagoda, and the top story gathers into a “bouquet,” with lions, elephants, bodhisattvas and guardian warriors clustered tier upon tier around the finial.
facts: Founded in the Tang and restored in the Dading era of the Jin; 40.5 m tall overall (another account gives 33.35 m), with four stories of brick imitating timber.

At the four corners of the first story, hexagonal annex chambers connect to the main pagoda, each with an arched doorway and an inverted-bowl top; this combination of “one main and four subsidiary” pagodas is seen nowhere else.

The bouquet-shaped body of the fourth story: its eight faces are modeled with lions, elephants, Buddhist niches and guardian warriors in staggered rows, eight tiers in all, which give the Flower Pagoda its name.
Together with the Xumi Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple, the Lingxiao Pagoda of Tianning Temple and the Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple, it is known as one of the “Four Pagodas of Zhengding.”

name: Yanshan Temple, Fanshi
lede: In Tianyan Village, the Manjushri Hall stills the noise of its courtyard amid the mountains. Within its broad plain walls and gently sloping eaves, Jin murals set the life of the Buddha and scenes of worldly town life on the same wall.
facts: The surviving Manjushri Hall is a Jin structure; an inscription beneath a beam records a restoration in the 2nd year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1315).
The Manjushri Hall is five bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and four-puzuo bracket sets.
The Jin murals inside the hall were completed in the 7th year of Dading (1167) and are the work of the painter Wang Kui and others.

sub: White Horse Temple · Jin brick pagoda

lede: East of White Horse Temple, Qiyun Pagoda draws a soft curve with thirteen tiers of close-set eaves. Its square shaft steps inward level by level, preserving the form of the brick pagoda rebuilt in the Jin, with a lineage distinct from the temple's Eastern Han founding.
facts: Rebuilding date: The Jin stele beside the pagoda, the Record of the Rebuilding of the Sakyamuni Relic Pagoda of the East White Horse Temple on the Left Street of Henan Prefecture, records its rebuilding in the 15th year of Dading (1175).
Form: A square multi-eaved brick pagoda of thirteen stories, stepping inward level by level from the sixth story up, and topped by a vase-shaped finial.
Temple and pagoda: The Qiyun Pagoda Court lies southeast of White Horse Temple; the history of the present pagoda and the later, newly built halls of the pagoda court are recorded separately.

name: Baolun Temple Pagoda
sub: Thirteen eaves drawn into a slender silhouette
yearNote: Entered according to the surviving pagoda rebuilt in the Jin; the founding date of the old Tang temple is not substituted for the date of the pagoda.
lede: In the 17th year of Dading in the Jin, the monk Zhixiu rebuilt the Baolun Temple Pagoda. Its square shaft tapers level by level, and thirteen close-set eaves trace a slender outline within the old city of Shanzhou.
facts: Jin rebuilding: The surviving pagoda was built in 1177; the history of the Tang temple and pagoda is recorded separately from this Jin pagoda.
Thirteen close-set eaves: The pagoda is 26.5 m tall; its brick eaves project with saw-tooth courses and corbelling, and at the bottom there is a separate platform and base.
Interior passage: Inside are a central chamber and stairways; its echo effect has earned it the popular name Toad Pagoda.

name: Erlang Temple of Wangbao, Gaoping
sub: Jin opera stage · Gable facing forward
lede: With its gable facing forward, a small one-bay stage carries a spreading hip-and-gable roof. The Erlang Temple at Wangbao preserves a Jin performance space at the south end of its courtyard, and the Dading date on its platform can still be traced.
facts: Jin stage: An inscription on the Sumeru-plinth platform records the 23rd year of Dading (1183), so the date of the surviving stage is clear; most of the temple's other buildings have been restored in the Ming and Qing.

Gable facing forward: The stage, one bay square, turns the gable of its hip-and-gable roof toward the audience; four round columns and stout bracket sets carry the roof, a form that is quite distinctive.
Surviving early stage: Official descriptions call it the earliest surviving stage in China; it sits at the south facing north and bears witness to early village temple fairs and performance spaces.

name: Lugou Bridge, Beijing
era: Completed in the Jin · Ming–Qing repairs
lede: Eleven stone arches extend beneath the low, gently sloping deck, and lion-topped balusters join into a long, slender edge. The plate views the bridge from a shallow oblique angle, keeping every arch open, and does not draw the shadows beneath the bridge as solid mass.
facts: Lugou Bridge was completed in 1192 under the Jin and later repaired in the Ming and Qing; the timeline uses the completion date and records the later repairs separately.

The bridge has eleven stone arches; this plate shows the abutments at both ends, the piers and the continuous stone-lion balustrade in full, distinguishing it from the single great arch of the Zhaozhou Bridge.

The colored plate follows the present appearance, with gray stone and lighter balustrade panels; all eleven arches are truly open, and the carved details of the stone lions are artistically simplified.

name: Taifu Temple, Fenyang
era: Jin · Hall of the Haotian Jade Emperor
yearNote: 1200 is an approximate sorting point for the period indicated by the altar record of the 5th year of Cheng'an; the main hall is dated to the Jin from its architecture and heritage sources, and the altar date is not forced on the hall as a precise completion year.
lede: The three-bay Haotian Hall stands on a terrace, its stout bracket sets holding up a single-eaved roof. The Jin timber structure of the main hall, the gilded melon-shaped studs on its doors and the later paintings and sculptures inside record the continuing building history of Taifu Temple.

name: Yongle Palace, Ruicheng
lede: The long eaves of the Sanqing Hall lift gently at both sides, and huge glazed dragon ridge-end ornaments guard either end of the main ridge. Inside, the mural Homage to the Primordial (Chaoyuan Tu) arrays hundreds of deities in a grand procession, so that Yuan timber architecture and murals reflect each other within a single space.
facts: Seven-bay hipped hall: The Sanqing Hall, also called the Wuji Hall, is the main hall of Yongle Palace, seven bays wide with a single-eaved hipped roof, and is dated to the 3rd year of Zhongtong (1262).
Chaoyuan Tu: The murals in the hall were completed in 1325 and are recorded separately from the construction date of the building.
Relocation for protection: For the Sanmenxia Reservoir project, the palace buildings and murals were moved to their present site in the 1960s, preserving the original halls and murals.

name: Dengfeng Observatory
sub: Front of the platform and stone scale
yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
lede: The brick-and-stone platform is divided into two chambers, with a narrow slit aligned with the stone scale that extends along the ground. The Dengfeng Observatory organizes the height, orientation and graduations needed to measure shadows into a clearly legible building.
facts: The observatory was built in the 13th year of Zhiyuan in the Yuan (1276) and is associated with the large-scale astronomical survey directed by Guo Shoujing.
A slit for measuring shadows is left between the two chambers on top of the platform, the stone scale is laid out on the north side, and twin stairways beside the platform lead to the top.
The plate shows only the observatory itself and the stone scale; the nearby Duke of Zhou's Shadow Measurement Platform is not split off as a separate entry.

name: Temple of the Holy Mother of the Nine Heavens
era: Restored in the 1st year of Jianzhong Jingguo, Song · Yuan offering hall
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Donghe Village
lede: The temple was founded in the Tang, its Holy Mother Hall was rebuilt in the early Northern Song, and the whole temple was restored in the 1st year of Jianzhong Jingguo (1101). The Yuan offering hall before the main hall is the most unusual: it is five bays deep, longer than its three-bay width, its main ridge runs along the depth, and its roof is the highest-ranking hipped type. From the front, in the courtyard, one sees its end face, so the drawing here shows its long side, where the main ridge and both ridge-end ornaments appear.
facts: The offering hall is a Yuan structure, three bays wide and five bays deep, with sixteen chamfered square sandstone columns all around and open on all four sides; its bracket sets are four-puzuo with a single projecting arm, and it stands on a bluestone platform one meter high.
The corner eaves of the three roofs, those of the offering hall, the main hall and the dance pavilion, interlock, which locals call “hooked hearts and fighting horns” (gouxin doujiao).
The Holy Mother Hall is a Song structure, three bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; in one village temple, timber buildings of the Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing follow one after another.

name: Xia Yu Shrine
place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Houbi Village
lede: On the Yuwang Hillock, the highest point of Houbi Village in the Zhuozhang River valley, a temple of a single courtyard packs Yuan, Ming and Qing timber buildings into 877 square metres: the gate is Ming, with a rear-facing stage on its upper floor looking straight at the Yuan main hall, while the side halls and wing rooms were added in the Qing. The plate shows the main hall, a surviving structure of 1336 (2nd year of Zhiyuan, Yuan), three bays wide under a gable roof with a two-rafter-deep front porch; its framing of four-rafter beam against front ru-beam on four columns is a ready textbook for Yuan village temples of southeastern Shanxi.
facts: Main hall: three bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, with a two-rafter-deep front porch; column-top bracket sets are four-puzuo with one downward ang, the three intercolumnar sets were added in the Qing; framing is a four-rafter beam against a front ru-beam, with four columns across the depth.

Dating: the shrine was founded in 1336 (2nd year of Zhiyuan, Yuan) and repaired repeatedly in the Ming and Qing; the hall keeps one Ming and two Qing inscribed wall stones and three stone offering tables of the Wanli reign; the gate is Ming, the side halls and wings Qing.

Layout: a single courtyard of only 877 square metres; the three-bay, four-rafter gate carries a rear-facing stage on its upper floor facing the main hall, and the convex altar terrace before the hall is carved in relief on three sides; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers the site as "Yuan to Qing", three dynasties of timber work in one yard.

name: Second Gate of Tiger Hill
sub: Suzhou · Duanliang Hall of Tiger Hill
era: Yuan · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Zhiyuan
lede: The main beam is 'broken': strictly, the ridge purlin is not a single timber but two round logs butted together at the middle, with the bracket sets and frames below spreading the load to either side, and it has held for more than six hundred years. The second gate of Tiger Hill is therefore called the Broken Beam Hall; rebuilt in 1338, the fourth year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan, it is three bays wide and two deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with one round-arched doorway at the centre of the front. Built in the same year as the main hall of Xuanyuan Palace at Dongshan on Lake Tai, the two are Suzhou's firmly dated Yuan timber buildings.
facts: Form: three bays wide and two deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with a round-arched doorway at the centre of the front. The ridge purlin is made of two round logs joined end to end rather than one piece, hence the name 'broken beam'; the hall is neither beamless nor left hanging after a fracture.

Dating: the present second gate was rebuilt in 1338, the same year as the main hall of Xuanyuan Palace at Dongshan; the temple on Tiger Hill rose and fell repeatedly from the Five Dynasties and Northern Song onward, most of its halls burnt in the Taiping war of 1860, and the second gate survived as the earliest building on the hill after the Five Dynasties Yunyan Temple Pagoda.

Value: the broken beam is often called a 'miracle' of carpentry, but it is in fact a splicing technique that lets the frames and bracket sets on either side share the load, reflecting the Jiangnan craftsman's habit of using timber as it came; together with the Yunyan Temple Pagoda completed in 959-961 on the summit, it forms Tiger Hill's sequence of early buildings from the Five Dynasties to the Yuan.

lede: Stout timber columns hold up deep eaves, and the offering pavilion joins the main hall behind it. Among the gray-brown old timbers, dark green glazed tiles outline the ridges and eave-tile ends; the Shrine of Grand Master Dou gathers its ritual space into a tight group of timber buildings.
facts: The shrine is dedicated to Dou Chou, a grand master of the state of Jin, and is also called the Lieshi Shrine and the Yingji Shrine; the early history of the shrine and the dates of the surviving buildings are described separately.

The surviving gate, offering pavilion and main hall were rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1343). The plate selects the offering pavilion and main hall and does not count the Qing side buildings as Yuan structures.

The hip-and-gable roof of the offering pavilion links with the overhanging gable roof of the main hall behind, and thick columns and massive bracket sets create a striking contrast of scale; the colored plate follows the surviving old timber, gray tiles and glazed tiles, and is not a reconstruction of historical painted decoration.

name: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass, Beijing
sub: Yuan base of a street-spanning stupa · Half-hexagonal arched passage
era: Built from the 2nd to the 5th year of Zhizheng
lede: A high white stone platform straddles the old passage, its body tapering upward and its top rail running flat. The half-hexagonal arched passage and the reliefs on its door frame remain from the stone base of a Yuan street-spanning stupa; the vanished stupa halls on the platform are not reconstructed.
facts: The Cloud Platform is the base of a Yuan street-spanning stupa, built in 1342–1345; the original stupa halls no longer stand on the platform today.

The inner opening of the central passage is half-hexagonal, and the door frame and passage walls bear reliefs and sutras carved in several scripts; the plate only suggests the carving with sparse lines.
The present-state drawing keeps the empty platform, stone balustrade, tapering body and arched passage, removes modern barriers and surroundings, and does not add the three historical stupas.

name: Beiyue Temple
sub: Front elevation of the Dening Hall (with gallery and platform)
yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau lists the present hall under the 7th year of Zhizheng (1347); the county gazetteer records completion in the 7th year of Zhiyuan (1270), so both construction phases need to be recorded.
lede: The Dening Hall of Beiyue Temple sits on a high platform, its two tiers of hipped eaves stretching horizontally. Once the place where the court made sacrifices from afar to the Northern Peak, Mount Heng, it preserves the memory of this ancient peak temple through its Yuan timber structure, murals and the steles of sacrifices from many dynasties.
facts: Date: The present hall is Yuan; sources record completion in 1270 and rebuilding in 1347 respectively, and the timeline enters it with an approximate Yuan value.
Hall: A double-eaved hipped roof with a surrounding gallery, nine bays wide and six bays deep overall; a central stairway climbs the high platform.
Sacrifices: Beiyue Temple was originally a temple for sacrifices to Mount Heng from afar; the hall preserves Yuan murals, and steles of many dynasties are gathered in the courtyard.

name: Main Hall of Xuanyuan Palace
lede: A small hall at Yangwan on Dongshan by Lake Tai, three bays square, its hip-and-gable roof pressed low and its eaves reaching far out; it was once the Temple of King Xu, dedicated to Wu Zixu, and only in the Republican era was it rededicated to the Yellow Emperor and renamed Xuanyuan Palace. The main hall was built in 1338, the fourth year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan, the same year as the second gate of Tiger Hill; it is 13.74 m wide and 11.43 m deep, with a ridge more than ten metres high. A major repair under Shunzhi in the Qing means that the Yuan frame and the traces of Ming-Qing repairs share the same building.
facts: Form: the main hall is three bays and 13.74 m wide, three bays and nine purlins or 11.43 m deep, under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with a ridge over 10 m high; the body is nearly square and the eaves are deep. The plate shows the front of the main hall.

Dating: the founding date is unknown; it was repaired and renamed the Temple of King Xu in the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song, and the main hall was built in 1338; a further major repair followed in 1649-1655, the sixth to twelfth years of Shunzhi, so what stands today is not an untouched Yuan original. It was listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

History: the site began as a shrine to Wu Zixu, who by tradition built the great city of Helü on the orders of the King of Wu; Suzhou's Xu Gate and Xukou take their names from him, and dragon-boat racing at the Duanwu festival in the Jiangsu-Zhejiang region is also seen as his commemoration. In the Republican era the temple was rededicated to the Yellow Emperor and first called Xuanyuan Palace.

name: Shisi Temple, Jingning
sub: Main hall · Yuan structure in a mountain village
lede: Between two tiers of flying eaves, deep bracket sets line up against white walls. With its light timber frame and low stone steps, the main hall of Shisi Temple lies hidden in an old temple in the mountain village of Daji.
facts: Yuan main hall: The hall was built in the 16th year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1356) and still retains many Yuan members.

Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof: The upper and lower eaves spread wide, the bracket sets of the upper eave show their full layering, and a central doorway with windows on either side forms a simple facade.
Several periods side by side: The temple's bell tower, Sanqing Hall and Mei clan ancestral hall form a complex spanning the Yuan, Ming and Qing; the plate takes only the Yuan main hall.

name: Stone Halls of Jijian Temple
lede: A small hall built in stone on the pattern of timber: stone columns, stone beams, stone purlins, even the roof is of stone slabs, and the back wall sits directly against the rock face of Tianchi Mountain. The stone hall of Jijian Temple, formerly Xitian Temple, was built in 1357, the seventeenth year of Zhizheng of the Yuan; it is three bays and 7.64 m wide, two bays and 5.52 m deep, under a low, compact single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. To the east and west stand two small stone shrines built around Buddha niches, one inscribed 'Tushita Palace' and the other 'Garden of Bliss', and the standing images inside them are Yuan originals as well.
facts: Form: the stone hall faces south, three bays and 7.64 m wide, two bays and 5.52 m deep, under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; columns, beams, purlins and roof are all carved in stone in imitation of timber, and the back of the hall sits against the natural rock face. The plate shows the front of the stone hall.

Dating: the Jijian Hermitage was founded in 1357, and became a temple after the Ming; the surviving stone hall, niches and images all date from the Yuan, and the site was listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Attached shrines: east and west of the hall stand two stone shrines built around Buddha niches in the manner of timber porches, each one bay wide and half a span deep: the west one has a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a standing Amitabha in its niche, inscribed 'Garden of Bliss'; the east one has a single-eaved roof and a standing Maitreya, inscribed 'Tushita Palace'. Yuan stone halls imitating timber are rare in the Jiangnan region, and this is a complete surviving group.

name: Qinglong Temple, Jishan
era: Late Yuan–early Ming · Middle hall murals
yearNote: The subject drawn is the middle hall murals, using the dating range of Sun Bo cited by the Yuncheng Museum; 1360 is only a sorting coordinate. It is not 1289, the completion year of the timber structure, and scholarly opinions on the dating of the murals still differ.
place: Shanxi · Jishan · Macun Village, Jifeng Town
lede: The earliest surviving wall painting of a Water-and-Land ritual in China is in the Middle Hall (yaodian) of Qinglong Temple at Macun: deities of Buddhism, Daoism and Confucianism parade in tiers, the Buddhas of the Three Ages enthroned at the top, drawn from the same southern Shanxi pattern books as the Yongle Palace one ridge away, yet in a manner of its own. An ink inscription of 1289 (26th year of Zhiyuan) under the hall's beams names the master carpenters; for the murals themselves there are two views, contemporary with the timber frame or repainted in the late Yuan to early Ming, and the timeline follows the latter. The plate redraws the Buddhas of the Three Ages in the upper part of the west wall and does not stand for all the murals and sculpture of the hall.
facts: Panels: each "Deities of the Three Realms" panel in the Middle Hall measures 223 cm high by 773 cm wide, principal Buddhas in the top register and lesser deities ranked below, linked by clouds; the line work is mainly iron-wire and nail-head-rat-tail strokes, the colouring based on azurite and malachite with vermilion, yellow, white and red.

Dating: the temple was founded in 662 (2nd year of Longshuo, Tang) and repaired repeatedly in the Yuan and Ming; an ink inscription under the ridge-brick tie beam of the Middle Hall reads "Great Yuan, 26th year of Zhiyuan, mid-autumn ... master carpenters ... respectfully recorded", i.e. the timber frame was completed in 1289; since Sun Bo's 2010 thesis the murals are dated to the Yuan, with a late-Yuan-to-early-Ming view as well.

Significance: the temple holds 196.38 square metres of Yuan and Ming murals; the Middle Hall cycle is regarded as the earliest extant Water-and-Land painting, its three-teachings pantheon leading on to Ming examples such as Pilu Temple; with the Sanqing Hall of Yongle Palace and the Mingying Wang Hall of the Water God Temple it belongs to the group of Yuan murals of southern Shanxi.

name: Pingyao City Wall
sub: Yingxun Gate and adjoining wall sections
yearNote: 1370 is used for sorting by the phase of the wall's expansion; the gate tower and surviving wall faces include later repairs.
siteCoordinateSource: Commons 2025-06-06迎薰门实拍的门前相机点37.198185,112.181053，仅作南门附近近似定位，非城楼中心测绘点。https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:20250606_Yingxun_Men.jpg
lede: After the enlargement and brick facing of 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming), this circuit of wall at Pingyao, over six thousand metres round and about twelve metres high, was never pulled down: six gates, four corner towers, seventy-two bastions and more than three thousand merlons can still be counted. It is the most complete county-town wall in China and the core of the "one city, two temples" World Heritage property of 1997. The plate takes the south gate, Yingxun Gate, where the arched passage, gate platform and double-eave gate tower stack into one group and the battlemented wall runs off east and west; both tower and wall surfaces include later repairs.
facts: Wall: about 6.4 km in circuit and about 12 m high, rammed earth faced with grey brick, paved on top with a horse ramp inside; a bastion with an enemy tower projects roughly every 50 m, 72 in all, with over three thousand merlons; the moat outside is about 4 m wide and 4 m deep.

History: tradition dates the first wall to King Xuan of Zhou; the present wall was enlarged and brick-cased in 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming) on the old town, and dozens of later repairs kept the early-Ming scheme; part of the south wall collapsed in 2004 and was rebuilt in 2005.

Heritage: in 1997 the Ancient City of Pingyao, with Shuanglin and Zhenguo temples, was inscribed as World Heritage, the wall enclosing a 225-hectare property; nearly four thousand Ming and Qing shops and dwellings inside bear witness to the town's years as China's financial centre from the 19th to the early 20th century.

name: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple
era: Rebuilt in the Hongwu era, maintained over the centuries
yearNote: 1371 is the recorded rebuilding of the Confucian Temple on its Yuan site; the Dacheng Hall retains Yuan building methods and has been maintained over the centuries, so not every surviving member can be assigned to 1371.
place: Shaanxi · Weinan · Old town of Hancheng
lede: Beneath a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, a broad front porch fronts the five-bay hall. The Hancheng Confucian Temple was rebuilt on its Yuan site, and between columns and architraves the continuation of earlier timber methods can still be seen.
facts: Rebuilding: The local gazetteer records rebuilding on the Yuan site in 1371, followed by repeated maintenance.
Main structure: The Dacheng Hall is five bays wide, its front porch spans three large bays, and it has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof.
Dating: It retains Yuan building methods; neither the whole temple nor all of its members are equated with a single year.

name: Jade Emperor Pavilion of Yuzhou
era: Founded in the 10th year of Hongwu
place: Hebei · Yu County · North city wall
lede: On the north wall of the old city of Yuzhou, Jingbian Tower spreads three tiers of eaves yet has only two stories. A gallery runs around the upper story, and here a defensive tower and the cult of the Jade Emperor overlap.
facts: Built in the 10th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1377) and also called Jingbian Tower, it is the landmark pavilion on the northern rampart of the old city of Yuzhou.
The main hall is five bays wide, with three tiers of eaves on two stories and a glazed-tile hip-and-gable roof; a waist eave gives the two-story pavilion the appearance of three eaves.
The upper story has a timber gallery around the building, and the lower story a surrounding colonnade; the surviving building preserves the historical layers of many Ming and Qing repairs.

name: Xi'an City Wall
sub: Arrow tower of Anding Gate · Ming rampart
lede: A massive wall platform carries a broad arrow tower, four rows of arrow windows stretch across it, and a single gate passage pierces the defenses. The layout of the west gate preserved at Anding Gate makes the scale and defensive purpose of the Xi'an City Wall clearly legible.
facts: Ming rampart: The main body of the surviving wall was built in the 7th to 11th years of Hongwu (1374–1378), extended from an earlier city site, and later gradually faced with brick and reinforced.

Anding Gate section: The plate takes the arrow tower of the main west gate and its single central arched passage; the broad tower has four rows of arrow windows, and the thick walls and gate tower together form a defensive space.

Repairs through the ages: Anding Gate has been repaired many times in the Ming, the Qing and the modern period and still preserves a defensive layout in which arrow tower, gate tower and barbican are linked.

name: Bell Tower and Drum Tower of Xi'an
era: Founded in the Hongwu era · Moved in the Wanli era
place: Shaanxi · Xi'an · Center of the prefectural city
lede: The Bell Tower stands with its pyramidal roof where streets meet, and the long ridge of the Drum Tower stretches across the south end of Beiyuanmen. These two Ming towers once announced the hours of the city with the sound of bell and drum.
facts: The Drum Tower was founded in 1380 and the Bell Tower in 1384; the Bell Tower was moved to its present site in 1582 on a newly built base, so the platform at the present site cannot be equated with the original founding date.

The Bell Tower is a triple-eaved pavilion with a four-sided pyramidal roof on a square platform; the Drum Tower stands on a rectangular platform, its body seven bays wide with a surrounding gallery and a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof on the upper story.

The plate sets near-frontal views of the Bell Tower and the Drum Tower side by side, keeping each one's complete outline; this is a composite of two subjects, not a view of the two towers actually standing next to each other.

name: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple
lede: Not a single piece of timber: the Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple is built entirely of brick, three barrel vaults running side by side from east to west carry the roof, the central one spanning eleven and a half metres and rising fourteen, and the front and rear walls are four metres thick. Built in 1381, the fourteenth year of Hongwu of the Ming, it originally housed the Buddha of Infinite Life, Wuliang, and 'Wuliang Hall' became 'Wuliang Hall', beamless, in speech; it is the largest brick hall of its kind in China. In the Xianfeng era the temple was all but levelled in war and only this brick hall stood; in 1931 it became the memorial hall of the cemetery for fallen soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army.
facts: Form: inside, five bays and 53.8 m from east to west, three bays and 37.85 m from north to south, with the roof 22 m high; a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in grey glazed tile carries three white glazed lama stupas on the ridge, the central one hollow at the base and open to the ceiling coffer inside to admit light. Three vaults run side by side, the middle one spanning 11.5 m and 14 m high, the side ones 5 m and 7.4 m; front and rear walls each open three doors and are about 4 m thick.

Dating: Linggu Temple was moved here from Dulongfu in 1381 and the Beamless Hall was completed the same year; in the Zhengtong era it housed three great Buddhas with the Twenty-four Devas along the sides and served as a sutra store, and it was repaired repeatedly under Jiaqing and Daoguang; in the Xianfeng era most of the temple's halls burnt in the fighting between Qing and Taiping forces, and only this brick hall survived.

Memorial hall: in 1928 the Nationalist government built the cemetery for fallen soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army on the old temple site, and in 1931 the restored Beamless Hall became its memorial hall, the Hall of Righteous Spirit; 110 slabs of Taihu bluestone set into the walls list 33,224 soldiers who fell in the Northern Expedition and in the fighting against Japan at Shanghai and in north China; the Nanjing municipal government restored it again in 1981.

name: Chongshan Temple, Taiyuan
sub: Hall of Great Compassion · Early Ming official-style timber structure
era: Hongwu era, Ming · Hall of Great Compassion
yearNote: 1385 is only an approximate timeline placement within the Hongwu reign, not a precise completion year. Neither the temple's history nor its Qing main gate replaces the date of the Ming main subject drawn.
lede: In 1381 (14th year of Hongwu, Ming) Zhu Gang, Prince Gong of Jin, enlarged this temple for his late mother Empress Ma; at 140,000 square metres with six great halls on the axis it was once the largest in Shanxi. After a fire in 1864 (3rd year of Tongzhi, Qing) only the fifth hall on the axis, the Dabei Hall, was left. Seven bays wide under double eaves and nearly twenty metres high, together with its three Hongwu-era painted statues over eight metres tall, it is the most dependable specimen of an early-Ming official-style Buddhist hall in Taiyuan. The plate shows the front of the Dabei Hall.
facts: Dabei Hall: seven bays wide and four bays deep, double-eave hip-and-gable (xieshan) roof, nearly 20 m high overall; in the centre stands the Thousand-armed, Thousand-eyed, Eleven-headed Guanyin, flanked by the Thousand-bowl Manjusri and Samantabhadra, all three original Hongwu-period statues over 8 m tall.

History: according to the Daoguang-era Yangqu County Gazetteer the site was a travel palace of Emperor Yang of Sui and was called Baima Temple in the early Tang; the enlargement ran from 1381 to 1391 (14th to 24th years of Hongwu), and the present name dates from the Jiajing reign; after the fire of 1864, Zhang Zhidong in 1882 (8th year of Guangxu) turned the ruined front part into the Taiyuan Prefectural Confucian Temple.

Scale: in the Ming the temple had nearly a thousand bays of halls, the axis running through the Vajra, Heavenly Kings, Mahavira, Vairocana, Dabei and Jinling halls, the Dabei Hall second only to the nine-bay Mahavira Hall; today the temple measures 119.2 m east-west by 71.7 m north-south, covering 8,547 square metres.

name: South Gate of Chongwu Ancient City
sub: Granite gate platform · South gate wall section
era: City built in the 20th year of Hongwu, later repaired
yearNote: 1387 is the founding date of the Chongwu stone city and an approximate timeline placement; the surviving south gate section has undergone later repairs, and the upper gate tower seen in photographs is not labeled as original 1387 fabric.
lede: China's most complete surviving granite coastal fortress town. In 1387 Zhou Dexing, Marquis of Jiangxia, was ordered to build the Chongwu Battalion (qianhusuo) city on the Hui'an headland against pirate raids: a wall of some 2,500 metres, seven metres high, with gates on four sides and barbicans added to the east and west gates. The plate shows a section at the South Gate, a low, massive granite platform with the arched gateway in the middle; the gatehouse above is as it appeared after the comprehensive 1980s restoration 'to the original appearance', and should not be taken as early Ming fabric.
facts: Scale: the walls are built entirely of granite blocks, 2,567 m in circuit, about 500 m north-south and 300 m east-west, 5 m thick at the base and 7 m high; there were originally 26 guard huts, 1,304 crenels and 1,300 arrow slits, with a two- to three-tier rampart walk. The South Gate platform and its arch are one section of this.

History: begun in 1387 and completed in 1394; in 1558 pirates besieged the city for six days and nights and took it; in 1567 Qi Jiguang garrisoned troops here and reorganised the defences. Five major repairs followed between the Yongle and Daoguang reigns, and in 1983-1987 the State Administration of Cultural Heritage funded three phases of restoration, rebuilding 2,517 m of wall to the original appearance.

Comparison: Chongwu was a battalion city in the early Ming coastal garrison (weisuo) system of Fujian, and survives whole because its stone was quarried from local Hui'an granite; within half a square kilometre the town still keeps over twenty temples and nunneries, dozens of ancestral halls and more than two hundred old houses, a live example of the social structure of a southern Fujian military town.

lede: Nine dragons twist among blue-green glazed tiles, with clouds and waves spreading along the long screen. The Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong contains its dense relief between a low coping and a layered Sumeru plinth, leaving behind the screen of an early Ming princely mansion.
facts: The Nine-Dragon Screen was originally the glazed spirit screen in front of the mansion of Zhu Gui, Prince of Dai. The Palace Museum records it as built in the 25th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1392), and it is assigned to the Ming according to the main body of the screen drawn.
The screen is about 45.5 m long and about 8 m high, with nine principal dragons arrayed along its continuous body; the hipped coping and the glazed Sumeru plinth form its upper and lower borders.

A spirit screen serves as a barrier and decoration in front of a building and is not a city wall or fortification. The plate removes the railings, trees and reflecting pool and simplifies the details of the cloud-and-dragon relief, while keeping the multicolored distribution of the actual glazes.

name: Shuanglin Temple, Pingyao
sub: Hall of Heavenly Kings · Painted sculpture
era: Restored in the 2nd year of Wuping, Northern Qi · Rebuilt in the early Ming
lede: It is the first thing you see inside the fortified gate: the five-bay, gable-roofed Hall of the Heavenly Kings, with four guardian Vajra figures three metres tall lined up in its front porch, the opening statement of Shuanglin Temple's more than two thousand Ming painted sculptures. The temple began as Zhongdu Temple; a Northern Song stele in the compound records a rebuilding as early as 571 (2nd year of Wuping, Northern Qi), while today's halls and statues mostly come from a Ming rebuilding, repainted in the Qing. In 1997 it was inscribed as World Heritage with Zhenguo Temple as part of the Ancient City of Pingyao. The plate shows the front of the hall and the porch guardians; the Maitreya, Indra, Brahma and Four Heavenly Kings inside are not in the picture.
facts: Hall of the Heavenly Kings: five bays wide and three deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof; four guardian Vajra figures about 3 m tall stand in the front porch; inside, the crowned Maitreya is 2.2 m high, the attendant Indra and Brahma about 1.75 m, the Four Heavenly Kings face inward from the south wall and the Eight Bodhisattvas line the sides.

Dating: the Gugu Stele of 1011 (4th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Northern Song) in the temple records that "Zhongdu Temple was rebuilt in the 2nd year of Wuping of Northern Qi (571)"; the Song renamed it after the Buddha's passing between twin sal trees; the existing halls and sculptures come mainly from a Ming rebuilding, repainted in the Qing, and the Ming rammed-earth enclosure with its battlements gives the temple the look of a fort.

Sculpture: ten halls hold 2,052 painted clay figures, 1,566 of them intact, the largest over 3 m and the smallest 30 cm, about three quarters modelled in suspended relief leaning forward 10 to 20 degrees; the clay is local red clay and the eyes are inlaid black glass.

name: Temple of Heaven, Beijing
sub: Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests
era: Founded in the 18th year of Yongle · Rebuilt in the 22nd year of Guangxu
lede: The Hall of Great Sacrifice was built in the 18th year of Yongle in the Ming (1420); in the Jiajing era it became a round, triple-eaved hall, and under Qianlong it received blue tiles and was renamed the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. Struck by lightning and burned in the 15th year of Guangxu (1889), it was rebuilt to the original design six years later — what we see today is timber of 1896.
facts: Round, triple-eaved and conical, with blue glazed tiles and a gilded finial; 32.72 m in diameter and 38 m tall overall, it stands on a three-tiered round terrace of white marble.
Twenty-eight columns stand inside: four Dragon Well Columns represent the four seasons, twelve golden columns the twelve months, and twelve eave columns the twelve two-hour periods of the day.
The hall has no great beams; columns, tie-beams and bracket sets support the conical roof layer by layer, the pinnacle of Ming–Qing official-style timber construction.

name: Pagoda of Great Bao'en Temple, Nanjing
era: Begun in the 10th year of Yongle · Completed in the 3rd year of Xuande
lede: Begun in 1412, the tenth year of Yongle of the Ming, and finished in 1428, the third year of Xuande, it had nine storeys and eight sides and rose 78.2 m, its body faced in white porcelain brick, its arched doorways set with lions, elephants and flying rams in five-coloured glazed tile, 152 wind bells hanging from the corner beams and more than a hundred lamps burning through every night; Europeans called it the Porcelain Tower of Nanjing and counted it among the seven wonders of the medieval world. It was blown up in 1856 during the Taiping internal purge at Tianjing, leaving only the finial and stone steles; the ink-numbered glazed components unearthed in 1958 and the Seven-Jewel Ashoka Stupa found in the crypt in 2008 are what remain of it in physical form. The plate is based on a reconstruction model.
facts: Form: the glazed pagoda had nine storeys and eight sides and a total height of 78.2 m, visible from the Yangtze tens of li away; the body was faced in white porcelain, the arched doors framed in glazed tile with lions, white elephants, flying rams and other motifs in five colours; the finial was set with gold, silver and jewels, 152 wind bells hung beneath the corner beams, and the inner walls were lined with Buddha niches.

Dating: in 1412 the Yongle Emperor ordered the Ministry of Works to rebuild Tianxi Temple, and in 1424 he named it the Great Bao'en Temple and composed its stele text himself; the pagoda was begun the same year and completed in 1428, after nineteen years, reportedly under the supervision of Zheng He, then garrison commander of Nanjing. Fire at the end of the Jiajing era left 'only the pagoda, the meditation hall and the kitchen standing'.

Destruction and finds: in 1856, during the Taiping purge at Tianjing, the North King Wei Changhui ordered it blown up to deny the Wing King's troops a platform for cannon, leaving only the finial and steles. In 1958 a large number of glazed components bearing ink-written serial marks were unearthed around Yaogang Village, and tradition says three identical sets were fired; in 2008 an iron casket at the site yielded the Seven-Jewel Ashoka Stupa containing the 'Buddha's parietal bone relic', and the site park opened in 2015.
captions: Nine stories, eight faces · Drawn from the Tushanwan model of the old pagoda
Original pagoda destroyed · Not the modern glass tower

name: Hunyuan Confucian Temple
place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan · Yong'an West Street
lede: At the prefectural school of Hunyuan below the Northern Sacred Peak, the Dacheng Hall is the one building in the compound with real presence: five bays wide and three deep, roofed in yellow and green glazed tile, its central and second bays fully fitted with six-rail lattice doors while the end bays are solid brick, and the brick rear wall carries the four large characters "loyalty, filial piety, chastity, righteousness". The gazetteer records a large-scale rebuilding in 1472 (8th year of Chenghua, Ming), and the surviving hall is generally taken as a Ming structure; the omission of the front interior columns and the plain four-puzuo bracket sets under the eaves keep an older feel. The plate shows the front of the Dacheng Hall.
facts: Dacheng Hall: five bays and 27.6 m wide, three bays and 14.6 m deep, single-eave hip-and-gable roof in yellow and green glazed tile; four-puzuo bracket sets with two intercolumnar sets each in the central and second bays, the front row of interior columns omitted; the terrace in front is about 13 m long, 6 m wide and 1.5 m high, with a two-dragons-and-pearl imperial ramp in the middle.

Dating: the Qianlong-era Hunyuan Prefecture Gazetteer says the temple predates the Liao and Jin, was enlarged in the early Yuan, rebuilt on a large scale in 1472 (8th year of Chenghua, Ming) and completed in the Wanli reign; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Ming to Qing, and the hall itself has no firm completion date.

Layout: along the axis only the Ji Gate, Dacheng Hall, Zunjing Pavilion and Chongsheng Shrine survive, the pavilion a brick vault below and a timber loft above; the "loyalty, filial piety, chastity, righteousness" brickwork resembles the carved brick inscriptions of nearby Yong'an Temple, whose glazed roof fittings also match those of this hall.

name: Diamond Throne Pagoda of Zhenjue Temple, Beijing
era: Completed in the 9th year of Chenghua
lede: Five small multi-eaved pagodas stand on a stone throne. Five rows of Buddha figures on the front, animal and floral patterns at the base and an arched entrance are layered one upon another, forming the most striking carved stone silhouette of Beijing's Five Pagoda Temple.
facts: The diamond throne was completed in the 9th year of Chenghua in the Ming (1473); the five pagodas and the throne form a single stone structure, not five separate brick pagodas.

The facade of the throne has five tiers of Buddhist niches, with additional bands of animals and floral patterns at the bottom. In the frontal view the two rear pagodas are hidden, and the five pagodas are not forcibly spread out in a row.

The pagoda eaves and niche figures are carved stone, and the present appearance is mainly gray-beige stone; the glazed members of the small pavilion over the stair to the top are colored separately from the stone pagoda eaves.

name: City God Temple of Yuci
sub: Xuanjian Tower · Music tower and stage
era: Ming · Xuanjian Tower and music tower
yearNote: Xuanjian Tower (1497) and the music tower (1511) are supported by stele records; the date of about 1523 for the stage in front is an inference by the cultural relics survey from a date on the screen wall.
lede: Xuanjian Tower is not one building but a group stacked up by three generations: in 1497 (10th year of Hongzhi, Ming) the five-bay, two-storey, triple-eaved tower, seventeen metres high, went up south of the main hall; later a music hall was fitted against its north eave, less than a metre between the two roofs, and a one-bay, round-ridged, hip-and-gable street stage pushed further north, flanked by Ming glazed-tile splayed screen walls. The peacock-blue glazed roofs rise and fall, and from the courtyard they read as a single whole. The plate shows this northern group; the main hall, Xianyou Hall, and the gate are not in the picture.
facts: Xuanjian Tower: five bays wide and four rafters deep, two storeys under three tiers of hip-and-gable eaves, 17 m high overall, peacock-blue glazed roof, three hollow caisson ceilings inside; to the north adjoins the two-rafter-deep music hall, and beyond it a one-bay street stage with a single round-ridged hip-and-gable roof, flanked by glazed splayed screen walls under hip-and-gable roofs.

Dating: the temple was founded in 1362 (22nd year of Zhizheng, Yuan), moved to the present site in 1431 (6th year of Xuande, Ming) and enlarged in the Chenghua and Hongzhi reigns; the tower was built in 1497 (10th year of Hongzhi), the gate in 1509 (4th year of Zhengde), and the music hall and stage were completed by the early Jiajing reign (around 1523), giving the present scale.

Significance: roofs of three periods interlock, and the screen walls and music hall enclose an acoustic space, a model of the Ming city-god-temple composite of tower, music hall and stage; it became a national key protected site in 1996 and was placed on the World Monuments Fund Watch list in 2000.

name: Gongzhu Temple, Fanshi
lede: This small temple in Princess Village, named for a Northern Wei princess, keeps its interest indoors: the Mahavira Hall is only three bays wide under a gable roof, with not even bracket sets under the eaves, yet its four walls are covered with Ming Water-and-Land murals in which Buddhas, bodhisattvas, devas and Daoist gods assemble in tiers, a complete Ming mural cycle of this genre. Tradition credits the founding to Princess Chengxin, fourth daughter of Emperor Wencheng of Northern Wei; the surviving halls are dated by a restoration of 1503 (16th year of Hongzhi, Ming), and the Mahavira Hall and the passage hall before it are the temple's only Ming structures. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall; the murals are inside.
facts: Mahavira Hall: three bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, no bracket sets under the eaves; the passage hall in front is three bays square under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with five-puzuo bracket sets, and these two are the only Ming buildings left in the temple.

Dating: tradition attributes the temple to Princess Chengxin, fourth daughter of Emperor Wencheng of Northern Wei; it was restored in 1503 (16th year of Hongzhi, Ming) and is registered by the National Cultural Heritage Administration as Ming to Qing; facing south with three courtyards, it covers 4,347 square metres with 1,116 square metres of buildings.

Murals: the Mahavira Hall preserves Ming Water-and-Land murals with Buddhist and Daoist deities painted in one assembly; the Qielan, Horse King, God of Wealth and Erlang halls on either side were all built in the Qing and belong to a different period from the murals inside.

name: Houtu Temple, Jiexiu
sub: Sanqing Tower · Hall and stage combined
yearNote: The construction of the Sanqing Tower and the Offering Tower in about the Zhengde period is used as the sorting point; the dates 1516 and 1519 in stele records and sources each refer to different things, and 1519 is not forced to stand as the completion year of every component drawn.
lede: Jiexiu's Houtu Temple stacks hall, stage and tower into one building: the lower floor of the Sanqing Tower is the Sanqing Hall, the upper floor is wrapped by a gallery on three sides, and the back is a stage facing the Houtu Great Hall, thirteen metres high, the tallest surviving Ming theatre stage; the double-eaved splayed screen walls on either side were forced up to match, with a brick eave below and a timber eave above. The Jiexiu heritage office records its founding in 1519 (14th year of Zhengde, Ming), and every roof in the temple is glazed, five-coloured except for the yellow of the Houtu Hall group; here glazed tile is not trim but the main event. The plate shows the stage on the north face of the Sanqing Tower with its splayed screen walls.
facts: Sanqing Tower: two storeys under three tiers of hip-and-gable eaves, 15.2 m high overall, with a two-storey, triple-eaved cross-ridged porch projecting in front to join the offering hall; the stage at the back is 13 m high, its lower level barely tall enough to stand in; the splayed screen walls on either side have double gable eaves, carved brick below and timber above, their bargeboards decorated with purple-and-white glazed "mice stealing grapes".

Dating: the Jiexiu heritage office dates the founding of the Sanqing Tower to 1519 (14th year of Zhengde, Ming); the restoration of 1516 (11th year of Zhengde) absorbed the Zhenwu Hall and Sanguan Shrine, the Earth God Temple of 1730 (8th year of Yongzheng, Qing) completed the layout of eight linked temples, and repairs followed in 1835 (15th year of Daoguang).

Glazed tile: all 29 buildings are roofed in glazed tile, the Houtu Hall group in yellow and the rest in yellow, green, blue, white and ochre, mostly replaced in Qing repairs, while a few Song tiles survive on the Sanqing Tower; the more than a thousand Ming Daoist painted statues inside are equally rare.

name: Iron Buddha Temple, Gaoping
era: Restored in the 1st year of Jiajing
place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mishan Town · Mixi Village
lede: In the lanes of Mixi Village, the three-bay main hall of the Iron Buddha Temple is finished with an overhanging gable roof and glazed ridge ornaments. Step inside and the Twenty-Four Devas unfold along the walls — glaring, smiling, eyes lowered — their beards, hair and streamers held out on iron wire, giving the clay figures expressions on the verge of movement.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof. The front-eave bracket sets are five-tiered (wucai) with double cantilevers (ang), and a glazed ornament of a lion bearing a treasure vase stands at the center of the ridge.

The Ming painted clay figures of the Twenty-Four Devas inside the hall are modeled in clay over wooden armatures; their beards, hair, headdresses and streamers are shaped with iron wire, making the details light yet full of tension.

The founding date is unknown. In the 7th year of Dading in the Jin (1167) an iron Buddha was cast and the temple restored; it was repaired again in the 1st year of Jiajing (1522) and the 3rd year of Wanli (1575) in the Ming, and in the Qing. The surviving buildings show a Ming–Qing style.

name: Feihong Pagoda of Guangsheng Temple
era: Begun in the 10th year of Zhengde · Completed in the 6th year of Jiajing
lede: Between 1515 and 1527 (10th year of Zhengde to 6th year of Jiajing, Ming) the monk Dalian raised funds for over a decade and set this brick pagoda, octagonal, thirteen storeys and over forty-seven metres high, at the very front of the axis of the Upper Temple on Mount Huo. Its outer skin, from eaves and bracket sets to Buddhas, guardians and coiling dragons, is entirely fired glaze in red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, making it the largest and most complete glazed pagoda surviving in China. It stands on the site of a Yuan predecessor and later rode out the great earthquakes of 1556 in Guanzhong and 1695 in Pingyang. The plate shows the whole Feihong Pagoda.
facts: Body: octagonal in plan, thirteen storeys, 47.31 m high overall (47.6 m in another source), tapering sharply into a cone; the core is brick and stone, and on every storey the eaves, bracket sets, niches, figures and coiling dragons are glazed components in red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

Dating: rebuilt on the Yuan site from 1515 (10th year of Zhengde, Ming) with funds raised by the eminent monk Dalian and completed in 1527 (6th year of Jiajing); it then survived unharmed the Guanzhong earthquake of 1556 (35th year of Jiajing) and the Pingyang earthquake of 1695 (34th year of Kangxi).

Connections: Guangsheng Temple was listed among the first batch of national key protected sites in 1961; the Yuan murals of the Lower Temple were sold in 1928 and are now divided among three American museums; the "Tang monk sweeps the pagoda" episode of the 1986 television series Journey to the West was filmed here.

name: Imperial Ancestral Temple, Beijing
lede: The Sacrificial Hall of the Imperial Ancestral Temple spreads its eleven-bay eaves over a three-tier white stone base. Here the emperors once performed rites to their ancestors; massive nanmu columns and a double-eaved hipped roof together hold up this solemn ancestral space.
facts: The Imperial Ancestral Temple was first built in the 18th year of Yongle (1420); this entry follows the date of the Sacrificial Hall's rebuilding in the 24th year of Jiajing (1545).
The Sacrificial Hall is eleven bays wide and six bays deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof of yellow glazed tiles.
The hall stands on a three-tier white marble Sumeru plinth, and its interior preserves sixty-eight columns, each made from a single nanmu trunk.

name: White Pagoda, Fuzhou
lede: The Black Pagoda is stone; the White Pagoda is brick. In 904 Wang Shenzhi built the Bao'en Dingguang Duobao Pagoda at the western foot of Yushan to earn merit for his parents, originally a seven-storey tower with a brick core and timber galleries. Struck by lightning and burnt in 1534, it was rebuilt in 1548, when the brick core was simply made the body of the pagoda itself, coated in white lime, octagonal and seven storeys high with a gourd-shaped finial. The clean, plain silhouette seen today is the Ming rebuilding.
facts: Form: an octagonal seven-storey pavilion-style brick pagoda, 41 m high, with plain white-limed walls and a gourd finial; the brick core contains a hanging-post spiral stair to the top. In 1963, while the surroundings were cleared, fifteen Tang-dynasty carved bluestone panels from a Sumeru-base waist were unearthed, with sea legends, lions and peonies, and are now set up on the spot.

History: the Shiguo Chunqiu records that in 904 Wang Shenzhi built the pagoda for his late parents; the original had a brick core with timber work outside. It was destroyed by lightning fire in 1534 and rebuilt as the present pagoda in 1548; the stair was replaced in a 1958 repair, and in 1991 it was listed as a Fujian provincial protected site.

Counterpart: it faces the Five Dynasties Black Pagoda at the eastern foot of Wushan across the old city; together they are the 'Three Hills and Two Pagodas' that have marked Fuzhou for a millennium, and the pairing of stone with brick, black with white, shows the different materials and methods of Five Dynasties and Ming pagoda building.

name: Twin Pagodas of Haihui Temple, Yangcheng
sub: Hexagonal brick pagoda · Octagonal glazed pagoda
yearNote: 1565 is only a sorting point for the construction period of the large Ming pagoda; sources give either 1561 or 1565–1568. The small pagoda was founded in the Five Dynasties and altered in the Song; the two pagodas were not built in the same year.
place: Shanxi · Yangcheng · Pagoda courtyard of Haihui Temple, Daqiao Village
lede: Two pagodas stand one behind the other, six centuries apart: the small one in front, hexagonal and ten storeys, is the relic pagoda built for the Chan master Shunmin in 922 (2nd year of Longde, Later Liang), studded with little niches and leaning slightly west; the great one behind, octagonal, thirteen storeys and about fifty-seven metres high, was built between 1565 and 1568 (Jiajing to Longqing reigns, Ming) with over two thousand taels of silver donated by the merchant Li Sixiao, its lowest three storeys wrapped in a battlemented wall like a castle while the tenth storey throws out a ring of glazed hanging galleries. Among the storeyed pagodas of north China there is no second example. The plate shows both pagodas together.
facts: Two pagodas: the small pagoda is grey brick, hexagonal, ten storeys with corbelled eaves, about 20 m high, its outer walls covered with Buddha niches; the great pagoda is octagonal, thirteen storeys and about 57 m high, its bottom three storeys enclosed by a battlemented masonry wall, and at the tenth storey a glazed balcony gallery projects, three bays to a side, twenty-four in all, with glazed columns, balustrades and brackets.

Dating: the stele "Later Record of Longquan Chan Cloister" of 956 (3rd year of Xiande, Later Zhou) in the temple dates the small pagoda to 922 (2nd year of Longde, Later Liang); the stele by Wang Guoguang, Ming Minister of Rites, "Record of Rebuilding the Precious Pagoda and Buddha Hall of Longquan Temple", dates the great pagoda to the Jiajing-Longqing years 1565 to 1568, with another view favouring 1561 (40th year of Jiajing).

Assessment: the great pagoda is also called the Glazed Pagoda for its glazed eave edges and galleries, and Zhang Yuhuan ranked it "the crown of the famous pagodas of Shangdang"; the temple housed the Haihui Academy in the Ming and Qing, was among the first provincial protected sites of Shanxi in 1965, and became a national key protected site together with the pagodas in 2006.

name: Guanyin Hall, Changzhi
lede: A small hall of three bays whose walls, roof frame and the spaces above doors and windows are entirely taken over by sculpture: Guanyin sits in the centre with Manjusri and Samantabhadra at her sides, celestial palaces rise tier upon tier behind her, the Eighteen Arhats, Twenty-four Devas and Twelve Bodhisattvas of Perfect Enlightenment ring the room in layers, and on the top tier the south wall carries Daoist immortals, the north wall Confucian worthies, so that Sakyamuni, Laozi and Confucius share one hall. Over five hundred suspended clay figures of around 1582 (10th year of Wanli, Ming) turn the belief in the unity of the three teachings into a visible world. The plate takes the central Guanyin and part of the celestial palaces and does not stand for the whole hall.
facts: Main hall: three bays wide and four rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof covered in yellow and green glazed tile with coiling-dragon and passion-flower patterns; inside are more than five hundred Ming suspended clay figures, gilded and painted, arranged in tiers on the walls, roof frame and upper parts of doors and windows.

Dating: the Guanyin Hall was built in 1582 (10th year of Wanli, Ming) and repaired in the Qing; the name board was written in 1583 (11th year of Wanli) by Gao Qin, Vice Minister of War; the temple faces west with two courtyards over 7,400 square metres, the main hall Ming and the rest Qing.

Subjects: the altar holds Guanyin, Manjusri and Samantabhadra, the rear wall shows the life of the Buddha, the sides carry the Eighteen Arhats, Twenty-four Devas and Twelve Bodhisattvas of Perfect Enlightenment, and the fourth tier has Daoist figures on the south wall and Confucian ones on the north, with Sakyamuni in the middle and Laozi and Confucius to either side, a physical record of the merging of the three teachings in a village temple.
