name: Hanging Temple, Hunyuan
sub: Pavilions on a sheer cliff · Unity of the Three Teachings
place: Shanxi · Hunyuan · Jinlong Gorge, Mount Heng
lede: The whole temple hangs in a recess halfway up Cuiping Mountain, its highest point more than ninety metres above the valley floor. It looks as if dozens of slender timber posts hold it up, but the real load is carried by twenty-seven beams driven into the rock; most of the posts are little more than reassurance. The north and south flying pavilions, three storeys and over ten metres high, float free on three sides and are linked by two plank walks wide enough for one person; the Three Teachings Hall on the top floor of the north pavilion seats Sakyamuni, Confucius and Laozi together. A Northern Wei founding has long been claimed, yet the surviving forty bays of timber work are all products of Ming and Qing rebuilding. The plate shows the two pavilions and the walkways between them.
facts: Structure: 27 timber beams about 50 cm in diameter, soaked in tung oil, are bedded under the temple, one end tenoned into the rock and the other carrying the buildings and projecting about 1 m to support the walkways; the temple has 40 bays and 152.5 square metres of timber building, the two flying pavilions each three storeys with nine-ridged roofs and posts more than ten metres long on the outer side.

History: one account has Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei found it in 491 (15th year of Taihe) to relocate the Celestial Masters' Daoist seat, another gives 398 (1st year of Tianxing); it was repaired in the Jin, Ming and the Tongzhi reign of the Qing, and most existing buildings are Ming and Qing rebuildings; the 1978 overhaul that replaced load-bearing beams reconfirmed the cantilevered-beam system.

Three teachings: the upper floor of the main hall holds the Three Buddhas Hall, Taiyi Hall and Guandi Temple; the south pavilion rises through the Chunyang Palace, Sanguan Hall and Leiyin Hall, the north pavilion through the Four Buddhas Hall, Three Sages Hall and Three Teachings Hall, where Sakyamuni, Confucius and Laozi share one shrine; the temple became a national key protected site in 1982.

name: Twin Pagodas of Yongzuo Temple, Taiyuan
yearNote: 1612 is only an approximate sorting point for the period in which the twin pagodas took shape; the two were built one after the other, and this year is not given as the founding year of both.
lede: On the high ground southeast of Taiyuan two thirteen-storey brick pagodas stand shoulder to shoulder, forty-six metres apart and both around fifty-four metres tall, the tallest pair of twin pagodas surviving in China. The east pagoda, Wenfeng Pagoda, came first, built in 1599 (27th year of Wanli, Ming) under Fu Lin and his son Fu Zhimo as a geomantic tower to mend the city's literary fortunes; the west pagoda, Xuanwen Pagoda, followed more than a decade later, completed in 1612 (40th year of Wanli) for the Prince of Jin by the eminent Wutai monk Miaofeng, its eaves edged entirely in peacock-blue glaze and named for the honorific title of the Wanli emperor's mother. The plate shows both pagodas, each with its own finial and taper.
facts: Twin pagodas: both are octagonal thirteen-storey brick pagodas of storeyed type, hollow double-shell structures with spiral stairs inside; the west Xuanwen Pagoda is 54.78 m high and the east Wenfeng Pagoda 53.3 m, 46 m apart, and all thirteen eaves of the Xuanwen Pagoda are edged with peacock-blue glazed tile.

Dating: Yongming Temple was founded in 1597 (25th year of Wanli, Ming) and the east pagoda finished in 1599; in 1608 (36th year of Wanli) Zhu Minchun, Prince of Jin, invited the Chan master Miaofeng to enlarge it, and in 1612 (40th year) the west pagoda and the beamless brick hall were completed and the temple renamed Yongzuo; additions in the Shunzhi and Kangxi reigns of the Qing gave it its present form.

Conservation: the east pagoda once leaned 2.87 m and was righted and strengthened in 1995 to 1996, the west pagoda was strengthened in 1981 to 1984, and only the west pagoda is now open to climb; the pair has been the emblem of Taiyuan since 1985, and the temple also keeps a Ming beamless brick hall and more than 260 stone steles.

name: Rulong Bridge
yearNote: According to the county gazetteer it was built in 1625; later repairs do not mean that every component of the bridge is original Ming fabric.

facts: Built in the Tianqi reign: the county gazetteer records that Rulong Bridge was built in the 5th year of Tianqi in the Ming (1625); it is one of the surviving Ming timber-arch covered bridges in Qingyuan.

Staggered heights: the bell tower at the north end, with a triple-eaved hip-and-gable roof, rises high and, together with the central roof and the south entrance, forms a layered outline along the long bridge.

name: Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
sub: Mahavira Hall · Hall of a Hundred Columns
era: Ming · Restored in the 10th year of Chongzhen
lede: Nine bays across the front under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof: the highest grade of Buddhist hall in China. The hall should hold a hundred stone columns, but to make room for the huge Five Buddhas and the worship space two rows of fourteen were omitted, leaving eighty-six, and the name 'Hall of a Hundred Columns' stuck anyway. More remarkable still are the twenty-four bracket sets carved as celestial musicians, kalavinka with human bodies, feathered wings and bird legs, holding instruments or scholars' implements: structural members that carry the beams and at the same time a scene of music before the Buddha. The present form dates from the rebuilding of 1637 by the general Zheng Zhilong and others.
facts: Form: nine bays wide and six deep, about 1,388 square metres in area, with a double-eave hip-and-gable roof about 20 m high; a palatial-type frame with two rows of 14 columns omitted in the middle, leaving 86 stone columns and 76 bracket sets; where the two central rows of stone columns meet the beams, the brackets are carved as 24 flying musicians.

History: founded in 686 (second year of Chuigong, Tang); the present plan and frame proportions largely follow the rebuilding of 1155 in the Southern Song, the outer eaves were extended in 1389, and the hall was rebuilt to its present state in 1637 by the general Zheng Zhilong and others. The Sumeru base of the terrace in front carries 73 panels of lions and sphinx-like figures, moved here during the Ming rebuilding from a Hindu temple abandoned at the end of the Yuan.

Plurality: the hall enshrines the Five Buddhas of esoteric Buddhism, each 6 m high; two Hindu stone columns under the rear gallery eaves were also reused in the 1637 rebuilding, nine of their 24 medallions showing Vishnu, Krishna and other myths. That a Buddhist hall was rebuilt with Hindu members is the most tangible evidence of the port's mixed cultures.

name: Xiaoxitian, Xi County
sub: Hall filled with suspended sculpture · Thousand Buddha Hermitage
lede: The Mahavira Hall is under one hundred and seventy square metres, yet nearly two thousand painted figures are packed into it: celestial palaces rise tier upon tier above the main Buddha, twelve musician bodhisattvas dance on the balustraded platform in front, human-faced apsaras and divine birds perch on clouds, the largest over three metres, the smallest no bigger than a thumb. All are clay, gilded and painted, suspended between roof frame and walls, begun in the Chongzhen reign at the end of the Ming and finished under Shunzhi in the early Qing. Qianfo Nunnery itself covers barely eleven hundred square metres, two thirds of its halls built in two storeys with cave-like openings for doors. The plate takes the central shrine and part of the celestial palaces and does not stand for the whole hall.
facts: Mahavira Hall: five bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, interior under 170 square metres; nearly two thousand suspended figures are arranged in tiers on the roof frame, walls and shrines, the largest over 3 m high and the smallest able to sit in a palm.

Dating: Qianfo Nunnery was founded at the end of the Ming by the Chan master Dongming; the suspended sculpture of the Mahavira Hall was begun in the Chongzhen reign and completed in the Shunzhi reign of the Qing, about thirty years in all; the temple faces east on the hillside in an upper and a lower court, and became a national key protected site in 1996.

Layout: the whole temple has little over 1,100 square metres of building, two thirds of its halls in two storeys, with cave-like doorways dividing the upper, middle and front courts; the upper court holds the Mahavira, Manjusri and Samantabhadra halls, the lower court the Wuliang Hall, Weituo Hall, Moyun Pavilion and the bell and drum towers.

name: Xianshen Tower, Jiexiu
sub: Street-spanning tower and music tower · Composite pavilion
era: Qing · Late Shunzhi to early Kangxi
lede: One building does three jobs: the street runs beneath it, making it the over-street tower of Shuncheng Gate Street; one floor up it is the gate of the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers; above that a five-bay theatre stage faces back to the north, the whole stacking into a four-storey silhouette. It is also the only surviving building in China linked to Zoroastrianism, the carved bull-headed and camel-headed beasts under its eaves read by Jiang Boqin as incarnations of Zoroastrian deities. Tradition credits the temple to Wen Yanbo of the Northern Song; it burned in the early Qing, and the present tower is a rebuilding of 1660 to 1668 (late Shunzhi to early Kangxi), with an inscription of 1667 (6th year of Kangxi) under the finial of the music hall ridge. The plate shows the over-street tower and the music hall.
facts: Form: the plan is T-shaped, about 20 m deep in all; the over-street tower at the front and the porch before the stage are each three bays square, the stage block behind is five bays wide and four deep with a surrounding gallery; the lower floor is the gate, the upper floor the stage, and with the music hall and double eaves it rises four storeys.

Dating: the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers burned in the early Qing and was rebuilt from 1660 (17th year of Shunzhi) to 1668 (7th year of Kangxi), with an inscription of 1667 (6th year of Kangxi) under the vase finial of the music hall ridge and an offering pavilion added in 1786 (51st year of Qianlong); in 1985 the over-street tower was jacked up 1.5 m as a whole and the restoration was completed in 1987.

Zoroastrian link: the stele record says Duke Wen Lu (Wen Yanbo) of the Song built the temple for the Xian god, and a Jiajing-era magistrate of the Ming turned it into the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers; Jiang Boqin judged from the bull- and camel-headed carvings under the eaves that it is the remnant of a Zoroastrian shrine, and Chen Mingda's 1951 survey already called its artistry outstanding and warned against dismissing it for its late date.

lede: Double green eaves spread over the seven-bay hall, and stone columns alternate with vermilion doors beneath them. Rebuilt in the Qing after an earthquake, the Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple remains the center of the worship of Mencius in Zoucheng.
facts: History: an earthquake in 1668 damaged the main hall, which was rebuilt five years later; it underwent a comprehensive repair in 1736, and its present state also reflects modern renovation.

name: Tiankuang Hall of the Dai Temple
lede: At the foot of Mount Tai, the Tiankuang Hall spreads two broad tiers of eaves to the scale of the rites to the sacred mountain. From its founding in the Song to its Qing restoration, its beam frame, doors, windows and murals layer the memories of different periods.
facts: The Tiankuang Hall is the main hall of the Dai Temple, dedicated to the god of Mount Tai; founded in the Song, it has been repaired many times since.
The hall is nine bays wide and five bays deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof covered in yellow glazed tiles.
The proportions and construction methods of the surviving timber frame show Qing characteristics, and the murals inside the hall were repainted in the early Qing.

A Kangxi-era stele records that the restoration was completed in 1677, keeping the usable beams and columns of the hall and replacing damaged members; the timeline places it approximately on this basis, with later repairs counted separately.

name: Forbidden City, Beijing
lede: The Hall of Supreme Harmony stands on a three-tier white marble base, commanding the Outer Court with its eleven-bay width and double-eaved hipped roof. Broad ceremonial stairs lift the hall on high; its present form comes from the rebuilding of the Kangxi reign.
facts: Work on the surviving Hall of Supreme Harmony began in the 34th year of Kangxi (1695) and was completed in the 36th year (1697).
Eleven bays wide and five bays deep, it is the foremost of the three great halls of the Outer Court of the Forbidden City.

The roof is a double-eaved hipped roof, with the number of ridge beasts on the eave corners increased to ten; important ceremonies such as enthronements and imperial weddings were once held in the hall.

name: Mimi Temple, Fanshi
place: Shanxi · Fanshi · Yantou Township · Mimo Cliff
lede: Thirty-eight kilometres southwest of Taihuai on Mount Wutai, this temple below Mimo Cliff on Mount Weiping was once the place of the saying that to visit Wutai without the Dragon Cave was to see only half the mountain. Tradition takes it back to the Northern Qi; the Tang monk Mucha retreated and built here, and it flourished in the Tang and Song, leaving outside the walls the Tang-founded, Ming-repaired pagoda of Patriarch Mucha and the pagoda of Master Xuanjue of 963 (7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han). The halls themselves are Qing rebuildings, the main halls of the front and middle courts both five bays wide. The plate shows the front of the Manjusri Hall: five bays with a front porch, a central stair climbing to the raised platform, and Qing paintings surviving on the porch panels and inside.
facts: Manjusri Hall: as drawn, five bays wide with a front porch under a flush-gable (yingshan) roof, standing on a raised platform reached by a central stone stair; in the temple the main halls of the front and middle courts are both five bays, the north and south sutra lofts five bays each, and only a five-bay north pavilion survives in the rear court.

Dating: the Qingliang Shan Gazetteer records that the Tang monk Mucha founded the temple while in retreat at Mimi Cliff, and another account has a Northern Qi nun's hermitage before it; of thirty-two hermitages once here the front, middle and rear courts and the West and Middle hermitages remain; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Qing, and it became a national key protected site in 2006.

Stonework: before the temple stand a Jin-dynasty stone pillar and two brick pagodas, the pagoda of Patriarch Mucha, Tang-founded and Ming-repaired, hexagonal, four storeys and about 10 m high, and the pagoda of Master Xuanjue of 963 (7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han), hexagonal and two storeys; the Golden Buddha Loft in the Middle Hermitage holds a stone Amitabha about 7 m high carved in 1535 (14th year of Jiajing, Ming).

name: Kang Baiwan Manor
era: Late Ming–early Qing · Extended over generations
yearNote: The Zhengzhou Municipal Bureau of Cultural Heritage dates the manor as a whole to the late Ming–early Qing, with continued construction in later periods. 1700 is only an approximate sorting point for the manor's Ming–Qing structures; the storied cave dwelling shown in the photographs has as yet no exact construction date of its own, and neither the Kang family's move here nor any individual's life dates are used as the date of the building.
lede: The facade of a storied cave dwelling and the buildings on either side enclose a long, deep inner courtyard. Kang Baiwan Manor combines caves dug into the cliff with siheyuan courtyard houses, preserving the living spaces of a merchant family of the Heluo region.

lede: The Octagonal Pavilion is not a small garden pavilion for enjoying the view but the ordination hall of a Dai Theravada Buddhist temple. name: Chengqi Lou, Yongding
sub: Gaobei tulou cluster · Circular rammed-earth dwelling
era: Completed in the 48th year of Kangxi
yearNote: The completion year of Chengqi Lou, 1709, is adopted; the start of construction in the Ming and the completion in the Qing are described separately. The plate shows the surviving exterior and does not reconstruct the interior from postage stamps.
lede: 'Four storeys high, four rings round, four hundred rooms up and down; circle within circle, ring within ring, three hundred years of weathering.' The local rhyme describes Chengqi Lou: inside a round building 73 metres across sit three concentric ring-houses and an ancestral hall, the outer ring four storeys with seventy-two rooms to a floor, the second ring two storeys, the third one, each stepping lower towards the centre. The Jiang clan is said to have broken ground in the Chongzhen era and finished only in 1709, the 48th year of Kangxi; at its peak more than six hundred people lived here. The plate shows only the complete exterior, with no section cut.
facts: Form: a four-ring concentric earthen building, 73 m in diameter on a site of 5,376.17 square metres; the outer ring is four storeys and 16.4 m high with 72 rooms per floor, the second ring two storeys with 40 rooms per floor, the third ring a single storey of 32 rooms, and an ancestral hall at the centre, over four hundred rooms in all, with 3 main gates and 2 wells. The rammed-earth outer wall is 1.5 m thick at the base and 1 m at the top, and the eaves project nearly 4 m.

Dating: ground is said to have been broken in the Chongzhen era of the Ming and the building completed in 1709, spanning three generations and about half a century. More than six hundred people lived here at its height and some three hundred of the Jiang clan still do; the Fujian dwelling in the 1986 Chinese folk-dwelling stamp series is this building.

Comparison: Chengqi Lou is the core of the Gaobei tulou cluster, home of the Yongding Jiang clan, together with Wuyun Lou, Shize Lou and Qiaofu Lou; by size and number of rings it ranks among the foremost surviving round tulou and is called the 'king of tulou'. In 2008 the Gaobei cluster was inscribed on the World Heritage List as part of 'Fujian Tulou', six clusters and four single buildings.

name: Guandi Temple, Xiezhou
sub: Chongning Hall · Ancestral temple of Guandi
yearLabel: Qing · Rebuilt after the Kangxi-era fire
yearNote: 1725 is only an approximate sorting point for the rebuilding phase in the early 18th century, not the exact completion year of the Chongning Hall; 1702 is the year of the temple fire.
lede: The ancestral temple of all Guandi temples, its main hall, Chongning Hall, is named for the title "Perfected Lord Chongning" conferred on Guan Yu by Emperor Huizong of Song in 1104 (3rd year of Chongning). The seven-bay hall under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof closes the axis of the front court, a ring of coiling-dragon stone columns in the gallery around it, and under its eaves hang imperial boards of four reigns: Kangxi's "righteousness lights heaven and earth", Qianlong's "divine valour", Xianfeng's "the pole of humanity for all ages" and Cixi's "awesome power shakes all". The temple was founded in 589 (9th year of Kaihuang, Sui); the existing buildings follow the rebuilding after the fire of 1702 (41st year of Kangxi, Qing). The plate takes the Chongning Hall alone; the Spring and Autumn Tower behind it is not in the picture.
facts: Chongning Hall: seven bays wide and six deep, double-eave hip-and-gable roof, with a surrounding gallery carried on coiling-dragon stone columns; a bell pavilion and a stele pavilion, added in the Qing, flank the front; inside and out hang the boards of Kangxi, Qianlong, Xianfeng and Cixi and dozens of late-Qing and Republican boards.

Dating: founded in 589 (9th year of Kaihuang, Sui) and rebuilt in 1014 (7th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Song), the temple was destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly; the rebuilding after the fire of 1702 (41st year of Kangxi, Qing) produced today's front-court-and-rear-palace layout, and it became a national key protected site in 1988.

Layout: the temple covers 220,000 square metres; to the south lies the Garden of the Sworn Oath of 1620 (48th year of Wanli, Ming), to the north the main temple, whose front axis runs through screen wall, Duan Gate, Zhi Gate, Meridian Gate, Imperial Calligraphy Tower and Chongning Hall, while the rear palace centres on the Spring and Autumn Tower flanked by the Sabre and Seal towers; with over a hundred bays of halls it is called the crown of martial temples.

name: Dongyue Temple, Wanrong
era: Restored in the 11th year of Qianlong
lede: This three-storey timber tower in the county town of Wanrong stands 23.19 m high. Four through-columns run from the ground floor straight to the top, and 345 bracket sets and 32 upturned eave corners project tier upon tier, so that from a distance clouds seem to gather about the tower, hence the name Feiyun, Flying Clouds. The timber is left unpainted. It stands at the very front of the axis of the Dongyue Temple; its founding date is unknown, a repair stele of 1617 (45th year of Wanli, Ming) already exists, and the present state is that of the repair of 1746 (11th year of Qianlong, Qing). The plate shows the front of Feiyun Lou.
facts: Form: square in plan, five bays wide and deep, three visible storeys with five inside, three tiers and four eaves, crowned by a cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof; on the second and third storeys a hip-and-gable baosha projects on each of the four sides above a balcony. The whole tower is jointed without iron nails; the four cypress through-columns are 0.7 m in diameter and over 15 m tall.

Dating: the Qianlong-era Record of Repairing Feiyun Lou says the Dongyue Temple already existed in the 1st year of Zhenguan (627); the tower's own founding date is unknown, steles record repairs in 1617 (45th year of Wanli, Ming) and 1746 (11th year of Qianlong, Qing), and the present fabric follows the latter. Listed as a national key protected site in 1988.

Assessment: Chai Zejun wrote that it 'holds an important place among surviving ancient storeyed buildings in China', and with the Yingxian pagoda it is called Shanxi's 'southern tower and northern pagoda'; behind it the Wumen gate and offering hall are Yuan structures, and the stone columns of the main Dongyue hall bear Ming inscriptions of the Zhengtong and Zhengde reigns, none of which is in the plate.

name: City God Temple, Jiexiu
yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate timeline position for the Qing building, not the exact completion year of the stage; the founding of the temple and the surviving Ming main hall have their own dates.
lede: The stage of the Jiexiu City God Temple is built 'reversed' beside the gate: toward the courtyard it throws out a hip-and-gable baosha as the stage front, with a round-ridged flush-gable backstage behind. The roof is covered in blue-green glazed tile, and along the main ridge pavilions, vases and ridge beasts stand in a row; beneath the platform a passage is left, so one enters the temple under the stage. The Jiexiu cultural heritage bureau records that the founding date is unknown and that steles note four repairs from 1495 (8th year of Hongzhi, Ming) onward; the roof glaze is among the few Ming remains left in Jiexiu. The plate shows the courtyard face of the stage and its glazed ridge.
facts: Stage: the main body has a round-ridged flush-gable roof, with a three-bay hip-and-gable baosha projecting both toward the courtyard and outward, the inner one serving as the stage; the platform is raised with a stone balustrade in front and a passage below; bell and drum towers flank it, and as drawn the sparrow braces under the eaves are carved all over with flowers.

Dating: steles record repairs in 1495 (8th year of Hongzhi), 1572 (6th year of Longqing), 1724 (2nd year of Yongzheng, Qing) and 1814 (19th year of Jiaqing); Wikipedia additionally gives a founding in 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming). Listed in 2013 in the seventh batch of national key protected sites.

Glaze: the glazed ridge tiles, owl-tail finials, immortals and beasts, pavilions and vases on the roof are Ming remains, complete in colour and form; the main hall, seven bays wide under a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, has slender columns and brackets of marked Ming character, and is not in the plate.

name: Dingcun Folk Houses
sub: Ding Kun Compound · Southern Shanxi courtyard house
era: Qianlong period, Qing · Ding Kun Compound
yearNote: 1760 is only for approximate sorting within the Qianlong period. The Ding Kun family built over three generations across about 50 years, and no precise completion year is invented for the hall drawn here.
lede: Dingcun lies on the east bank of the Fen River and keeps more than twenty Ming and Qing residences: the northern group are single-court siheyuan from the Wanli reign of the Ming onward, the central and southern groups two-court compounds of the Yongzheng to Xianfeng reigns of the Qing. The Ding Kun compound, now Courtyard No. 1 and the Dingcun Folk Museum, was founded in 1745 (10th year of Qianlong, Qing); its owners Ding Kun and his son Ding Jialun both purchased the status of imperial student, and the grandson Ding Xilian purchased a sub-prefectural post in 1795 (60th year of Qianlong), whereupon the 'Xuandelang' archway was raised before the gate. The plate shows the three-bay hall inside the courtyard and the wing rooms on either side.
facts: Courtyard: as drawn, a three-bay hall with a front porch, with wing rooms on both sides enclosing a long narrow court; Dingcun houses are northern siheyuan of brick, stone and timber, richly carved on eave boards, sparrow braces, column bases and gate stones, and in one Qianlong-era house the railing panels of the central hall carry 'hundred plays' carvings such as 'Ningwu Pass' and 'Yue Fei's mother tattooing'.

Dating: the earliest house of the northern group dates to 1593 (21st year of Wanli, Ming), the central and southern groups to the Yongzheng-Xianfeng reigns of the Qing; Courtyard No. 1 was founded in 1745 (10th year of Qianlong), and the 'Xuandelang' archway was erected after Ding Xilian's purchase of office in 1795 (60th year of Qianlong). The Dingcun residences were listed as a national key protected site in 1988.

Value: Dingcun is a group of residences built continuously by one family in one village for over two hundred years; the Dingcun Folk Museum, opened in 1985, was China's first folk museum of the Han people. The Dingcun site on the Fen River terrace beside the village is a Palaeolithic site, protected separately from the houses.

name: Quanzhou Prefectural Confucian Temple
sub: Dacheng Hall · Qing structure in Song style
lede: A Hall of Great Achievement for a prefectural school, yet roofed with a double-eave hip roof, yellow glazed tiles and stone columns carved with coiling dragons: extraordinarily rare among Confucian temples anywhere in China. The temple moved to its present site in the early Taiping Xingguo era of the Northern Song and took its 'school on the left, temple on the right' layout after a rebuilding in 1137; the hall was rebuilt in the Xianchun era and the present hall was thoroughly repaired in 1761, yet its column grid, beam frame and true cantilever brackets keep twelfth-century practice. The six relief dragon columns along the front eaves are known locally as 'six dragons bearing up the sage'.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and five deep, about 801 square metres in area, with a double-eave hip roof of yellow glazed tiles; the hall body is carried on 48 round white stone columns in a two-ring 'double-trough' grid, with six relief dragon columns at the front eaves and two more dragon columns inside; the bracket sets use true ang inside and out, the beams are fully painted, and the ridges carry cut-porcelain ornament.

Dating: moved to the present site early in the Taiping Xingguo era of the Northern Song and rebuilt in 1137; the hall was rebuilt in the Xianchun era (1265-1274), and the present hall is the product of a major repair in 1761 that kept its Song structural character. A 2014-2015 restoration to the original form and materials was named one of the outstanding heritage conservation projects of 2020 nationwide.

Significance: the Quanzhou Confucian Temple and its school symbolised the officials and scholars of Song-Yuan Quanzhou, and its building scale is the largest among Confucian temples in China's seven southeastern provinces; the waist of the Sumeru base of the terrace in front still carries Song bluestone reliefs of scrolling foliage. In 2021 it was inscribed as a component of the World Heritage property 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.

name: Longxing Temple, Xinjiang County
era: Qing · Qianlong restoration with added stories
yearNote: This year is the date of the Qing restoration that added stories, producing the surviving thirteen-story exterior; neither the temple's Tang history nor early remains inside the pagoda are equated directly with the date of the exterior.
lede: The Longxing Pagoda on the high ground north of the old Jiangzhou city is octagonal and thirteen storeys, over 42 m high, the highest point in the town. The pagoda originally had eight storeys; it collapsed in 1777 (42nd year of Qianlong, Qing) and was rebuilt in 1784 (49th year of Qianlong), cased in grey brick and raised to thirteen storeys, and the flat corbelled brick eaves and taper seen today were fixed then. The temple was founded in the early Tang as the Biluo Daoist abbey and renamed Longxing Temple in 670 (1st year of Xianheng); early remains inside the pagoda do not date its exterior. The plate shows the whole pagoda.
facts: Form: an octagonal brick pagoda of pavilion type, built of grey brick, thirteen storeys tapering upward, each storey divided by corbelled brick eaves, with brick-carved bracket sets under the first-storey eaves; its height is given as 42.4 m by one source and 43.7 m by another, and each storey carries a plaque, from 'one column holding up heaven' to 'ten continents and three isles'.

Dating: originally eight storeys, the pagoda fell in 1777 (42nd year of Qianlong, Qing) and was rebuilt in 1784 (49th year of Qianlong) at thirteen storeys; another account has it cased and heightened during the 1777 repair. Repaired in 1941, with a Record of Repairing the Longxing Temple of Xinjiang. The whole temple became a national key protected site in 2006.

Curiosity: the county gazetteer and steles record 'smoke rising' from the top of the pagoda on several occasions, in 1875 (1st year of Guangxu), 1937, 1971, 1976 and 1993, the 1971 episode lasting over ten days, its cause unexplained; the temple also holds a Yuan main hall and the Tang Biluo Stele, not in the plate.

name: Jiwang Temple, Jishan
sub: Offering Hall · Bell and drum towers
yearNote: The Offering Hall, bell and drum towers and Houji Tower drawn here are Qing rebuildings; the Yuan-dynasty Jiangyuan Hall in the temple is not drawn.
place: Shanxi · Jishan · West Street of the county town
lede: The sparrow braces under the front eaves of the offering hall of the Jiwang Temple carry no dragons or phoenixes; they show Hou Ji teaching the people to farm, spring sowing and the grain harvest. On either wing of this small three-bay hall stands a bell or drum tower, four metres square under a double-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, and behind rises the thirty-metre Hou Ji Tower, three glazed roofs crowded together. The temple was founded in 1345 (5th year of Zhizheng, Yuan), burned in the Daoguang reign of the Qing, and was rebuilt in 1843 (23rd year of Daoguang) by subscription led by the magistrate Li Jingchun; all three buildings drawn belong to that rebuilding. The plate shows the offering hall and the bell and drum towers, with only the upper eaves of the Hou Ji Tower visible.
facts: Offering hall: three bays and 14 m wide, 10 m deep, roofed in coloured glazed tile, the roof described as overhanging-gable by one source and flush-gable by another; the sparrow braces under front and rear eaves are wood reliefs of farming, Hou Ji teaching agriculture in the central bay, spring ploughing in the east bay and harvest in the west bay. The bell and drum towers are 4 m square under double-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roofs.

Dating: founded in 1345 (5th year of Zhizheng, Yuan), the temple burned down in the 10th year of Daoguang (some say the 16th) and was rebuilt in 1843 (23rd year of Daoguang) by subscription led by magistrate Li Jingchun; his seven-character poem on its completion is carved in the west gable wall, and the eight views of Jishan in the east. Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Comparison: the temple is known for the 'three marvels' of glaze, wood carving and stone carving; the gallery of the Hou Ji Tower has twenty carved stone eave columns and fifty-two carved stone balustrade panels. The Jiangyuan Hall inside is a Yuan structure and the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers the temple as 'Yuan to Qing', but everything drawn is Qing.

name: Ancient Opera Stages of Ninghai
sub: Hu Clan Ancestral Hall, Aohu · Chongxing Temple · City God Temple
era: Qing to Republic · Aohu stage, 4th year of Xianfeng
lede: Ninghai County has 125 surviving old opera stages, ten of them listed as national protected sites, all built inside ancestral halls and temples between the Qing and the Republic. A stage one bay square is raised half a person's height into the air, the upturned corners of its hip-and-gable roof curling like ox horns, and inside a caisson ceiling spirals upward.
facts: Most stages are one bay wide, with the stage floor raised off the ground and a carved balustrade around the stage front; the column heads support the eaves with carved brackets (niutui, “ox legs”) rather than bracket sets.

Caisson ceilings are the specialty of Ninghai's stages: the stage of the Hu Clan Ancestral Hall in Aohu and its linking corridor have three caisson ceilings in a row, one of only three surviving “three linked caisson ceilings” in Zhejiang.

The Hu Clan Ancestral Hall in Aohu was built in the 4th year of Xianfeng in the Qing (1854); the stage connects with viewing galleries on either side, from whose upper floors the audience watched performances.

name: Houtu Shrine, Wanrong
era: Qing · Rebuilt in the 9th year of Tongzhi
place: Shanxi · Wanrong · Ronghe Town · Miaoqian Village
lede: Emperor Wu of Han sacrificed to Houtu at Fenyin and, boating on the Fen, wrote the Song of the Autumn Wind; two thousand years later this tower still bears its name. It stands at the northern end of the Houtu Shrine on a brick-and-stone platform sixteen metres square, three storeys and over thirty-two metres high, galleried on all four sides under a cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof; the platform is pierced east-west like a street gate, with 'Gazing at Lu' over the east arch and 'Looking to Qin' over the west. As the Yellow River repeatedly shifted, the shrine was moved east again and again; the present site was rebuilt in 1870 (9th year of Tongzhi, Qing) by magistrate Dai Ruzhen, and the tower was then moved to the rear of the temple. The plate shows the front of Qiufeng Lou.
facts: Form: platform 16 m square, tower of three storeys, 32.6 m high (33 m by another account), five bays wide and deep, cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, galleries on each storey, a warrior figure on each upturned corner; inside the south gate of the platform a small niche is inscribed 'Sweeping-the-ground Altar', and the storeys hold, from bottom to top, modern, Qing and Yuan carvings of the Song of the Autumn Wind.

History: in the Yuan an Autumn Wind Pavilion behind the temple held the stele of the song carved in 1271 (8th year of Zhiyuan); in the Longqing reign of the Ming the pavilion was lost to the Fen and a tower built before the temple; in 1662 (1st year of Kangxi, Qing) the river breached and the tower was lost, and it was rebuilt elsewhere the next year; destroyed again in 1862 (1st year of Tongzhi) and moved to the present site in 1870 (9th year of Tongzhi). After the Guangxu-era Ronghe County Gazetteer.

Background: the Houtu Shrine at Fenyin was the imperial temple for sacrifice to the earth established by Emperor Wu of Han, and emperors of Han, Tang and Song sacrificed here in person; a temple-plan stele of 1137 (15th year of Tianhui, Jin) depicts the layout after the Northern Song enlargement. Apart from the Yuan gate, most of today's shrine is late Qing; listed as a national key protected site in 1996.

name: Hōryū-ji
era: Asuka period · Second half of the 7th century
lede: Beneath its two tiers of tiled roofs, the Kondō of Hōryū-ji forms a distinctive outline with cloud-shaped bracketing, an upper-story railing and a low pent roof (mokoshi). This Asuka-period timber building faces the five-story pagoda on the west side of the courtyard, preserving clues to the space of early East Asian Buddhist temples.
facts: The temple was founded in 607; the surviving Kondō belongs to the Western Precinct (Sai-in Garan), rebuilt after the fire of 670, and is dated to the second half of the 7th century.
The main structure is five bays across and four bays deep, with a two-tiered irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof; a board-roofed mokoshi surrounds the first story, forming a shallower eave line below.
Cloud-shaped bearing blocks and bracket arms (kumoto and kumohijiki), slightly swelling round columns and the geometric railing of the upper story are important features of the Kondō's exterior.

name: Tōshōdai-ji
era: Nara period · Second half of the 8th century
lede: Eight round columns carry the broad single-eaved roof of the Kondō of Tōshōdai-ji, and the open portico in front adds a quiet layer of transition between the courtyard and the inner chamber where the Buddha images stand. After Jianzhen (Ganjin) founded the temple, his disciples completed this Kondō in the second half of the 8th century.
facts: Jianzhen (Ganjin) founded Tōshōdai-ji in 759, while the surviving Kondō was built in the second half of the 8th century; the temple's official account links its construction to his disciple Nyohō.
The Kondō is seven bays across the front and four bays deep, with a yosemune (hipped) roof covered in hongawara tiles; the front bay is left open to form a colonnade.

Three-stepped bracket sets (mitesaki kumimono) beneath the eaves carry the deep overhang, and the shibi ridge-end ornaments at both ends of the ridge and the broad single eave together define its exterior.

name: Byōdō-in
lede: Across the Aji Pond, the central hall and its two wing corridors spread like a bird with outstretched wings, and twin phoenixes face each other on the ridge. The Amida Hall built by Fujiwara no Yorimichi in 1053 sets the Heian-period vision of the Pure Land above the waters of Uji.
facts: Heian structure: the Phoenix Hall was built in 1053 by Fujiwara no Yorimichi; the surviving central hall and wing corridors reflect the layout of an Amida hall of the late Heian period.

Twin phoenixes and two wings: the left and right wing corridors enclose the central hall, and a pair of phoenixes stands on the ridge; the name Phoenix Hall gradually came into use in the Edo period, and the phoenixes now on the roof are replacements installed in 1968.

Worship across the pond: the building sits in the west facing east, and worshippers on the east bank of the Aji Pond face west to venerate the Buddha; garden and hall together express the image of the Western Pure Land.

name: Tōdai-ji
lede: With round columns rising straight to the heights and tier upon tier of tie beams passing through them, the Nandaimon shows the structural power of the Daibutsuyō style. Three passages run beneath the broad double eaves, and Niō guardian statues on either side protect the entrance to Tōdai-ji.
facts: The surviving Nandaimon was rebuilt under the direction of Chōgen; its ridgepole was raised in 1199, and it was completed in 1203 together with the Kongō Rikishi statues within the gate.
The gate has an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof, five bays across the front with three central doorways and double eaves; it is an important surviving example of Daibutsuyō architecture.
The gate has 18 great round columns in all, with six columns across the front dividing it into five bays; according to the temple, the gate is 25.46 m tall above the platform.

name: Kiyomizu-dera
lede: The main hall of Kiyomizu-dera lays its broad cypress-bark roof over the slope of Mount Otowa, and the Kiyomizu stage in front of the eaves projects out from the cliff. Beneath the stage, rows of tall timber posts interlace with horizontal tie beams, revealing the support system of Japanese kakezukuri (cliffside) architecture.
facts: The temple was founded in 778; the surviving main hall and stage shown here were rebuilt in 1633 and are registered as Edo period.
The main hall has a yosemune (hipped) roof with cypress-bark roofing; the small gables on both sides of the south face and the stage projecting at the center form its main outline.
The Kiyomizu stage stands nearly 13 m above the ground, supported by 18 zelkova columns linked by horizontal tie beams; it was originally used for performances offered to Kannon.

name: Tō-ji
lede: The five-story pagoda of Tō-ji tapers story by story beneath five broad tiled eaves, with a slender spire of rings (sōrin) at the top. About 55 m tall, this timber pagoda is a striking historic building in southern Kyoto, its outline following the tiered eaves and railings of Japanese Buddhist pagodas.
facts: The surviving five-story pagoda was rebuilt in 1644 and is the fifth pagoda on the site, after four fires; it is not registered by the founding date of the temple or of the first pagoda.
The pagoda is a five-story square timber structure with hongawara tile roofing; a complete spire of rings stands above the five broad eaves, and the total height is about 55 m.

Inside the first story, the central pillar (shinbashira) running through all the stories symbolizes Dainichi Nyorai and is surrounded by images of Nyorai and Bosatsu, forming an Esoteric Buddhist space.

era: Begun in the 10th year of Guangxu · Completed in the 32nd year
yearNote: Begun in 1884 and completed in 1906; the drawing shows the street-front exterior in 2023 photographs, which predate the 2025 repairs.
lede: Fujianese merchants brought the bricks, tiles, timber and stone of Quanzhou, and its craftsmanship, to Yantai. Red walls, fire-break gables and swallowtail ridges give this guild hall in a northern port city a distinctly southern Fujian appearance.
facts: The Fujian Guild Hall was funded by Fujianese merchants; work began in 1884 and it was completed in 1906. It is also called the Tianhou Palace.
Its bricks, tiles, timber and stone were procured and worked in the Quanzhou area, then shipped to Yantai for assembly.

name: Nine-Top Pagoda
yearNote: 750 is used only to place it approximately in the Tang on the timeline, not as an exact construction year; the surviving pagoda includes later repairs, and the date of the folk-culture park is not counted as the date of the ancient pagoda.

facts: The Nine-Top Pagoda stands on the site of Jiuta Temple; its surviving main structure is generally identified as a Tang remain, but its exact construction year has not been confirmed in the materials for this batch.
The body is a single octagonal story, with corbeled eaves projecting outward and carrying eight small outer pagodas and one central small pagoda.
The perspective drawing shows only the small pagodas visible from this angle and does not force the back into view; the pagoda was repaired in 1962.

name: Yan Temple of Qufu
era: Fusheng Hall rebuilt in the 2nd year of Zhengde, Ming
yearNote: The plate corresponds to the seven-bay Fusheng Hall as rebuilt in 1507, which continued to be repaired in the Ming and Qing and in 1934, 1978 and 2006; neither the date of the Yan Temple's relocation in the Yuan nor the 1509 construction date of the stele pavilion is used to date this hall.
lede: The Yan Temple is dedicated to Yan Hui, and its main hall, Fusheng Hall, spreads across seven bays beneath a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Carved stone dragon columns and the balustrade of the terrace before the hall give concrete form to the ritual order of a Confucian temple through columns, steps and eaves.
facts: Fusheng Hall was originally a five-bay, double-eaved Yuan building; rebuilt in the 2nd year of Zhengde in the Ming (1507), it became seven bays wide and has since been repaired many times.
Four carved stone dragon columns in the front gallery, together with the other octagonal stone columns, carry a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green tiles; a terrace lies in front of the hall.

The Yan Temple is a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level; the plate shows only Fusheng Hall, which has its own card separate from the Dacheng Hall of the Qufu Confucian Temple.

The cast-iron body is octagonal with nine stories; each story is divided into body, balcony platform, railing and bracketed eaves, giving it the character of a timber pavilion-style tower.

name: Stone Shrine of the Guo Family Tomb on Mount Xiaotang
sub: Eastern Han stone chamber · Modern shelter excluded
yearNote: The plate shows the Eastern Han stone shrine itself inside its shelter; “about the 1st century” is an archaeological dating, not an exact construction year.
lede: A small stone chamber stands inside a later protective building. Its stone slabs imitate the tile ridges and projecting eaves of a Han roof, and the pictorial carvings inside preserve early above-ground architecture and funerary imagery together.
facts: The shrine was built roughly in the early Eastern Han and is one of the earliest surviving above-ground buildings constructed and carved in stone.

“Guo family” is the inherited heritage name; the precise identity of the tomb's occupant is still debated, and legend is not taken as grounds for identifying him as Guo Ju.

name: Qingjing Mosque, Quanzhou
era: Founded in the 2nd year of Dazhong Xiangfu
yearNote: 1009 is the founding year of Qingjing Mosque; the surviving gatehouse has gone through a restoration in the 3rd year of Zhida in the Yuan (1310) and later repairs. The plate shows its present state and does not claim that every stone is Song work.
lede: Entering from Tumen Street means passing through three successively narrowing pointed arches: this is the only surviving stone mosque gatehouse in mainland China. The mosque was founded in 1009, the second year of Dazhong Xiangfu of the Northern Song, under the Arabic name Masjid al-Ashab, the Mosque of the Companions; two lines of Arabic inscription above the arch record that a Muslim merchant from Shiraz rebuilt it in 1310, and the diabase-and-granite gatehouse seen today is essentially what that rebuilding left. The plate shows the gatehouse and the stone wall attached to it; the prayer hall inside is not included.
facts: Form: the gatehouse is 12.3 m high overall and 6.6 m wide at the base, built of diabase and white granite; it consists of three tiers and four connected pointed-arch openings, the first two passages pointed-arched with half-dome vaults and the third domed, with supports under the arches reminiscent of Chinese sparrow braces. The roof is a platform for sighting the moon during Ramadan, and its brick portions were rebuilt in the 17th-18th centuries.

Inscriptions: the Arabic inscription above the arch records that the mosque was built in AH 400 (1009-1010) as the first mosque of the local community, and that some three hundred years later Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Qudsi of Shiraz restored and renewed it, raising a dome, widening the passage and rebuilding the gate, completed in AH 710 (1310-1311). An imperial edict stele of 1407 (fifth year of Yongle) is set into the north wall.

Significance: one of the oldest surviving mosques in China, its gatehouse in West Asian mosque form is physical evidence of the Persian and Arab Muslim merchant quarter of Song-Yuan Quanzhou; the Stele on Re-erecting the Qingjing Mosque written by Wu Jian in 1350 is among the earliest datable Chinese-language stelae of any mosque in China. In 2021 it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site as part of 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.

name: Anping Bridge
era: Begun in the 8th year of Shaoxing · Completed about the 22nd year of Shaoxing
yearNote: Begun in 1138; the Quanzhou Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism records its completion in 1152, while other sources record that it was finished in 1151. The plate shows only one section of the surviving deck and does not let this detail stand for the full length.
lede: 'No bridge under heaven is longer than this one.' In 1138 Huang Hu of Anhai and the monk Zhiyuan each gave ten thousand strings of cash and the monk Zupai directed the building of a bridge across the bay; both died midway, and work stopped for more than a decade until the prefect Zhao Lingjin took office in 1151 and took it over, finishing the bridge the following year. About 2,255 m long and known locally as the Five-Li Bridge, it is the longest surviving sea-crossing beam bridge in stone in China. The plate shows only a stretch of deck and a few nearby piers, not the whole bridge in miniature.
facts: Form: a stone beam bridge running east-west, about 2,255 m long with a deck 2.9-4 m wide, paved with stone slabs and railed in granite; 360 masonry piers of three types, rectangular, single-pointed boat-shaped and double-pointed boat-shaped, chosen to suit the depth and current of each channel, with huge stone slabs 5-11 m long laid across the piers as the deck.

Technique: the pier foundations use the 'sleeping timber' method, with timber piles driven into the seabed, a layer of timbers laid across them, and the stone piers built on top, saving stone and labour compared with the dumped-rock raft foundations of Luoyang Bridge; around the Shuixin Pavilion at mid-bridge survive 16 stelae recording repairs, the earliest the Record of Repairing Anping Bridge of 1459.

Significance: Anping Bridge was the overland node between Quanzhou and the Zhangzhou and Guangzhou regions to the south, built jointly by officials, monks, merchants and townspeople; the Ruiguang Pagoda at the east end, the Shuixin Pavilion at mid-span and the Wanggao and Tingchao gate towers at the two ends still stand. In 2021 it was inscribed as a component of the World Heritage property 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.

lede: The North Pagoda has stacked pavilion stories below, a round drum in the middle and a tall, tapering bell shape on top; beyond the pagoda, the thousand-year history of carving the Yunju Temple stone sutras continues.

“Pagodas and Stone Sutras of Yunju Temple” is the name of the national protected site; the sutras and the pagodas each have their own chronology and cannot be merged into a single construction date.

name: Yongtong Bridge
sub: Zhao County · Single-span open-spandrel stone arch bridge
yearNote: According to the Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau, the bridge was built in the Mingchang reign of the Jin (1190–1195); 1192 is a sorting point within that range, and earlier legends are not used to date the surviving structure.
lede: Each shoulder of a single low stone arch opens into two small arches, and the deck rises gently between stone balustrades. At a smaller scale, Zhao County's Little Stone Bridge carries on the structural language of the open-spandrel stone arch.
facts: This plate shows the full side elevation of Yongtong Bridge, including the main arch, the four small spandrel arches and the stone balustrades.
The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau gives the bridge's construction as the Mingchang reign of the Jin (1190–1195).
The official main span is about 26 m; it is entered separately from Anji Bridge to avoid confusing identical names or aliases.

lede: A tall ground story of carved brick supports thirteen closely set, tapering tiers of eaves. Although Tiangong Temple itself is gone, the coiled-dragon engaged columns and stacked eaves still give this Liao pagoda a fine, close-knit rhythm.
facts: The pagoda stands within the former grounds of Tiangong Temple in Fengrun and was founded in the 8th year of Qingning in the Liao (1062).
The plate shows the whole octagonal thirteen-story multi-eaved pagoda, keeping the Sumeru plinth, the upturned lotus and the coiled-dragon engaged columns.

facts: Shi'en Temple was founded in 1470; its other halls have been destroyed, and the surviving main structure is the Main Hall.

facts: The gate was formally opened and built in the 1st year of Shunzhi in the Qing (1644); the earlier wall and passage have a separate history.

name: Xu Guo Stone Archway
yearNote: The construction year of the stone archway is used; the plate shows only the front elevation of one side of the eight-pillared, four-sided archway.
siteCoordinateSource: Wikimedia Commons分类页所列29°52′03.5″N,118°25′50″E，供歙县地图展示点参考，非测绘成果。
lede: Eight stone pillars enclose a four-sided memorial archway: the Xu Guo Archway turns a flat gateway into a stone space one can walk through. Beams, bracket sets and stone lions are all carved from the same gray stone, and it still stands at a street junction in the old Huizhou town.
facts: Built in the 12th year of Wanli in the Ming (1584) in honor of Grand Secretary Xu Guo, it is also called the Grand Secretary's Archway; it was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1988.

It has four sides and eight pillars: the front and back each have three bays, four pillars and three roofed tiers, and the left and right sides each a single bay, two pillars and three roofed tiers, together enclosing a rectangle; carving covers the stone beams and bracket sets that imitate timber construction.

The plate shows only the front elevation of one side, presenting four front pillars and three passages rather than lining up all eight pillars in a row; inscriptions and the street background are omitted.

name: Zhenfeng Pagoda, Anqing
sub: Yingjiang Temple · Seven-story octagonal brick-and-stone pagoda
yearNote: The pagoda body drawn is dated to the Longqing reign of the Ming and placed at the commonly cited completion year of 1570; local records also give a completion date of 1572. The attached eaves, roofs and finial show the repaired state seen in the photographs.
siteCoordinateSource: Wikimedia Commons分类页所列30°30′13.07″N,117°02′57.48″E，供安庆地图展示点参考，非测绘成果。
lede: Zhenfeng Pagoda stands within Yingjiang Temple on the north bank of the Yangtze, its seven white stories and dark-gray eave bands tapering level by level. Balconies and small arched openings between the stories give the heavy masonry a rhythm that climbs tier by tier.
facts: The surviving pagoda body was built in the Longqing reign of the Ming, with a commonly cited completion date of the 4th year of Longqing (1570); it has been repaired repeatedly since and was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 2006.

It is an octagonal, seven-story pavilion-style brick-and-stone pagoda; beneath the eaves, brick and stone imitations of timber members project outward, and each story has a balcony with railings and arched openings. The attached eave at ground level is not counted as a separate story.

The plate checks the pagoda body and ground-story outline against on-site photographs and takes its colors from more recent ones; the red finial, dark-gray roofs and pale walls are the present state after repairs, not a reconstruction of the Ming original.

name: Huaxi Opera Tower, Bozhou
sub: Great Guandi Temple · Courtyard opera stage
yearNote: The year 1676, when the courtyard opera stage was added, is used rather than 1656, the founding year of the Great Guandi Temple; the woodcarving, painted decoration and roof have undergone later restoration.
siteCoordinateSource: Wikimedia Commons分类页所列33°53′11″N,115°46′03″E，供亳州地图展示点参考，非测绘成果。
lede: Red columns support a roof of blue-green glazed tiles, and pale woodcarving hangs tier upon tier beneath the eaves. Huaxi Opera Tower carves opera scenes into its beams and hanging fascia; it is a guild-hall stage left in Bozhou by medicine merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi.
facts: The Great Guandi Temple was founded in the 13th year of Shunzhi in the Qing (1656); merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi added the opera tower in the 15th year of Kangxi (1676), and it was later enlarged and restored several times. Huaxi Opera Tower was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1988.

The stage sits on the south side facing north and projects into the courtyard; the woodcarving and painted decoration beneath its eaves mostly depict opera stories. The carved-brick gate, the iron flagpoles and the stage woodcarving are separate parts.

The plate shows only the central courtyard stage and the passage beneath it, keeping the material colors of the glazed roof, red columns and hanging fascia; the gate archway and the viewing galleries on either side are not merged into the main subject.

lede: The fifteen multi-eaves of the square brick pagoda project tier upon tier, drawing inward in a soft curve as they rise. The plate takes the upper part of the Tang pagoda at Fawang Temple, keeping the rhythm among the brick eaves, the small round-arched openings and the damaged top.
facts: Subject drawn: The great fifteen-tier square multi-eaved pagoda is chosen from the Fawang Temple pagoda group and registered as a Tang survival; the dates of the nearby Yuan and Qing pagodas are not mixed in.

name: Imperial Tombs of the Northern Song
yearNote: 1063 is the construction date of the Yongzhao Mausoleum, and the subject is an original stone civil official before the tomb; it does not mean that all the Song tombs were built in the same year, nor are the modern reconstructed gate towers counted as Song structures.
lede: Robes falling long and hands holding a tablet of office, the stone civil official stands at attention beside the spirit way of the Yongzhao Mausoleum. Weathering has softened the details but has not erased the solemn, quiet figure of a Northern Song tomb honor guard.
facts: Date of the tomb: The Yongzhao Mausoleum is the tomb of Emperor Renzong of Song, Zhao Zhen, begun in 1063; this entry uses its original stone carvings to represent the Northern Song imperial tombs, without counting the individual tombs separately.

Surviving carvings: The spirit ways of the Song tombs set out a ceremonial order with human and animal statues; the stone carvings are physical evidence for the study of Song sculpture and the imperial funerary system.

Plate scope: The plate shows the first stone civil official from the south in the east row at the Yongzhao Mausoleum; based on on-site photographs from 2025, it keeps the damaged crown, the tablet-holding pose and the stone base, and does not include the modern reconstructed gate towers.

lede: A round-ridge roof spreads above woodcarving and painted decoration, and red door columns frame the dark entrance of the hall. With its worship hall joined to the main hall, Bixia Palace on Mount Fuqiu preserves the dense craftsmanship of a popular Ming–Qing temple.
facts: Construction and repairs: Sources record the main hall's founding as the 21st year of Jiajing in the Ming (1542), followed by many repairs and expansions in the Ming and Qing; the present appearance does not mean every member is original to the first construction.

Hall arrangement: A round-ridge hip-and-gable worship hall at the front joins a main hall with an overhanging gable roof behind; the woodcarving of the front eaves, pierced-carved windows and painted decoration make up a rich facade.

View notes: Drawn from a 2024 frontal on-site photograph of the front worship hall, omitting neighboring halls, trees, offering furnishings and text; the platform edge and side steps are generalized, and the hidden carved central imperial way is not reconstructed.

lede: At the northern foot of the Liupan Mountains, the grottoes are spread along the undulating cliffs. The Tang Maitreya Buddha of Cave 5 faces the valley with broad shoulders, long ears and a full, round face, its drapery still falling gently from the chest.
facts: Dating of the subject: The grottoes were first cut in the late Northern Wei and developed through the Western Wei, Northern Zhou, Sui and Tang; this plate shows the Tang Maitreya Buddha of Cave 5 and does not treat the Northern Dynasties caves as Tang.

The great Buddha: A large seated Maitreya. Materials from the Ningxia Department of Culture and Tourism give its height as about 20.6 m, while another introduction gives 20.06 m; the approximate figure is kept here, without claiming measured precision on the basis of descriptive texts.

Detail drawn: Based on a 2017 on-site photograph, the plate shows the head, the drapery folds on the chest and the knees, keeping the weathering damage; it does not invent the unseen hands, feet or lotus seat, nor reconstruct the painted color.

yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate sorting point for the Western Xia period, not the exact construction year of Tomb No. 3; Tomb No. 3 is generally considered to be Li Yuanhao's Tailing, but the attribution of its occupant is not treated as a proven conclusion.
place: Ningxia · Yinchuan · Xixia District · Eastern foot of the Helan Mountains
lede: At the eastern foot of the Helan Mountains, the rammed-earth tomb tower exposes layer upon layer of weathered shoulders. The original architectural cladding is gone, yet the remaining earthen core still gives this imperial necropolis a sharply defined profile.
facts: Period of the necropolis: The Western Xia Imperial Tombs took shape between the 11th and 13th centuries as the burial ground of the Western Xia imperial house; Tomb No. 3 is generally thought to be associated with the founding emperor Li Yuanhao, and the plate does not treat this presumed occupant as established fact.

Form of the remains: This plate shows only the surviving rammed-earth tomb tower of Tomb No. 3, keeping its taper, banding and irregular damage as photographed; it does not follow the museum's reconstruction model or add eaves and a finial.

World Heritage: The Western Xia Imperial Tombs were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025; the property comprises nine imperial tombs, satellite tombs and related buildings, and flood-control remains, and this plate does not represent the whole necropolis.

place: Ningxia · Wuzhong · Qingtongxia · West bank of the Yellow River
lede: On the west bank of the Yellow River, brick pagodas are ranged row by row down the hillside, spreading from a single pagoda at the top into a triangle. Each pagoda is small, yet together they form an exceptionally striking order within Ningxia's Buddhist architecture.
facts: Twelve rows of pagodas: From top to bottom they are arranged in rows of 1, 3, 3, 5, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17 and 19, totaling 108; the bases and bodies of individual pagodas differ slightly and cannot be treated as identical copies of a single type.

Dating and repairs: The Qingtongxia municipal government's introduction adopts the view of a Western Xia founding, while the 1988 list of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level records them as Yuan; this entry is classified by the founding view and states the discrepancy in registration explicitly, and it does not regard all of the surviving brick cladding as original Western Xia work.

Scope drawn: The plate takes only the top three rows of seven pagodas and the terrace supporting them, emphasizing the larger top pagoda and the 1, 3, 3 arrangement; this seven-pagoda detail is not passed off as a complete panorama of all 108 pagodas.

name: Huangze Temple Cliff Sculptures
sub: Cliff group of five figures, detail
yearNote: The Huangze Temple cliff sculptures are characterized chiefly by Tang works; the exact carving year of the selected niche has not been determined from the image.
place: Sichuan · Guangyuan · West bank of the Jialing River
lede: On the cliff of the west bank of the Jialing, the 'group of five', a Buddha in the centre with disciples and bodhisattvas standing on either side, is the commonest arrangement at Huangze Temple, and the plate takes a detail of one such niche; the niche number has not been verified. The carvings were begun in the late Northern Wei, continued through Western Wei, Northern Zhou and Sui, and reached their peak in the early and high Tang; 57 niches with more than 1,200 figures survive. The temple takes its name from Wu Zetian, and here the caves came first and the temple later. The drawing follows a Tang niche and leaves out signboards and modern railings.
facts: Form: the main image sits in the centre of the niche with a disciple and a bodhisattva on each side, making a group of five; the largest, Cave 28 or the Great Buddha Cave, has Amitabha as its main image, about 6 m high, adds two guardians, and carries the Eight Classes of Beings on the back wall. The five figures in the plate are a detail of one such niche; its number and dimensions were not confirmed from the photograph.

Dating: carving began in the late Northern Wei and continued through Western Wei, Northern Zhou and Sui, peaking in the early and high Tang and declining after the mid-Tang; Yang Xiu, Prince of Shu and son of Emperor Wen of Sui, cut niches here. Listed in 1961 in the first group of Major National Historical and Cultural Sites, it is with Qianfoya among the earliest cave sites of Sichuan.

Significance: like Dunhuang, Huangze Temple had its caves cut before the temple was built; the temple is named for Wu Zetian and holds a stone image said to be her 'true likeness'. Published niche counts differ (47, 50, 57); this entry follows the survey of the Sichuan Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, 57 niches and over 1,200 figures, with subjects including sutra pillars, multi-figure groups, Buddhas of the Three Ages and Sakyamuni and Prabhutaratna seated together.

name: Thousand-Buddha Cliff Sculptures, Guangyuan
yearNote: Work on the Thousand-Buddha Cliff spans several dynasties; the niche drawn has not been confirmed from the photographs as a specific numbered niche.
place: Sichuan · Guangyuan · East bank of the Jialing River
lede: Along 388 m of cliff on the east bank of the Jialing, niches large and small are stacked one above another like a honeycomb. This is one of the earliest cave sites in Sichuan, begun in the late Northern Wei and most active in the Tang; when the Sichuan-Shaanxi highway was blasted through in 1935 about two thirds of the carvings were destroyed, yet more than 950 niches and 7,900 figures remain. The 146 inscriptions on the cliff run from the Wu Zhou period to the Republic, the best known being the merit cave of Wei Kang, inspector of Jiannan, dated 722 (Kaiyuan 10). The plate takes a seated Buddha with attendants from one niche and does not stand for the whole cliff.
facts: Form: the cliff runs 388 m north to south, closely packed with niches above and below; more than 950 niches and 7,900 figures survive, with subjects including Amitabha, Vairocana, Sakyamuni and bodhisattvas. The plate shows a detail of one niche, a seated Buddha with attendants on either side; its number was not confirmed from the photograph.

Dating: carving began in the late Northern Wei; the Northern Dynasties to the Tang were the main period, the Tang the richest, while the Five Dynasties, Song, Yuan and Qing mostly repainted. The cliff carries 146 inscriptions, the earliest of the Wu Zhou period (696–697); the inscription of Cave 513, the Wei Kang cave, is dated 'the seventh day of the sixth month of Kaiyuan 10', and Niche 211 was made by Su Ting. The site was called Baitang Temple in the Tang and renamed Qianfoya in the Yuan.

Significance: there were once more than 17,000 figures; in 1935 the building of the Sichuan-Shaanxi highway blasted away over a hundred metres of cliff, and Liang Sicheng reported to the government that year that 'about two thirds have been destroyed'. Listed in 1961 among the first Major National Historical and Cultural Sites, it was systematically consolidated again after the Wenchuan earthquake of 2008. It is the earliest cave site in south-west China and the largest cave complex in Sichuan.

name: Song Stone Inscriptions in the Suzhou Confucian Temple
lede: A city map carved in stone: on a slab 2.84 m high, the walls of Southern Song Pingjiang, its five land-and-water gates, 359 bridges, 61 wards and 264 lanes are all drawn in single incised lines, canals running parallel to streets in a double chessboard. Carved in 1229, the second year of Shaoding, it is the earliest surviving city plan in China; set against today's old city of Suzhou, Xuanmiao Temple and the twin pagodas of Luohan Cloister still stand where the map places them. The plate only summarises the structure of the map and is not meant as a legible reproduction.
facts: Form: the stele is 2.84 m high, 1.46 m wide and 30 cm thick, carved in single incised lines; the scale is roughly 1:2,500 north-south and 1:3,000 east-west, with walls, bridges and buildings drawn as simplified elevations at their plan positions. The original is kept in the Suzhou Confucian Temple, now the Suzhou Museum of Stone Inscriptions.

Dating: the stele bears no date; the modern scholar Wang Jian checked it against the rebuilding works of 1229 recorded in the Wujun Gazetteer, finding that everything built before that spring and summer appears on the map and nothing built after the autumn does, and so concluded it was carved in 1229, the second year of Shaoding of the Southern Song.

Content and value: the city is a rectangle longer north-south, with land and water gates drawn at each of the five gates, Qi, Lou, Feng, Pan and Chang, and the prefectural seat slightly southeast of centre; the map marks 359 bridges, 61 wards, 264 lanes, 24 alleys and 67 temples, many names still in use. Checked against archaeology and surviving buildings, it shows that Suzhou has been rebuilt again and again on the same site.

name: Bronze and Iron Buddhist Statues of Shengshou Wannian Temple, Mount Emei
sub: Bronze Samantabhadra riding a white elephant
yearNote: The cast-bronze Samantabhadra riding an elephant is a Northern Song survival; the name of the protected site also covers the other bronze and iron Buddhist statues in the temple.
lede: A bronze six-tusked white elephant carries the bodhisattva Samantabhadra; the elephant is taller than a living one, and image and mount together stand 7.85 m high and weigh about 62 tonnes. It was cast in 980 (Taiping Xingguo 5), when Emperor Taizong of the Northern Song granted the gold and sent the eunuch Zhang Renzan to Chengdu to oversee the work; it was cast in sections and carried up to a monastery a thousand metres above sea level, and how it was moved remains a puzzle. The wooden pavilion that once sheltered it burned in 1599 (Wanli 27), and two years later it was covered by the beamless brick hall that still stands. The plate shows this bronze inside the hall, not the modern colossus on the Golden Summit.
facts: Form: a bronze Samantabhadra riding an elephant, 7.85 m high in all and about 62 tonnes in weight; the bodhisattva is 3.64 m high, wears a two-tiered jewelled crown and sits cross-legged on a lotus seat on the elephant's back, the seat 1.39 m high and 2.22 m across; each of the elephant's four feet rests on a lotus. Above the lotus the alloy is brass, the elephant is bronze, cast in sections, and the elephant's belly and the figure are hollow to hold sutras.

Dating: the Southern Song Fozu tongji of Zhipan records that in the first month of 980 (Taiping Xingguo 5) Zhang Renzan was ordered to Chengdu to cast a gilt-bronze Samantabhadra; the Emei shan zhi says the monk Maozhen of Baishui Temple, after an audience at court, was granted three thousand liang of gold for the casting. The scholar Hu Zhaoxi dates completion between 980 and 1012. Listed in 1961 as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site under the name 'bronze and iron Buddhist images of Shengshou Wannian Temple on Mount Emei'.

Significance: the beamless brick hall housing the bronze was built in 1601 (Wanli 29) with gold granted by the Empress Dowager Cisheng, a brick-vaulted structure in the manner of Indian temples using no timber at all; when Wannian Temple burned in 1946 this hall alone survived, and the bronze with it. The protected site also includes other bronze and iron images in the temple, such as the three bronze Buddhas cast by the monk Biechuan in 1534 (Jiajing 13), none of which appears in the plate.

name: Humble Administrator's Garden
sub: Hall of Distant Fragrance, present state
era: Garden created 1509 · Most surviving buildings from the Qing
yearNote: 1509 is the year the garden was created, and most surviving buildings were rebuilt after the 10th year of Xianfeng in the Qing; 1860 is only an approximate sorting point for the garden's present Qing state, not the exact construction year of the Hall of Distant Fragrance.
lede: The Hall of Distant Fragrance is a 'four-sided hall': no walls on any side, only floor-length lattice windows, so that from inside the lotus pond, the islands and the two small pavilions become pictures framed in the openings. It stands on the site of the Ming Ruoshu Hall, three bays wide, with a broad terrace on the north reaching the water, and is the main hall of the garden's central section. The garden began in 1509, the fourth year of Zhengde, but most of today's halls were rebuilt after 1860: in the Tongzhi era the site served first as the Loyal King's palace, then became the Eight Banners guild hall, and was repaired again in 1887, the layout surviving since. It was inscribed as World Heritage in 1997.
facts: Form: a four-sided hall three bays wide, built on the site of the Ruoshu Hall of the Ming Wang family garden; floor-length lattice windows on all sides open the view in every direction, and a broad terrace on the north reaches the pond, facing across the water the two islands that carry the Xuexiang Yunwei and Daishuang pavilions. The name board was originally written by Shen Deqian of the Qing, destroyed in the Cultural Revolution, and is now a replacement by Zhang Xinjia.

Dating: the garden was founded in 1509; the central section is what survives of the late-Qing Eight Banners guild hall, established in 1872 and repaired in 1887, and most of the existing buildings were rebuilt after 1860, the tenth year of Xianfeng. The hall was shaken and damaged by bombing in 1937 and thoroughly repaired in 1980.

Value: the central section covers about 18.5 mu, centred on a pond that takes up roughly a third of the area, with every pavilion built at the water's edge, and it still keeps the solid, open and uncluttered layout of a Ming garden; it was listed among the first national key protected sites in 1961 and inscribed with the other classical gardens of Suzhou as World Heritage in 1997.

name: Luding Bridge
sub: Iron-chain bridge span and abutments on both banks
era: Bridge built in the Kangxi reign · Battle of 1935
lede: Thirteen iron chains span the Dadu River, nine laid as the deck and four as rails, made of more than twelve thousand flat iron links; each chain is over 127 m long and weighs about two and a half tonnes, and its ends run into wells six metres deep behind the stone abutments on either bank, locked to cast-iron 'earth-dragon' and 'sleeping-dragon' piles. Work began by imperial sanction in 1705 (Kangxi 44) and the bridge was finished the next year; before it the river could only be crossed by bamboo or rattan ropes or by ferry. On 29 May 1935 twenty-two Red Army soldiers crawled along the chains to seize the bridge, and it entered another history. The plate shows the chain bridge and the abutments on both banks.
facts: Form: an iron-chain suspension bridge of 101.6 m span and 2.8 m width, its deck about 14.5 m above low water; of the 13 chains 9 form the deck and 4 the handrails, the deck chains 33 cm apart and covered with cross-planks and eight runs of longitudinal boards; each chain is 127.45 m long, weighs about 2.5 tonnes and is made of eight or nine hundred flat links. The abutments on both banks are of dressed stone, 20 m high, with timber bridge pavilions on top.

Dating: begun in 1705 (Kangxi 44) and completed in 1706 (Kangxi 45); because it was built by the Kangxi emperor's sanction it was once called the 'Imperial Bridge'. The eastern pavilion holds the Kangxi stele 'Imperial Record of Luding Bridge' telling how it was built, and on the west stands a stele with 'Luding Bridge' in the emperor's own hand. After a new bridge on the Sichuan-Tibet highway opened in 1950 it ceased to carry traffic, and the whole bridge was restored in 1977.

Significance: the chains are anchored in wells 6 m deep behind the abutments, to seven or eight 'earth-dragon' piles and a 'sleeping-dragon' pile weighing 1,800 jin, so that the mass of abutment and piles together takes the pull, the mature practice of Qing iron-chain bridges. On 29 May 1935 the Central Red Army 'took Luding Bridge by storm'; bridge and battle together were listed in 1961 among the first Major National Historical and Cultural Sites.

yearNote: 1163 is placed according to the official Hangzhou record of the reburial; the plate shows the burial mound, tombstone and offering altar seen today, whose stone elements have been repaired in later periods and are not regarded as entirely original Southern Song work.
lede: The burial mound and stones below Qixia Ridge preserve the memory of Yue Fei after his death. The plate focuses on the present state of the area in front of the tomb and does not treat the whole Temple of King Yue as the tomb.
facts: Official Hangzhou sources record that after Yue Fei was exonerated, he was reburied at the present site in 1163, and a shrine was built in 1221.

The present tombstone, offering altar and stonework have been repaired in later periods; the plate does not reproduce the inscriptions, nor does it date the offering altar as original Southern Song structure.

name: Kinkaku-ji
yearNote: The timeline uses 1955, the year the surviving Shariden was rebuilt; the original structure from the time of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu burned down in 1950.
lede: Beside the Kyōko-chi pond, the three-story Golden Pavilion stacks floors of differing styles. The Shariden seen today was rebuilt in 1955 according to old records, and its gold-leaf surface has undergone later repairs.
facts: The Shariden of Rokuon-ji, popularly called the Golden Pavilion, was originally associated with Ashikaga Yoshimitsu's Kitayama villa; it was destroyed by fire in 1950, and the present building was rebuilt in 1955.
The first floor is the Hōsui-in, the second the Chōondō and the third the Kukyōchō; the second and third floors are covered in gold leaf, and a phoenix stands on the roof.
The plate focuses on the surviving three-story Shariden and does not record the reconstruction as a Muromachi original untouched by fire.
