name: Ginkaku-ji
yearNote: Temple records state that the ridgepole of the Kannon-den was raised in 1489 and that it was still unfinished when Ashikaga Yoshimasa died in 1490; the timeline marks the documented year of the ridgepole raising and does not presume a completion year.
lede: The Silver Pavilion was never covered in silver leaf. Amid the tree shadows and pond water of Higashiyama, the two-story Kannon-den retains its dark timber frame, broad eaves and upper-floor window lattices; it is a surviving pavilion of the Muromachi period.
facts: Construction of Ashikaga Yoshimasa's Higashiyama villa began in 1482, and the ridgepole of the Kannon-den was raised in 1489; Yoshimasa did not live to see it completed.
The Kannon-den is a surviving Muromachi-period pavilion and garden building and has since been repaired; the plate is based on its present state.
“Silver Pavilion” is a popular name; the building is in fact the Kannon-den of Jishō-ji and should not be drawn in silver because of its name.

name: Sensō-ji
yearNote: The timeline marks the 1958 completion of the reinforced-concrete main hall seen today, rather than the temple's founding legend or the old Edo-period main hall.
lede: The broad roof of Sensō-ji's main hall bears down on a deep, long veranda, and worshippers walk from Nakamise toward the Kannon Hall. The surviving main hall is a religious building rebuilt after the war.
facts: The original main hall, a National Treasure, burned in the 1945 air raids on Tokyo, and the present main hall was completed in 1958.
Official temple records state that the present main hall has a reinforced-concrete structure and an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof; the roof was re-covered with titanium tiles in 2010.
The plate shows only the front of the main hall and does not mix in the Kaminarimon, rebuilt in 1960, or the five-story pagoda, rebuilt in 1973.

name: Himeji Castle
lede: White plastered walls rise tier upon tier above the stone ramparts, and the gables and dark tiled eaves of the main keep overlap into the silhouette of the “White Heron Castle.” The plate takes the surviving main tower as its subject.
facts: Ikeda Terumasa carried out a large-scale rebuilding of Himeji Castle from 1601, and the five-tiered main keep was completed in 1609.
The castle also has smaller keeps, connecting turrets, gates and baileys; the plate shows only the main keep and the high stone wall supporting it.
The surviving keep has undergone repairs in the Shōwa and Heisei eras; 1609 is the completion year of the main structure, not the age of all its surface materials.

name: Itsukushima Shrine
sub: Seaside main shrine buildings and corridors
era: Built in the 12th century · Main surviving buildings rebuilt in 1241
yearNote: The UNESCO evaluation records that the main surviving shrine buildings were rebuilt in 1241; the main shrine complex has undergone repeated repairs and additions, and the timeline point indicates only the rebuilding phase of the main surviving structures.
lede: Vermilion shrine buildings and corridors stand over the tide, their roofs unfolding layer upon layer along the shore. The plate chooses the seaside buildings of the main shrine and does not let the great torii in the sea stand in for the shrine buildings.
facts: Taira no Kiyomori promoted the building of Itsukushima's shrine halls over the sea in the 12th century, and today's layout preserves the style of that time.
The main surviving shrine buildings were rebuilt after a fire in 1223, with the work completed by 1241; the individual buildings have since undergone separate repairs.
The plate shows the low shrine buildings, the vermilion colonnades and the corridors from the sea side; its scope is the building complex, not a survey of any single hall.

facts: The Ninomaru Palace of Nijō Castle was built in the time of Tokugawa Ieyasu and later extensively renovated in 1624–26 to receive an imperial visit by Emperor Go-Mizunoo.

name: Square Fort and Ming Tower, Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum
yearNote: 1398 places the early Ming mausoleum phase; it does not represent the construction date of every surviving component of the Ming Tower.
lede: A square fortress with a tower on top: the combination began here, and every imperial tomb afterward, at the Ming Tombs outside Beijing and the Qing Eastern and Western Tombs, copied it. The Square City of the Ming Xiaoling is built of huge stone blocks, and the Soul Tower above it is brick, 39.25 m from east to west and 18.4 m deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in yellow glazed tile; the central arched passage leads to the burial mound behind, inside which Zhu Yuanzhang and Empress Ma lie. The tower's roof burnt in 1853 and for more than a hundred and fifty years only the four walls stood; the present roof was added in 2009, so the plate shows what is seen today, not an early Ming original.
facts: Form: the Soul Tower is brick, 39.25 m wide east to west and 18.4 m deep north to south, under a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of yellow glazed tile, its outer walls washed red and inner walls yellow; three arched openings face south and one each faces east, west and north. The Square City below is built of huge stone blocks, its central arched passage leading to an inner court before the mound, from which stepped ramps climb to the tower.

Dating: work on the Xiaoling began in 1381, the fourteenth year of Hongwu, the sacrificial hall and other main structures were finished in 1383, and the whole was completed in 1405, the third year of Yongle; in 1853, in the fighting between Qing and Taiping forces, the timber parts, including the hall and the tower's roof, all burnt. In 2007 the Zhongshan Cemetery Administration decided to rebuild the tower's roof, the State Administration of Cultural Heritage approved it in 2008, and it was completed in July 2009.

Value: the pairing of Square City and Soul Tower with the walled mound took its fixed form at the Xiaoling, and the imperial tombs of the Ming and Qing followed it for more than five hundred years; the mound covers an underground palace cut into the body of Wanzhu Peak, heaped with cobbles and loess into a rounded hill about 400 m across, and magnetic survey in 1998 traced the entrance tunnel east of the tower, about 120 m long. The Ming Xiaoling was inscribed as World Heritage in 2003.
captions: Square Fort and Ming Tower, Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum

name: Sacrificial Hall, Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum
sub: Sacrificial Hall and main stone stairway
lede: From the Bo'ai Gateway to the Sacrificial Hall is seven hundred metres and a climb of seventy-three, and the plan of the whole mausoleum is a bell. Lü Yanzhi won first prize in the design competition of 1925 with this scheme; work began in 1926, the hall was finished in the spring of 1929, and on 1 June that year Sun Yat-sen's coffin was interred. The hall is a stone palace imitating timber: 28 m long, 22.5 m wide and 26 m high, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in blue glazed tile, three arched doors on the front inscribed 'Nationalism, Democracy, People's Livelihood', and fortress-like square turrets at the four corners, a Chinese great roof and a Western tripartite composition laid over one another in a single building.
facts: Form: the hall faces south, a stone palace imitating timber construction, 28 m long, 22.5 m wide and 26 m high; the double-eaved hip-and-gable roof is covered in blue glazed tile with two tiers of stone bracket sets beneath the eaves; the three arched doors on the front carry bronze doors with pierced plum-blossom lattice, the lintels bear Zhang Jingjiang's seal-script 'Minzu', 'Minquan' and 'Minsheng', the band between the eaves holds Sun Yat-sen's inscription 'Righteous Spirit of Heaven and Earth', and each corner has a fortress-like square turret.

Dating: in 1925 the funeral preparatory committee held a prize competition for designs and Lü Yanzhi's scheme took first place; the first phase, covering the hall, the tomb chamber, the terrace and the steps, began on 15 January 1926 and was finished in the spring of 1929, Lü Yanzhi dying of illness that March; the state funeral was held on 1 June, and the whole project was completed by the end of 1931.

Interior and value: inside stand twelve stone columns with reinforced-concrete cores clad in black Qingdao granite; slightly north of centre sits the marble statue of Sun Yat-sen by Paul Landowski, 4.6 m high; the tomb chamber behind is a hemisphere 18 m across and 11 m high. The whole mausoleum is bell-shaped in plan, 700 m horizontally and 73 m in height from gateway to hall, and it is regarded as a representative work of modern China's fusion of Chinese and Western architecture.

name: Luoyang Bridge
sub: Stone beam bridge · Run of piers (detail)
era: Completed in the 4th year of Jiayou
yearNote: Begun in 1053 and completed in 1059; the plate takes only one section and does not use this detail to represent the whole bridge.
lede: At the mouth of the Luoyang River the Song builders did three things that later generations never tired of praising: they dumped rock along the bridge line to form a low submerged dyke as a 'raft foundation', they farmed oysters on the footing stones so that the shellfish cemented the blocks together, and they used the rise and fall of the tide to float stone beams of more than ten tonnes on rafts and set them onto the piers. Begun in 1053 by Wang Shi and others, the bridge was completed in 1059 under the prefect Cai Xiang, and is the earliest surviving sea-crossing stone bridge in China. The plate takes a stretch of several consecutive boat-shaped piers and their beams.
facts: Form: a stone beam bridge running northeast-southwest, now about 731 m long and 4.5 m wide, with 47 spans and 45 stone piers in the main section, built in two parts around the mid-river islet of Zhongzhou; every pier has a boat-shaped cutwater on the upstream side; the deck beams are single slabs of stone up to 11 m long, 0.98 m wide and 0.8 m thick, weighing over ten tonnes.

Dating: in 1053 Wang Shi, Lu Xi and thirteen others jointly began a stone bridge and failed to finish it in three years; between 1056 and 1059 Cai Xiang, twice prefect of Quanzhou, directed its completion and wrote the 153-character Record of Wan'an Bridge, carved on a stele. The bridge was repaired 27 times down to 1993 and came through the great Quanzhou earthquake of 1604 unharmed.

Significance: the earliest surviving sea-crossing stone bridge in China, it opened three centuries of bridge building in Song-Yuan Quanzhou; its raft foundations, oyster-cemented footings and tidal floating of beams were inherited by Anping Bridge and others. Seven stone pagodas from the Song onward and four guardian stone generals survive on the bridge and the islet, and in 2021 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List.

name: Tianhou Temple, Quanzhou
sub: Main hall · Southern Fujian upswept ridges
era: Founded in the 2nd year of Qingyuan
yearNote: 1196 is the founding year of the Tianhou Temple; the main hall has been repaired in successive periods, and the plate shows its present state.
lede: Leaving Quanzhou by the south gate, Deji Gate, one came first to the Tianhou Temple and then went down to the Jin River to put to sea: this was the first stop for sailors paying their respects to Mazu in the Song and Yuan. The temple was built in 1196 as the Shunji Palace; in 1232 the prefect Zhen Dexiu came in person to sacrifice, bringing Mazu into the official cult, and in 1278 the court titled her 'Celestial Consort'. The main hall in the plate is five bays wide under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof with steeply upturned ridges; its surviving main structure took shape in the 19th century, and it sits on a granite platform a metre high.
facts: Form: the main hall is five bays (24.6 m) wide and five bays (23 m) deep under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof with the high upswept ridges of southern Fujian; it stands on a granite platform 1 m above the ground whose four faces carry reliefs of carp turning into dragons, galloping steeds and cranes among clouds. The surviving main structure took shape in the 19th century.

History: founded in 1196 as the Shunji Palace; brought into official ritual after Zhen Dexiu's sacrifice in 1232; Mazu was titled Tianfei in 1278 and the investiture was conducted in 1281 by Pu Shiwen, superintendent of the Maritime Trade Office; Zheng He petitioned for repairs in 1407 and Shi Lang for the title 'Tianhou' in 1684; the hall was repaired to its original regulations in 1815 and 1821.

Layout: set at the southern end of the old city, linking the town within to the port without, the temple keeps a front-hall-and-rear-chamber layout formed before the 16th century, with gate, stage, worship court, main hall, rear chamber and dressing tower along the axis on a site of about 6,800 square metres; the rear chamber holds a reused pair of Yuan-dynasty sixteen-sided Hindu diabase columns. Inscribed as World Heritage in 2021.

name: Zhangzhou Stone Memorial Archways · Sanshi Zai'er Archway
yearNote: Sources differ on the exact construction year of the Sanshi Zai'er Archway, so it is placed approximately in the Wanli reign; the plate shows only this archway and does not represent the whole group of four.
place: Fujian · Zhangzhou · Hong Kong Road, Xiangcheng
lede: On Hong Kong Road in the old town of Zhangzhou, two Ming stone archways face each other 28.5 m apart along a north-south line; this is the northern one. In 1619 the court raised it to honour Jiang Mengyu, Right Vice Minister of Personnel at Nanjing, together with his father and grandfather, three generations in all; the two faces of the tablet read 'Three Generations of Vice Ministers' and 'Served with Distinction in Both Capitals'. It is 8.09 m wide and 11 m high, three bays, five roofs and twelve columns, built of alternating grey-green and white stone, a representative use of southern Fujian stone carving in a commemorative gateway.
facts: Form: a stone archway of three bays, five roofs and twelve columns, 8.09 m wide and 11 m high, oriented north-south; built of alternating bluestone and white stone, with fish-shaped ridge ornaments on the roofs, upturned eave corners, and beams and lintels dividing the tiers below the main tablet; brackets, sparrow braces, panels and hanging posts are all carved in stone.

Date: according to the Fujian Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau the archway was erected in 1619, the 47th year of Wanli, to honour Jiang Mengyu, Right Vice Minister of Personnel at Nanjing, and his father and grandfather; the main tablet is inscribed in regular script 'Sanshi Zai'er' on one face and 'Liangjing Yangli' on the other. The 'Minister and Third-Place Graduate' archway just to the south, for Lin Shizhang, is fourteen years older.

A set of four: the national heritage listing 'Zhangzhou Stone Archways' comprises the two Ming archways on Hong Kong Road and two Kangxi-era archways for military commanders on Yuekou Street; the panels of the latter even carry carved foreigners with curly hair and hats, a reflection of overseas trade in the Yuegang era. The plate shows only the Sanshi Zai'er archway.

name: Jiangdong Bridge
yearNote: Built 1237–1241; the bridge was repeatedly repaired in later periods, and the plate shows a surviving section of stone beams and piers.
place: Fujian · Zhangzhou · North Stream of the Jiulong River
lede: Each stone beam is twenty-two or twenty-three metres long and weighs close to two hundred tonnes; how craftsmen eight centuries ago set them onto piers in a racing current was something the bridge engineer Mao Yisheng, writing in 1962, still called 'not fully understood'. Jiangdong Bridge, formerly Hudu Bridge, was rebuilt in stone after the timber bridge burnt in 1237, at the urging of the Zhangzhou prefect Li Shao, and took a little over three years. Today only five intact piers on the west bank, two spans of deck and nine ruined pier bases remain, with a 1970 road bridge carried above them. The plate takes a surviving stretch of beams and piers.
facts: Form: a multi-span stone beam bridge. Surviving are 5 intact piers, two spans of original deck, 9 ruined pier bases and the east and west abutment walls, a remnant 100.35 m long; the piers are built of interlocking stone blocks 0.35 x 0.4 x 5.2 m into a ship's-prow shape, 11.4 m long and 5.3 m wide; each span carries 3 to 5 stone beams 22-23 m long, 1.15-1.5 m wide and 1.3-1.6 m thick, weighing nearly 200 tonnes.

Dating: a pontoon bridge was laid here in 1190 and the prefect Zhuang Xia replaced it in the Jiading era with a timber bridge on stone piers; after the timber bridge burnt in 1237 the prefect Li Shao urged a stone rebuilding, completed in a little over three years. The Longxi County Gazetteer records it as 'twenty chi wide and two thousand chi long' with fifteen openings. In 1970 a reinforced-concrete road bridge was raised on top of the old bridge.

Significance: counted with the Luoyang, Anping and Longjiang bridges as the four great stone bridges of Fujian, its beams are of a size rare in the history of bridge building anywhere, and Joseph Needham's Science and Civilisation in China calls it 'an interesting historical problem'; Zheng Chenggong defeated Qing forces here in 1652, and Japanese bombing in the war of resistance left only the five piers on the west bank.

name: Guandi Temple, Dongshan
sub: Gate tower · Southern Fujian cut-porcelain ridge decoration
era: Founded in the 20th year of Hongwu
yearNote: 1387 is the temple's founding year; the plate takes the surviving gate tower and entrance, and the ridge decoration and buildings have been repaired.
lede: The temple gate is not a wall but a pavilion carried on six stone columns, known locally as the Taizi Ting. The three columns on either side lean slightly inward to form a triangular brace; above them close-set bracket clusters carry a palace-style pavilion roof whose ridges are covered in jianci diao, cut-porcelain mosaic: shards of coloured ware pieced into the Eight Immortals crossing the sea, auspicious beasts and figures from Tang and Song tales, their colours unfading. The temple was founded in 1387, the twentieth year of Hongwu, and was enlarged and rebuilt in the Zhengde and Kangxi reigns; it is the ancestral temple from which many Guandi temples in Taiwan drew their incense. The plate shows this gate pavilion and the stone steps before it.
facts: Form: the gate is of the pailou type, six round stone columns carrying tiers of brackets and a palace-style pavilion roof, the three columns on each side leaning inward for triangular stability; the roof and ridges are covered with cut-porcelain mosaic, the Eight Immortals and beasts such as qilin, elephant and lion on the front, Tang and Song story figures on the back. The whole temple is three bays wide and six deep, on a site of more than 680 square metres.

Dating: founded in 1387 (Hongwu 20), enlarged from 1508 (Zhengde 3) and completed in 1512 (Zhengde 7), rebuilt in 1680 (Kangxi 19); repeatedly added to since, so that the timberwork is partly Ming and partly Qing and modern. The halls still keep a carved wooden couplet composed by Huang Daozhou and a board inscribed by the Xianfeng emperor reading 'Wanshi renji'.

Significance: together with the Guandi temples at Yuncheng in Shanxi, Luoyang in Henan and Dangyang in Hubei it is counted among the four great Guandi temples of China, and it is the ancestral temple of nearly a thousand Guandi temples in Taiwan. The Taizi Ting, with its leaning columns and bracket sets, has stood through centuries of island typhoons and earthquakes, a representative work in which Minnan builders fused structural mechanics with cut-porcelain ornament.

name: Eryi Building, Hua'an
era: Built in the 5th year of Qianlong
lede: A huge ring 73.4 m across, four storeys and 16 m high, its outer wall 2.53 m thick at the base, yet not the gallery-type round house of the Hakka but a Minnan unit house: sixteen units, each with its own stair running from ground to top, divided from one another by walls and linked only by a concealed corridor along the outer wall. Jiang Shixiong of the fourteenth generation of the Jiang clan began it in 1740, the fifth year of Qianlong, and the work took thirty years. More than two hundred murals and as many painted panels survive inside. The plate shows the rammed-earth face of the outer ring.
facts: Form: a double-ring round tulou; the outer ring is four storeys, 16 m high and 73.4 m in outer diameter, with a wall up to 2.53 m thick. It is divided into 16 units with 213 rooms in all, each unit with its own stair; there is no continuous front gallery, but a concealed corridor runs along the inner face of the outer wall. The single-storey inner ring is joined to each unit by a passage.

Dating: begun in 1740 (Qianlong 5) by Jiang Shixiong, fourteenth generation of the Jiang clan and holder of the honorific 'xiangyin dabin', and completed around 1770 (Qianlong 34), after thirty years. Inside survive 226 murals, 228 painted panels, 349 wood carvings and 163 couplets, direct evidence for the mid-Qing date of its fittings.

Comparison: Eryi Lou combines features of the Hakka inner-gallery type and the Minnan unit type; in 1996 it became the first tulou listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site, and in 2008 it was inscribed as World Heritage together with the tulou of Yongding and Nanjing as 'Fujian Tulou', of which it is the largest single building by area.

name: Hegui Building, Nanjing County
yearNote: Placed approximately in the Yongzheng reign of the Qing; the traditionally reported year is not treated as a verified construction date for each story.
place: Fujian · Zhangzhou · Pushan Village, Nanjing County
lede: A five-storey square building 21.5 m high, the tallest of all the Fujian tulou, yet built on a swamp. When the Jian clan of Changjiao raised it in 1732 they first drove more than two hundred pine piles into the soft ground, laid timber over them and built a cobblestone footing before ramming up the earth walls; after more than two centuries the building still stands level. Each floor has 28 rooms, 140 in all, with a single door in the middle of the front. The plate takes the five-storey earthen front and the low wall before it, without showing the inner court.
facts: Form: a square tulou of the inner-corridor type, five storeys and 21.5 m high, on a site of 1,547 square metres with a floor area of 3,574 square metres; 28 rooms per floor and 140 in all, one central door and a stair at each of the four corners; the massive rammed-earth outer wall is pierced by close rows of small windows, a defensive form different from the round tulou.

Dating: built in 1732, the tenth year of Yongzheng, by Jian Ciping of the thirteenth generation of the Changjiao Jian clan at a cost of fifteen thousand taels of silver; first raised to four storeys and given a fifth when rebuilt. It stands on marshland, on a foundation of more than two hundred pine piles and timber bedding with a cobblestone wall footing, which is why it has stayed sound for over two hundred years.

Comparison: Hegui Lou is known as the 'tallest' of the Fujian tulou, also called Shanjiao Lou, and is one of the few single tulou listed individually as World Heritage; in 2008 it was inscribed together with Huaiyuan Lou and the Tianluokeng and Hekeng clusters as the Nanjing portion of 'Fujian Tulou'.

name: Hulishan Fort
yearNote: The plate shows part of the surviving Krupp gun emplacement; 1894 is an approximate placement for the fort's late Qing construction phase and does not mean all installations were mounted in the same year.
lede: A Krupp breech-loading coastal gun of 280 mm calibre, thirteen metres long and fifty tonnes in weight, still mounted on the emplacement it occupied more than a century ago: the largest surviving nineteenth-century coastal gun in the world. Hulishan Fort was built on the memorial of Peng Chuhan, commander of the Fujian naval forces, and Bian Baodi, governor-general of Fujian and Zhejiang; work began in the third month of 1894 and finished in the tenth month of 1896, a half-bunker, half-rampart fort commanding the entrance to Xiamen harbour. The plate takes only the Krupp gun and its emplacement on the east battery, not the whole fort.
facts: Form: a fort of half-bunker, half-rampart type with east and west batteries for the main and supporting guns, over 70,000 square metres in all, of which the citadel is over 13,000; the gun platforms are rammed from a mortar of camphor-tree sap, glutinous rice, lime, paper fibre and sand. The surviving east gun has a calibre of 280 mm, a length of 13.13 m and a weight of 50 tonnes, turns through 360 degrees and has a range of 16,000 m.

Dating: begun on the eighth day of the third month of 1894 and completed on the eighth day of the tenth month of 1896, a construction period of two years and eight months; the east gun is marked '28 cm K.L/40 C/87', made by Krupp in Germany in 1887; the west gun was scrapped in the Great Steel Drive of 1958, and the two 150 mm secondary guns were carried off by the Japanese occupying Xiamen in 1938.

Significance: in the late Qing four 280 mm coastal guns were bought from Krupp to strengthen the southeastern coast; the two at Dianguangshan at the mouth of the Min River are gone and this is the only one left at Hulishan, certified in 2000 as the largest surviving 19th-century coastal gun in the world. Its crossfire with the Yuziwei fort on the opposite shore closed the channel, a surviving piece of the Self-Strengthening Movement's coastal defences.

name: Laojun Rock Statue, Mount Qingyuan
sub: Seated Lord Lao · Song stone carving
yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate placement on the Song timeline, not a confirmed carving date for Laojun Rock; the subject is registered under the third-batch listing of the Laojun Rock Statue.
lede: A single natural granite boulder, lightly carved to follow the shape of the rock, became a seated Laozi leaning on an armrest with his beard falling to his chest. The Quanzhou Prefectural Gazetteer puts it plainly: 'the stone image was formed by heaven; enthusiasts merely added a little carving.' At 5.63 m high it is the largest surviving Song-dynasty Daoist stone statue in China. A group of Daoist halls, the Zhenjun and Beidou halls, once stood below Qingyuan Mountain; the buildings are all gone, and only this Laojun remains seated at the foot of the hill, looking south over Quanzhou and the Jin River.
facts: Form: carved from one free-standing natural granite boulder, 5.63 m high, 8.01 m wide and 6.85 m deep; the Old Lord has a bald, high forehead, ears reaching his shoulders and a flowing beard, wears a Daoist robe with overlapping lapels and sits on the ground, right hand on an armrest, left hand on his knee, legs folded, the robe folds rendered in a few clear lines. The stone armrest shows Yuan-dynasty furniture features and is probably a later addition.

Dating: He Qiaoyuan's Minshu records that Zhu Xi visited this 'Yuxian Rock', so the statue existed by the 12th century; stone building members excavated around it, including cap-blocks with wedge tenons and arch keystones, match the work of the Southern Song twin pagodas of Kaiyuan Temple and the Liusheng Pagoda, the archaeological basis for dating it to the Song.

Significance: the largest surviving Song Daoist stone sculpture in China, which together with the Confucian Temple represents the native mainstream culture behind the Song-Yuan port of Quanzhou; it is the largest of the seven groups and nine Song-Yuan stone statues on Qingyuan Mountain, and in 2021 was inscribed as one of the 22 component sites of the World Heritage property 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.

name: Fuzhou Confucian Temple
era: Present structure from the Xianfeng reign
yearNote: The Confucian Temple has earlier origins; the Dacheng Hall is placed approximately by its 1851–1854 construction phase, and the plate shows its present state after the 2026 restoration.
lede: In the eighth month of 1851 a fire destroyed the Fuzhou Confucian Temple; rebuilding began that twelfth month and was finished in the sixth month of 1854, and what stands today is that layout. The Hall of Great Achievement is seven bays wide and four deep under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, on a stone platform a metre and a half high; a ring of twenty-two stone eave columns runs under the lower eaves, the eight stone interior columns weigh about nine tonnes each, and timber columns are jointed onto the stone column heads, a Fujian practice of mixing stone and timber. At the end of 2025 it completed its first major repair in the more than 170 years since the rebuilding.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and four deep, with a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, 19.6 m high, standing on a stone platform 1.46 m above the forecourt; the lower part of the column-and-tie timber frame is stone, 22 stone eave columns and 8 stone interior columns, with 18 full-height timber columns jointed above their heads; between the upper and lower eaves are 42 bracket sets of five tiers and eight layers, and the ceiling well is painted with a star chart.

Dating: in 773 the commissioner Li Yi moved the prefectural school here, a temple to Confucius was first made in the Taiping Xingguo era of the Song, and the Hall of Great Achievement was built in 1374; fire struck on the third day of the eighth month of 1851, and the surviving temple was built between the twelfth month of 1851 and the sixth month of 1854. The year-long major repair of 2024-2025 was the first in more than 170 years since the rebuilding.

Layout: the surviving temple covers 7,552 square metres with about 4,000 square metres of buildings; along the axis from south to north are the outer forecourt, Lingxing Gate, the half-moon pool, Dacheng Gate, the moon terrace and the Hall of Great Achievement, flanked by galleries, official halls and shrines to local worthies; the hall's floor area ranks among the largest of its kind in China, and inside stand bluestone seated figures of Confucius and his four attendants with the seventy-two disciples.

name: Dacheng Hall, Tainan Confucian Temple
yearNote: 1665 marks the founding of the temple and school, and the Dacheng Hall was enlarged in 1712; the surviving hall was dismantled, restored and rebuilt in 1917, and the timeline is placed by the most recent large-scale restoration of the present main structure.
lede: Swallowtail ridges sweep upward, and beneath two tiers of red-tiled eaves stands the Dacheng Hall of the Confucian Temple. The Tainan Confucian Temple dates from 1665; the hall seen today has gone through Qing enlargement and a modern dismantling and restoration.
facts: In 1665 Chen Yonghua oversaw the founding of the Temple of the Former Teacher; during a major rebuilding in 1712, the Dacheng Hall, the Qisheng Shrine and other buildings were enlarged.

In 1917 the Dacheng Hall and other buildings were dismantled and restored. The plate shows the front of the surviving Dacheng Hall and does not take the 1665 founding as the date of all its surviving components.

The two tiers of eaves, the paired dragons and central ornament on the ridge, the vermilion columns of the front veranda and the central stone steps make up the front view; the side corridors to left and right are outside the scope of the plate.

name: Five-Door Hall, Lukang Longshan Temple
yearNote: The temple moved to its present site in 1786, and the 1831 renovation established its scale; the plate shows the present state of the Five-Door Hall after component replacements in the 1960s and later restoration, and does not date every column and beam to the Qing.
lede: The Five-Door Hall stretches wide, its raised central red-tiled ridge joining the lower side eaves in an undulating outline. It is the gate hall that follows the front gate on the way into the main courtyard of Lukang Longshan Temple.
facts: Longshan Temple moved to its present site in 1786 and completed a major renovation in 1831; the Five-Door Hall belongs to the spatial sequence leading from the front gate through the inner courtyard to the main hall.

The front has five openings, with two carved dragon stone columns at the center and a round decorative window on each of the left and right walls. The plate shows only the Five-Door Hall, without the front gate before it or the main hall behind it.

Some eave columns and beams of the surviving Five-Door Hall were replaced in the 1960s, followed by later restoration; the colored plate is based on 2013 photographs showing red clay tiles, gray-white ridge ornaments, gray stone and old timber.

name: North Gate of Taipei Prefectural City
era: Completed in the 10th year of Guangxu (1884)
lede: An arched passage pierces a massive gray stone platform, topped by red walls and a tiled roof with upturned corners. Cheng'en Gate is a Qing city gate surviving from Taipei Prefectural City.
facts: The North Gate of Taipei Prefectural City was completed in 1884, its plaque inscribed "Cheng'en Gate"; the surviving gate is one of the original gates of Taipei Prefectural City.

The stone-built lower platform is pierced by a single arched passage, and the red upper walls carry a single-eaved tiled roof; the round window on the front and the narrow windows on the sides are kept in the plate.
The plate takes an oblique view of the surviving gate from the northwest and shows only the gate tower itself; the demolished barbican and connecting city walls are not reconstructed.

name: Leshan Giant Buddha
yearNote: The timeline is placed by 803, the year the Buddha statue was completed. The plate covers the surviving head down to the chest and abdomen and does not represent the complete 71-meter seated figure.
lede: Tightly coiled snail-shell curls and long ears emerge from the cliff, and below the broad face fall the folds of the robe. Carved over several decades in the Tang, the Leshan Giant Buddha remains joined to the sandstone of Mount Lingyun.
facts: Carving began in 713 and was completed in 803; the plate depicts the present state of the head down to the chest and abdomen.
The Buddha itself is a cliff carving whose image is shaped by the snail-shell curls, long ears and robe folds; the plate does not add the legs or base that the photographs do not include.

The surviving surface has undergone weathering and repeated maintenance. The colored plate follows the pinkish-brown and grayish-brown of the present sandstone and is not a reconstruction of Tang painted decoration.

name: Bao'en Temple, Pingwu
yearNote: Work on the temple began in 1439, its main buildings had taken shape by 1446, and the whole was completed in 1460. The Mahavira Hall is placed at about 1450 within this construction period; no unconfirmed completion date is given for the single hall.
lede: Beneath double eaves, densely set bracket sets support blue-green glazed tiles. The Mahavira Hall of Pingwu Bao'en Temple preserves the open front of an early Ming official-style hall.
facts: Wang Xi and his son Wang Jian oversaw the building of Bao'en Temple; work began in 1439, and the whole temple was completed in 1460.

The Mahavira Hall stands in the temple's second courtyard, forming the main worship space together with the Dabei Hall and the Huayan Repository, which face each other; the plate shows only the front of the main hall.

The five-bay width and the double-eaved hip-and-gable roof serve as the structural basis; the colored plate follows photographs in keeping the blue-green tiles, grayish-brown timberwork and red doors and columns.

name: Wuliang Pagoda
yearNote: The State Council's sixth-batch list dates it to the Song. The timeline position of about 1000 is for placement within the dynasty and is not a confirmed completion year; the traditional attribution to the Jianlong reign is not presented as a proven exact date.
lede: The White Pagoda beside the Jialing River projects eave after eave, its pale body tapering story by story. Built in brick in imitation of a timber pavilion, Wuliang Pagoda leaves the slender outline of an old pagoda of northern Sichuan.
facts: Wuliang Pagoda, also called the Nanchong White Pagoda, stands on Heming Hill in Gaoping District; the sixth-batch national protected site list records its date as Song.
The pagoda is a square, thirteen-story pavilion-style brick pagoda; its eaves diminish gradually, and its carved brick decoration imitates timber architecture.

Accounts of its construction year differ, and this entry gives only an approximate Song placement; the plate is based on photographs of the surviving pagoda and does not reconstruct historical colors.

name: Zhang Huanhou Shrine
yearNote: Diwan Tower belongs to the surviving Ming–Qing shrine complex; about 1600 is only a timeline placement, does not assert that all components were built in the same year, and is certainly not based on the year of Zhang Fei's death.
lede: A raised small tower meets broad lower eaves, and between red columns stands the Diwan Tower of the Zhang Huanhou Shrine in Langzhong. The shrine commemorating Zhang Fei took its present layout through Ming and Qing restorations.
facts: The Zhang Huanhou Shrine is popularly known as the Zhang Fei Temple; the surviving shrine is a Ming–Qing building complex, and the national protected site list likewise dates it to the Ming and Qing.
Diwan Tower is one of the buildings on the shrine's central axis; the plate takes the tower and its connected front eaves and excludes the main hall, the tomb pavilion and Zhang Fei's tomb.

The upper tower, the broad lower eaves and the doors and windows between the columns are rendered from photographs; the visible components have undergone repairs, and no claim is made that all are original Ming fabric.

name: Luodai Guild Halls
era: First built in the Qing · Rebuilt 1913
yearNote: Yuwang Palace was first built in the Qianlong period of the Qing and rebuilt in 1913 after a fire in 1912. The timeline uses the rebuilding year of the surviving main structure and does not follow the parent unit's "Qing" label to mark the present gate tower as original Qianlong work.
lede: Undulating fire walls carry cloud and dragon ornaments, and three arched gateways lead into the Huguang Guild Hall of Luodai. Yuwang Palace is one of the guild halls where migrants who came to repopulate Sichuan kept up hometown bonds far from home.
facts: The Luodai Guild Halls national protected site includes the Guangdong, Huguang, Jiangxi and Northern Sichuan guild halls, among others; the plate shows the gate tower of Yuwang Palace, the Huguang Guild Hall.
The Huguang Guild Hall was first built in the Qianlong period of the Qing and rebuilt the year after a fire in 1912; the date of its present state and its founding date are recorded separately.

Of the gate tower's three arched gateways the central one is taller, and the top of the wall has an undulating outline; the cloud motifs, dragon ornaments and deity figures are simplified from photographs, and the shops along the street are not drawn.

name: Que of Lord Shen
era: Eastern Han stone que · Approximate date
yearNote: The que is an Eastern Han relic; about 150 is a placement within the dynasty on the timeline, not a precise construction date from an inscription. The plate shows only one surviving main que and does not add the lost subsidiary que.
lede: A single sandstone shaft carries tiers of bracket sets imitating timber, with reliefs of birds and beasts on the stone face. The Que of Lord Shen preserves the image of Han timber construction in the stone carving of Qu County.
facts: The Que of Lord Shen was listed in the first batch of national protected sites in 1961 and later merged with the other Han que of Qu County; this subject is still recorded under the first batch, in which it was first announced.
The surviving east and west que form the remains of a spirit-way entrance; the plate takes one of the main que and does not present a single plate as a reconstruction of the whole group.

The form follows a 1914 photograph, and the coloring also draws on modern photographs of the ocher-brown sandstone and the dark gray weathered stone top; the carved decoration has been artistically simplified.

name: Shibaozhai
era: Founded in the Ming · Enlarged in the Qing
yearNote: Founded in the Wanli reign of the Ming and enlarged several times from the Kangxi to the Tongzhi reigns of the Qing; about 1800 places the surviving tower within the dynasty. Sources differ on when the top three stories took shape, and the whole present tower is not dated to 1956.
lede: The vermilion tower climbs against Yuyin Hill, its tiers of upturned eaves narrowing beside the rock face. Shibaozhai binds timber construction tightly to the hill, forming a distinctive vertical silhouette on the bank of the Yangtze.
facts: Shibaozhai was founded in the Ming and enlarged and repaired several times in the Qing; it was listed in the fifth batch of national protected sites in 2001.
The surviving tower consists of nine lower stories and the three-story Kuixing Pavilion above; the timber structure is supported by the hill, with round and square windows alternating.

The plate keeps the surviving twelve stories and the adjoining rock face, omitting the river, the protective embankment and the suspension bridge; an archival photograph of 1909 already shows the upper pavilion, and no enlargement year is forced.

name: Huguang Guild Hall, Chongqing
era: Qing guild hall · Enlarged in the Daoguang reign
yearNote: The guild hall complex took shape in the Qing and was enlarged in the Daoguang reign; about 1846 places the surviving Qing structure, and the plate shows the opera stage as repaired in 2003–2005, without asserting that every beam and column is original 1846 work.
lede: Carved wooden balustrade panels run across the front of the raised stage, and beneath the flying eaves a three-bay stage opens. The opera stage of the Huguang Guild Hall in Chongqing hosted the public life of migrant gatherings, rituals and theatergoing.
facts: The Huguang Guild Hall of Chongqing, in the Dongshuimen area of Yuzhong District, is a Qing complex of migrant guild halls and is now in the sixth batch of national protected sites.

The guild hall was enlarged in the Daoguang reign, and its present state has also undergone modern conservation repairs; the plate takes the front of one opera stage and does not draw the whole group of courtyards.

The balustrade panels, beams and backstage decoration come from photographs; the colored plate keeps the dark brown carved wood, red backstage and bluish-gray tiles, rather than tinting the Qing building uniformly in a dynasty color.

name: Diaoyu Fortress Site
era: Fortifications expanded 1243 · Gate tower built later
yearNote: 1243 is a key milestone in the building of the Southern Song defensive system at Diaoyu Fortress, and the timeline is placed by the site. The upper timber gate tower of Huguo Gate was built later, and not all the structure in the photographs is taken as original Song work.
lede: A thick stone wall is pierced by a single arched opening, and stone steps up to the walls cling to the cliff. Huguo Gate condenses the strategic terrain and mountain-fortress defenses of Diaoyu Fortress into a narrow entrance.
facts: Diaoyu Fortress is the site of a Southern Song mountain fortress, expanded in 1243, that endured a long war of siege defense.
The plate takes the stone gateway of Huguo Gate, the later gate tower and the stone steps in front, keeping the passage along the cliff; it does not reconstruct the whole fortress.
The original fourth-batch national protected site list registered it under "Hechuan City, Sichuan Province"; it now lies within Chongqing, and the page uses Chongqing as its region.

name: Cliff Carvings of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan
era: Head carved in the Tang · Whole statue completed 1151
yearNote: The Buddha's head was carved in the Tang and the body continued in the Northern Song, with the whole statue completed in 1151; the surviving gold leaf includes the results of conservation and restoration in the 2010s, and the timeline is not placed by the temple's founding year.
lede: Gold leaf covers the broad face and flowing robe folds, and dark snail-shell curls set off the Great Buddha's calm. The head and body of the Tongnan Great Buddha were carved in turn, and the seated figure was completed only after spanning the Tang and Song.
facts: The head was carved first, the body was continued in the Northern Song, and the whole statue was completed in 1151; the plate takes this Great Buddha and does not represent all the cliff niches and figures of the temple.

The surviving seated figure rests its right hand flat before the abdomen and its left hand on the knee, with snail-shell curls on the head and a kasaya draped over the body; the feet hidden by the offering table are not conjecturally completed.

The gilding has been renewed over the centuries and has undergone modern conservation and restoration. The colored plate follows photographs of the gold leaf and dark snail-shell curls, and this artistic rendering is not a reconstruction of the original Song finish.

name: Zishou Temple, Lingshi
sub: Front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings
yearNote: 1500 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The front of the Heavenly Kings Hall of Zishou Temple is not a row of lattice doors but a solid wall of grey brick with a single doorway in the middle, over which hangs the plaque 'Secluded Delight of Hills and Woods'; the grey-tiled roof is edged in blue-green glaze and the main ridge is crowded with glazed pavilions and beasts. The temple is at Suxi village in Jingsheng town, Lingshi; steles record its founding in 870 (11th year of Xiantong, Tang), destruction by fire at the end of the Jin, rebuilding in 1467 (3rd year of Chenghua, Ming), large-scale repair in 1521 (16th year of Zhengde) and its present extent by 1622 (2nd year of Tianqi), the surviving halls all being Ming. The plate shows the front of the Heavenly Kings Hall.
facts: Heavenly Kings Hall: as drawn, a single-eaved hall whose front is a brick wall without lattice doors, with one central door, a pair of stone lions before it, bracket sets under the eaves, a grey-tile roof with glazed edging and a glazed main ridge; bell and drum towers stand to either side, and inside, along both sides, four Heavenly Kings about 3 m tall.

Dating: founded in 870 (11th year of Xiantong, Tang), burned at the end of the Jin, repaired in the Yuan, rebuilt in 1467 (3rd year of Chenghua, Ming), repaired in 1521 (16th year of Zhengde) and brought to its present form in 1622 (2nd year of Tianqi); about 17,000 square metres in two courts, front and rear. Listed as a national key protected site in 2001.

Loss: the temple is known for its Ming painted sculpture and murals, with 248.34 square metres of murals and over a hundred statues; in 1993 the heads of its eighteen arhats were cut off, stolen and sold abroad, later bought back and returned by the Taiwanese businessman Chen Yongtai, one of the cases of lost Shanxi relics coming home.

name: Ruicheng City God Temple
sub: Gable side of the main hall
era: Original Song structure · Repaired over the centuries
yearLabel: Original Song structure · Repaired over the centuries
yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted gable side of the main hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The earliest surviving City God temple in Shanxi. Its main hall is a Song structure under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with five-puzuo bracket sets and two downward cantilevers of split-bamboo profile on the front column heads; seen from the gable end, a Ming glazed panel of 'two dragons playing with a pearl' is set in the gable, the owl-tail finials and ridge ornaments are glazed too, while below is plain red wall. Known locally as the 'South Temple', it was founded according to the Republican-era Ruicheng County Gazetteer in the Dazhong Xiangfu reign of the Northern Song (1008-1016) and repaired under the Yuan, Ming and Qing; on the axis the offering pavilion is Yuan and the offering hall and rear hall Qing, so four dynasties of carpentry stand in one court. The plate shows the gable end of the main hall.
facts: Main hall: five bays wide and three deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the front column-head bracket sets are five-puzuo with two downward cantilevers of split-bamboo profile and grasshopper-head beam ends; the gable carries a Ming glazed panel of two dragons playing with a pearl, the glazed owl-tails and ridge ornaments are bright in colour, and the red wall sits on a grey-brick dado.

Dating: according to the Republican-era Ruicheng County Gazetteer the temple was founded in the Dazhong Xiangfu reign of the Northern Song (1008-1016) and repaired in the Yuan, Ming and Qing; the main hall is original Song work, the offering pavilion Yuan, the offering hall and rear hall Qing, and the gate, stage and bell and drum towers recent rebuildings. Listed as a national key protected site in 2001.

Steles: the stele gallery displays 98 steles and image steles from the Northern Wei to the Ming and Qing, among them the Preface to the Jingyuan Daoist Hall of Mount Zhongtiao of 798 (14th year of Zhenyuan, Tang), composed by Wang Yan, prefect of Guozhou, and written by Yuan Zi; the offering pavilion, a four-rafter hall with two columns spanning the full depth, has massive architraves and leaning corner columns, typical of Yuan work, and is not in the plate.

name: Qiao Family Compound
sub: Inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard
yearNote: 1800 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The proper name of the Qiao Family Compound is Zaizhongtang, the residence of the Shanxi merchant Qiao Zhiyong. An eighty-metre stone walk divides six large courts into a northern and a southern row, and seen from above the whole house forms the character for double happiness; each court is a long narrow one like this, wing rooms on both sides closing in the yard and a two-storey main house at the far end. Building began in 1755 (20th year of Qianlong, Qing), with enlargements in the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns, and the present extent was reached only in the early Republic, so any single court can be dated only approximately. The plate shows the end house and the flanking wing rooms of one court of Zaizhongtang.
facts: Courts: Zaizhongtang covers 10,642 square metres with six large courts, twenty small ones and 313 rooms; the main gate faces east, an arched gateway with a tower above. As drawn, the two sides are single-storey wing rooms and the end house is two storeys with an upper gallery, grey brick walls, lattice doors and brick carving and painting under the eaves stacked tier on tier.

Dating: begun in 1755 (20th year of Qianlong, Qing), enlarged in the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns and completed in the early Republic; the courts were built in stages and no single court has a firm completion date. Listed as a national key protected site in 2001; made the Qixian Folk Museum in 1985 and opened the next year.

Family: the Qiaos rose from Qiao Guifa, who 'went west beyond the pass' to Baotou in the early Qianlong years and founded the Fushenggong firm, giving rise to the saying 'first Fushenggong, then Baotou city'; under Qiao Zhiyong the firm's branches spread far and wide. The Dexingtang, Ningshoutang, Baoyuantang and garden are recent reconstructions on their old sites and are not in the plate.

name: Wang Family Compound
sub: Courtyard walls and roofs of Hongmen Fort (detail)
yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted courtyard walls and roofs of Hongmen Fort on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The Hongmen Fort of the Wang Family Compound is a fort in earnest: a wall eight metres high and two thick encloses a circuit of over six hundred metres, inside which eighty-eight courtyards climb the slope in four tiers with a single main street running up the middle, so that the plan resembles the character wang. Seen from above, grey-tiled roofs, brick courtyard walls, openwork screen walls and one small gatehouse after another pile up in layers, and that is the corner the plate takes. Hongmen Fort, also called Hengzhen Fort, was built in the Qianlong reign of the Qing and housed eight generations of the Jingsheng Wangs, from the fourteenth to the twenty-first; the compound as a whole went up over nearly ninety years from the Kangxi to the Jiaqing reigns.
facts: Fort: Hongmen Fort, or Hengzhen Fort, is the west compound of the Wang Family Compound, laid out on the hillside in four tiers of courtyards from low to high, symmetrical left and right, with 88 courtyards and 776 rooms in all; the wall is 8 m high, 2 m wide and over 600 m round, and the south gate bears the stone plaque 'Hengzhen'. The plate shows the layering of roofs, screen walls and courtyard gates inside the fort.

Dating: Hongmen Fort was built in the Qianlong reign of the Qing, and Gaojiaya to its east in the Jiaqing reign by the brothers Wang Rucong and Wang Rucheng of the seventeenth generation; the compound was built mainly over nearly 90 years from Kangxi to Jiaqing, with 123 courtyards and 1,118 rooms. Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Family: the Jingsheng Wangs moved here as farmers in 1313 (2nd year of Huangqing, Yuan), took to trade in the Ming, grew rich on salt and tea in the Qing, and declined after the fall of Yangzhou in 1853 (3rd year of Xianfeng). The total area is given as 150,000 or 250,000 square metres, making it one of the largest Qing residential complexes in Shanxi.

name: Dai County Confucian Temple
sub: Front and platform of the Dacheng Hall
era: Ming–Qing buildings · Repaired over the centuries
yearLabel: Ming–Qing buildings · Repaired over the centuries
yearNote: 1500 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front and platform of the Dacheng Hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The largest surviving prefectural Confucian temple in north China. The Dacheng Hall is seven bays wide and ten rafters deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof entirely covered in peacock-blue glazed tile, with nine-step bracket sets of one upward and three downward cantilevers under the eaves and a row of front lattice doors in twelve different patterns; it stands on a white-marble platform with stone balustrades on three sides and a carved dragon ramp in the centre. The temple is said to have been founded in the Tang; it was rebuilt from 1367 (27th year of Zhizheng, Yuan) and completed in 1369 (2nd year of Hongwu, Ming), enlarged in the Chenghua and Jiajing reigns and repeatedly repaired in the Qing, the surviving fabric being mainly Ming. The plate shows the front of the Dacheng Hall and its terrace, with the steles in the foreground omitted.
facts: Dacheng Hall: seven bays wide (five according to the Daixian county government page), ten rafters deep, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof in peacock-blue glazed tile; nine-step bracket sets with one upward and three downward cantilevers under the eaves; front lattice doors in twelve patterns; inside, a caisson ceiling converging on an eight-trigram apex, square, octagonal and round tiers carried on four layers of brackets.

Dating: traditionally founded in the Tang, destroyed by war at the end of the Yuan, rebuilt from 1367 (27th year of Zhizheng) and completed in 1369 (2nd year of Hongwu, Ming), enlarged in the Chenghua and Jiajing reigns and repeatedly repaired in the Qing; it survived after 1949 by serving as a granary. The National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Ming to Qing; listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Layout: about 14,400 square metres in four courts, the axis running Wanren archway, Lingxing gate, Pan pool, Ji gate, Dacheng Hall and Jingyi pavilion, with the shrines of worthy officials and local worthies east and west of the pool; the Lingxing gate has six columns and five roofs, its side roofs set with glazed coiled-dragon roundels. The plate takes only the Dacheng Hall.

name: Ciyun Temple, Tianzhen
yearNote: 1450 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the Mahavira Hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The Mahavira Hall of Ciyun Temple is only three bays square under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, its bracket sets stepping out tier on tier beneath the eaves, and inside it keeps over fifty square metres of Ming murals: the twelve bodhisattvas of complete enlightenment on the main wall, the twenty-four devas and the eight classes of beings on the sides. The temple stands on West Street in the county town of Tianzhen; originally Fahua Temple, it was founded in the Tang according to the Guangxu-era Tianzhen County Gazetteer, repaired in 1019 (8th year of Kaitai, Liao) and again from 1428 to 1430 (3rd to 5th years of Xuande, Ming), when the chiliarch Xiong Liang petitioned for the name Ciyun Temple, 'the great monastery north of the pass'; today's layout is that left by the Xuande repair. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall and the steps before it.
facts: Mahavira Hall: also called the Sakyamuni Hall, three bays wide and deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, standing on a high platform reached by a central stone stair, with dense bracket sets under the eaves as drawn; inside are over 50 square metres of Ming murals and a seated Sakyamuni flanked by the Medicine Buddha and Amitabha.

Dating: the Guangxu-era Tianzhen County Gazetteer records that the temple was 'built in the Tang, originally named Fahua', repaired in 1019 (8th year of Kaitai, Liao), rebuilt from 1428 to 1430 (3rd to 5th years of Xuande, Ming) and granted the name Ciyun Temple, with further repairs in 1539 (18th year of Jiajing, Ming) and 1761 (26th year of Qianlong, Qing). Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Bell and drum towers: the bell and drum towers before the Heavenly Kings Hall are octagonal in plan with round domed roofs, a brick chamber ringed by eight columns below and an open railed storey above, a form found nowhere else among Yuan and Ming bell and drum towers in Shanxi; the bell tower hangs an iron bell of 1432 (7th year of Xuande, Ming). The temple has 31 surviving buildings on about 1.6 hectares.

name: Wuyue Temple, Jiexiu
yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the opera stage on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: The Wuyue Temple of Jiexiu merges gate, stage and bell and drum towers into one building, known locally as the Haishen Lou, the 'mirage tower'. On the courtyard side the upper storey is five bays wide, the central bay pushed forward as the stage front under a small hip-and-gable roof, with the gables of the two wings turned to face front; below are five brick arches, the middle one the passage into the temple. The roofs are of peacock-blue glaze; Jiexiu calls itself the home of glazed tile, and the colour here is among the purest. The temple was founded in 1456 (7th year of Jingtai, Ming), destroyed in 1750 (15th year of Qianlong, Qing) and rebuilt in 1763 (28th year of Qianlong), so the surviving buildings are Qing. The plate shows the courtyard front of the stage.
facts: Stage: built on a high platform, five bays wide, the central bay projecting one bay northward, with elaborate bracket sets under the eaves; the upper stage front has a wooden railing and the gables of both wings face forward, while below a central passage is flanked by four arched openings; gate, stage and bell and drum towers form one body, called the Haishen Lou.

Dating: according to temple steles, founded in 1456 (7th year of Jingtai, Ming), destroyed in 1750 (15th year of Qianlong, Qing), rebuilt in 1763 (28th year of Qianlong) and repaired in 2001; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Qing, and it was listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Glaze: the peacock-blue glazed roof ornaments are pure in colour and fine in form, and the Jiexiu cultural heritage bureau calls them another treasure of the 'home of glazed tile'; the temple faces south in two courts on 4,149 square metres, with 13 surviving buildings including screen wall, offering pavilion, main hall and rear hall, the main hall five bays under a flush-gable roof.

name: Pingyao City God Temple
yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the front hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
lede: To enter the Pingyao City God Temple one first passes through a low gateway beneath a tower; over the passage hang the two characters 'Dare you enter', the 'enter' written like a knife. The tower is the stage, the Zhaoge Lou, double-eaved hip-and-gable and three bays wide; on its south face a hip-and-gable baosha projects above the passage, thick with bracket sets, and the bell and drum towers join it on either side. The temple's founding date is unknown; it was repaired after a fire in 1554 (33rd year of Jiajing, Ming), another fire in 1859 (9th year of Xianfeng, Qing) left only the rear hall, and most of the surviving buildings date from the rebuilding of 1864-1869 (3rd to 8th years of Tongzhi). The plate shows the south face of this tower and the passage.
facts: Stage: two storeys under a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, three bays wide, glazed tile; the south plaque reads 'Dare you enter' and the north 'Zhaoge Lou', and the passage beneath leads into the front court; ten earthenware jars are buried under the stage floor to resonate with the ceiling. The bell and drum towers join it east and west; the plate shows the south face and the baosha.

Dating: founding date unknown; repaired after the fire of 1554 (33rd year of Jiajing, Ming), reduced to the rear hall by the fire of 1859 (9th year of Xianfeng, Qing), rebuilt from 1864 to 1869 (3rd to 8th years of Tongzhi), the Procession of the City God painted in the main hall in 1868 (7th year of Tongzhi). Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Layout: the temple and the Pingyao county yamen stand on opposite sides of South Street in east-west symmetry; three courts on 7,302 square metres, the axis running archway, gate, stage, offering hall, main hall and rear hall, with the Six Bureaus and the Earth God shrine on the sides and the Kitchen God and God of Wealth temples east and west of the rear court, 'all the gods dwelling in one temple'.

name: Former Site of Rishengchang
era: Former Qing draft bank · Surviving street frontage
yearLabel: Former Qing draft bank · Surviving street frontage
yearNote: 1823 is the commonly cited year the draft bank opened; the construction year of the surviving frontage itself is undetermined, and the timeline places it approximately by that period.
lede: This row of shopfronts on the south side of West Street in Pingyao was the head office of China's first draft bank. The front is a run of dark wooden plank doors with a line of small painted panels above the lintels and a grey-tiled pitched roof above that, as unassuming as any shop; behind it two parallel courts face north, with a floor area of over 1,700 square metres. Rishengchang was reorganised from the Xiyucheng dye shop; the customary date is 1823 (3rd year of Daoguang, Qing), though the steles allow the reorganisation to be placed only between 1819 and 1838, and no record gives the construction date of the shopfront itself. The plate shows the street front.
facts: Shopfront: the head office stands on the south side of West Street, facing north, with two courts side by side, on 2,324 square metres of land and over 1,700 square metres of floor area; as drawn the front is single-storey, a continuous row of plank doors with a line of small painted windows above and the plaque 'Rishengchang Ji' under the eaves.

Dating: Rishengchang was reorganised from the Xiyucheng dye shop of the Li family of Dapu, with the owner Li Daquan contributing 300,000 taels and Lei Lütai 20,000; a stele of 1819 (24th year of Jiaqing) still lists Xiyucheng and one of 1838 (18th year of Daoguang) no longer does, so the change fell between, conventionally in 1823 (3rd year of Daoguang). Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Influence: Rishengchang pioneered remittance between cities, with branches in Hankou, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou and elsewhere, and by 1891 (17th year of Guangxu) remitted thirty million taels a year; it was sealed in 1914 over a guarantee case and closed in 1932. Pingyao thereby became the financial centre of all China in the nineteenth century, and was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1997.

name: Pujiu Temple Pagoda
era: Rebuilt in the Jiajing reign (Ming) · Thirteen-story brick pagoda
yearLabel: Rebuilt in the Jiajing reign (Ming) · Thirteen-story brick pagoda
yearNote: The surviving pagoda was rebuilt after an earthquake in the Jiajing reign of the Ming; sources differ on the exact year of rebuilding, and the timeline uses an approximate value of around 1560.
lede: In the Romance of the Western Chamber the student Zhang 'climbed the pagoda and walked the whole cloister'; this is that pagoda. A square brick pagoda of thirteen storeys with close-set eaves, 39.5 m high and 8.3 m on a side, its eaves corbelled and its taper slight, it is close in form to the Great Wild Goose Pagoda of Xi'an. In 1555 (34th year of Jiajing, Ming) a great earthquake at Puzhou destroyed temple and pagoda alike; in 1564 (43rd year of Jiajing) the prefect Zhang Jiayin gave his salary to lead the rebuilding, and the pagoda rose six storeys higher than its Tang predecessor to thirteen, the present Yingying Pagoda. The other halls were later lost to fire and rebuilt from 1986 to 1990; the pagoda is the only Ming survivor. The plate shows the whole pagoda.
facts: Form: square in plan, a thirteen-storey brick pagoda with close-set eaves, 39.5 m high and 8.3 m on a side, with a door on the south; the first storey has no windows and a Buddha niche on the north wall, from the second to the ninth storey brick stairs spiral up inside the walls and each storey has window openings; the square cloister round it, eleven bays to a side, was rebuilt after 1986.

Dating: a Ming stele in the temple says Pujiu Temple was 'founded in the Sui and Tang', and an excavated sutra pillar is dated 872 (13th year of Xiantong, Tang); the pagoda fell in the earthquake of 1555 (34th year of Jiajing, Ming) and was rebuilt in 1564 (43rd year of Jiajing) by Zhang Jiayin, whose poem stele stands before it. The pagoda was listed as a provincial protected site in 1965 and a national key protected site in 2019.

Echo: strike a stone on the ground before the pagoda and it answers from within like a croaking frog, for which it is counted among China's four great echoing buildings; Ding Shizhang and others of Shanxi University found the cause in the eaves of each storey, unequal in length and concave, and the smooth surface of the body, which send sound waves back and forth around the pagoda into resonance.

name: Daxiangguo Temple
era: Qianlong rebuilding phase (Qing), not the Northern Qi founding year
yearNote: The Qianlong rebuilding phase of the Qing, not the Northern Qi founding year of the temple.
lede: In 1642 a breach of the Yellow River buried Kaifeng, and Daxiangguo Temple with it, under silt; the halls seen today follow the layout fixed by a rebuilding in 1661 (Shunzhi 18) and a renovation in 1766 (Qianlong 31). The Daxiong Baodian (Mahavira Hall) shown here stands at the centre of the second courtyard: seven bays wide, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, set on a Sumeru-base terrace ringed by stone balustrades whose posts are carved with small lions. The Northern Song complex of sixty-four cloisters is long gone, but the scale of a Qing state-sponsored monastery remains.
facts: Form: the Daxiong Baodian is seven bays wide and five deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of yellow and green glazed tile and a total height of about 13 m. In front lies a Sumeru-base terrace; white stone balustrades surround hall and terrace, their post-heads carved with more than fifty small lions, no two alike.

History: in 712 (Yanhe 1) Emperor Ruizong of Tang bestowed the name Xiangguo Si. After the flood of 1642, the gate, Hall of Heavenly Kings and Daxiong Baodian were rebuilt in 1661 (Shunzhi 18) and renovated again in 1766 (Qianlong 31); the existing halls took their present form then, and Qianlong wrote the plaque 'Imperially Built Xiangguo Si'.

Fortunes: in 1927 troops of Feng Yuxiang destroyed every Buddhist image in the temple except the Thousand-Armed Guanyin and turned the temple into the Zhongshan Market; the main hall long stood empty and was used for exhibitions. In Northern Song the temple governed sixty-four cloisters on 540 mu of land; what stands today is only a corner of that core.

name: Zhengzhou City God Temple
sub: Front of the three-bay main hall
era: Surviving Ming–Qing historic buildings; exact construction year of the individual building unknown
yearNote: Surviving Ming–Qing historic buildings; the exact construction year of the individual building is unknown.
lede: The best-preserved group of Ming-Qing buildings in old Zhengzhou is not a government office but this City God Temple. The Republican-era Zhengxian Gazetteer records renovations led by seven prefectural magistrates between 1501 (Hongzhi 14) and 1890 (Guangxu 16), and the gate, passage hall, stage, main hall and rear chambers still line up on one axis. The three-bay front shown here, with its green glazed-tile overhanging-gable roof, four small-octagonal stone columns in the central bay and three pairs of red plank doors, corresponds in the gazetteer's description to the temple's front gate hall; the main hall proper, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, stands north of the stage.
facts: Form: the front shown is three bays wide and two deep, with a green glazed-tile overhanging-gable roof and seven-tier bracket sets with three ang under the eaves, the ang-tips shaped as triple clouds and the beam-ends as elephant trunks. Four small-octagonal stone columns stand front and back in the central bay; three pairs of solid plank doors hang on the through-columns, with a fan-shaped flight of six steps and a pair of stone lions before them.

History: originally named the Temple of the City God, Marquis Lingyou, it enshrines Ji Xin, a general of Liu Bang of Han, and was founded in the early Ming. According to the Republican-era Zhengxian Gazetteer it was repeatedly renovated by magistrates: Shi Chuncui in 1501 (Hongzhi 14), Liu Ru in Jiajing 6, Li Shixuan in Longqing 4, and others in the Kangxi, Qianlong and Guangxu reigns. A stele with the cursive 'Eulogy of Fortune' by the early-Ming deputy magistrate Zhang Dayou survives in the temple.

Comparison: on the axis, the stage is a two-storey hip-and-gable pavilion whose nineteen roof ridges cross and overlap; the main hall is three bays square under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with gilt-style bracket sets in the central bay; the five-bay rear chamber has an overhanging-gable roof fronted by a rolled-ridge worship porch. With gate, tower, hall and chamber roof types all present, it is one of the larger and more complete surviving City God temples in Henan.

name: Jia County Confucian Temple
era: Surviving Dacheng Hall with Ming–Qing repairs; Five Dynasties founding year not used
yearNote: Surviving Dacheng Hall with Ming–Qing repairs; the Five Dynasties founding year of the temple is not used.
lede: The four front-eave columns of the Dacheng Hall are carved through their whole length with coiling dragons, their capitals cut as tiger heads, and the dragon columns are of wood: Qing wooden dragon columns of this kind survive nowhere else in Henan. The hall is five bays wide under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green glazed tile, and the dragon slab before its terrace shows two dragons playing with a 'spider' rather than a flaming pearl. The temple began as a Kong family shrine completed in 954 (Xiande 1 of Later Zhou) and became the official Confucian temple in 1206 (Taihe 6 of Jin); the Dacheng Hall shown here is the Qing timber structure left by repeated Ming and Qing renovations.
facts: Form: the Dacheng Hall is five bays wide and three deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green glazed tile, 15.5 m high and 19.7 m across the front. The four wooden eave columns are carved through with coiling dragons, their capitals cut as fanged tiger faces looking down on the dragons; the column bases are covered with auspicious scenes, and the architraves, bracket sets and sparrow braces are also pierced with figures, carts, birds, flowers and clouds.

History: descendants of Confucius built a family shrine here in 954 (Xiande 1 of Later Zhou); in 1206 (Taihe 6 of Jin) the magistrate Zhang Zhixing enlarged it on the same site into the official Confucian temple. The Dacheng Hall was restored and its dragon slab carved under the Yingzong emperor of Ming (1459); the temple was rebuilt eleven times, and the surviving Dacheng Hall, Ji Gate and side halls are all Qing timber structures.

Comparison: the wooden dragon columns are later than the Song dragon columns of the Sage Mother Hall at Jinci, yet they are the only surviving example in Henan. The outer bracket sets and purlins keep original painted decoration that is neither the Beijing 'palace style' nor the Suzhou-Hangzhou 'Su style' but a Central Plains local manner. The temple retains 22 buildings with 71 bays, laid out with the school on the left and the shrine on the right, serving as both Kong family shrine and county school.

name: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Jia County
sub: Gate tower with bell and drum towers
era: Qing buildings; exact dates of the individual buildings in the surviving group unknown
yearNote: Qing buildings; the exact dates of the individual buildings in the surviving group are unknown.
lede: Seen from the street, the three-bay gatehouse is flanked by the bell and drum towers; its upper storey is the theatre stage, which faces north into the courtyard where the audience filled the open ground. The Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall of Jiaxian was founded in 1693 (Kangxi 32) by merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi as a way-station and guild house where the old Nanyang-Luoyang and Xuchang-Luoyang roads crossed. Shown here are the gatehouse and the two towers: each tower stands on a 4 m base, with twelve round timber columns carrying a cross-beamed roof under two tiers of flaring eaves, rising above the ridge of the gatehouse.
facts: Form: the gatehouse is three bays wide, the central bay for passage and the side bays for gatekeepers and reception; the open three-bay upper storey faces north as the stage, its brick-carved ridge crowned at the centre by a qilin bearing a treasure vase. The bell and drum towers on either side stand on bases 4 m high, each with twelve round timber columns supporting cross beams, double tiers of flaring eaves and solid bracket sets.

History: the guild hall was founded in 1693 (Kangxi 32) with funds from Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants and is also called the Shan-Shaan Temple or Guandi Temple. It faces south over a watercourse on a site of 6,300 square metres; the river-guarding screen wall before the gate is 8 m wide, 7 m high and 1 m thick, with a brick-carved coiled dragon on a red-sandstone base.

Comparison: the east and west galleries have eleven bays each, the courtyard could hold a thousand spectators, and to the north stand the five-bay Guan Gong Hall and, behind it, the Spring-and-Autumn Pavilion. Jiaxian lay where the Nanyang-Luoyang and Xuchang-Luoyang roads met; the tea route north from Nanyang branched here toward Shanxi, and the hall is regarded as a surviving relic of the Qing 'Ten-Thousand-Li Tea Road' in Henan.

name: Linfeng Fortified Village
sub: West Gate and connected red-stone wall
era: Red-stone walls rebuilt in the 1st year of Tongzhi
yearNote: Red-stone walls rebuilt in the 1st year of Tongzhi.
lede: The red-stone plaque above the gate is cut with the two characters 'Linfeng', and the iron sheathing of the doors is chiselled 'first year of Tongzhi, the year renxu': this wall wears its own birthday on its face. Linfeng Fort was originally a late-Ming earthen stockade; in 1862 (Tongzhi 1) the villager Zhu Zifeng led its rebuilding in purplish-red ashlar, an oval ring 1,100 m around and 6.6 m high, with five watch-towers and eight hundred merlons, and three gates set by the trigram directions to the north-west, south-west and south-east. Shown here are the west-facing Linfeng Gate and the wall joined to it.
facts: Form: the wall is stone outside and earth within, built of purplish-red ashlar on an oval plan 1,100 m around and 6.6 m high, with five watch-towers and 800 merlons. Each gate is a barrel-vaulted opening fitted with a pair of elm doors sheathed in 10 cm iron plate, with flood gates and drainage culverts outside; a moat 13 m wide circles the fort.

History: the Zhu clan is said to have moved here from Hongtong, Shanxi, in the Wanli reign of Ming and first raised an earthen stockade. In 1862 (Tongzhi 1) Zhu Zifeng, a native holding a purchased magistrate's rank, led the building of the red-stone fort; the words 'first year of Tongzhi, the year renxu' chiselled on the iron of the north-west gate are still legible. Inside survive one Ming courtyard house and more than a hundred Qing buildings with over four hundred bays.

Comparison: after 1949 village walls were pulled down across the region, but Linfeng's low-lying site and the need for flood defence saved it; Luo Zhewen called it 'the first red-stone fort of the Central Plains'. It was listed as a Chinese Historic and Cultural Village in 2005, among the first batch of Traditional Chinese Villages in 2012, and from 2014 the National Cultural Heritage Administration funded its overall restoration.
