name: Gaoge Temple
sub: Pavilion and upper part of the high platform
era: Ming building with later repairs; approximate timeline placement
yearNote: Ming building with later repairs; approximate timeline placement.
lede: The one pavilion-hall left from a Ming princely palace. In 1404 (Yongle 2) the Yongle emperor enfeoffed his third son Zhu Gaosui as Prince of Zhao; the prince took up residence at Zhangde (Anyang) in 1425 (Hongxi 1) and turned the prefectural offices into his palace. The palace was abolished with the fall of the Ming in 1644, and by the Republican era only this Dashi Pavilion remained; because it stands on a brick platform about 8 m high it is known as Gaoge Si, the 'High Pavilion Temple'. The existing pavilion was rebuilt in 1470 (Chenghua 6), with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of glazed tile; shown here are the pavilion body and its two tiers of eaves above the stone balustrade of the platform.
facts: Form: a pavilion on a high platform, more than 20 m in total height. The square brick platform is about 8 m high and 13 m on a side, with a flight of 32 stone steps on the south; white marble balustrades with carved lions line the steps and the platform top. The pavilion is three bays square, about 9 m each way, under a double-eaved nine-ridge hip-and-gable roof of glazed tile, with four round timber through-columns rising inside to the top beams.

History: Zhu Gaosui was made Prince of Zhao in 1404 (Yongle 2), took up residence at Zhangde in 1425 (Hongxi 1) and converted the prefectural offices into the Prince of Zhao's palace, of which the Dashi Pavilion was one hall; the existing building was rebuilt in 1470 (Chenghua 6). The Zhao line passed through eleven generations until the palace was abolished in 1644 (Chongzhen 17); by the Republican era its buildings had collapsed, leaving only this pavilion.

Comparison: most Ming princely palaces were demolished after the dynasty fell, and what survives elsewhere, such as the gate of the Jingjiang palace in Guilin, the Longting of the Zhou palace in Kaifeng or the Wangjing Tower of the Lu palace in Xinxiang, are fragments; Gaoge Si is the only building left of the Zhao palace. Twenty-five dragons carved in stone, interspersed with Sanskrit script, run around the outer walls of the pavilion, a rare decoration for a princely hall.

name: Wenzhi Pavilion, Xun County
sub: Surviving crossroads bell and drum tower
era: Surviving pavilion rebuilt in the Kangxi period according to research, approximately placed on the timeline; the Ming date in the national list is for the city wall and Wenzhi Pavilion as a whole
yearNote: According to research, the surviving pavilion was rebuilt in the Kangxi period, and its timeline placement is approximate; the Ming date in the national protected site list refers to the city wall and Wenzhi Pavilion as a whole.
lede: The east-west and north-south main streets of old Junxian cross here; the base is pierced by vaulted openings on all four sides, and carts and pedestrians pass beneath the pavilion. It is at once the bell-and-drum tower at the heart of the town and a gate-tower over the street. Originally called the Central Pavilion, of unknown founding date, it received the town bell after 1615 (Wanli 43) and has been known as the Bell-and-Drum Tower ever since; it burned in 1649 (Shunzhi 6) and was rebuilt in 1709 (Kangxi 48) by magistrate Liang Tongluo, who renamed it Wenzhi Ge, 'Pavilion of Civil Rule'. Shown here are the brick base and the two-storey, double-eaved pyramidal-roofed pavilion that make up the surviving structure.
facts: Form: about 20 m high in all, in two parts, base and pavilion. The square brick base is about 12 m on a side, with an arched vault through the middle of each face so that the four openings align east-west and north-south. On top stands a two-storey square pavilion about 10 m high, with a double-eaved four-sided pyramidal roof, upturned corners and ornamental ridges trimmed with glazed tile; the lower storey opens on all four sides, and the platform is ringed by a gallery and a 1 m parapet with square openings.

History: the Jiaqing-era Junxian Gazetteer records that 'after the yimao year of Wanli (1615) the bell was moved to the Central Pavilion'. It was destroyed by fire in 1649 (Shunzhi 6) and rebuilt in 1709 (Kangxi 48) by magistrate Liang Tongluo, who renamed it Wenzhi Ge after the idea of 'ruling by civil virtue'; Zhang Xi wrote a 'Record of the Rebuilding of Wenzhi Ge'. The present pavilion is the structure left by that rebuilding, with later repairs.

Comparison: above the four vaults are Qing bluestone horizontal tablets, 'Red glow streams from the eastern wall' and 'Jade pours from the western hills' by Zhao Sulu on the east and west, 'Clear waters ring the Li' and 'Dark mist guards the Pi' by Zhang Zhe on the south and north. The pavilion is listed together with the surviving stretch of city wall on the Wei River, first built in 1370 (Hongwu 3), and is one of the heritage points of the Junxian section of the Grand Canal.

yearNote: Official sources record its founding in about 1560; the main hall was repaired in 1928, in 1952–1960 and at other times, so not all the surviving decoration can be regarded as original 16th-century work.
lede: Low-sweeping roofs spread to either side, and the layered gables and fine gold ornament reflect the lightness of the timber structure. The sim of Wat Xieng Thong rests quietly on its platform beneath the traditional roof curves of Luang Prabang.
facts: The depicted subject is the sim and its supporting platform, excluding the later Royal Funerary Carriage House; the tiles, timberwork and gold ornament are colored from photographs of their present state.
Official tourism sources record the founding of the temple in about 1560 and repeated repairs to the main hall; the founding phase and later decoration are described separately.

sub: Surviving main shrine tower with entrance and base
yearNote: Official Khánh Hòa Province sources give the late 13th–early 14th century; 1300 is only for approximate ordering, and the construction date of the tower is not inferred from the life dates of the king worshipped there.
place: Khánh Hòa Province · Phan Rang–Tháp Chàm
lede: The red-brick tower body is divided by pilasters and false doors, and the layered brick ornament of the upper tiers tapers steadily. The main tower of Po Klong Garai preserves the outline of a Cham temple tower and also carries on local ritual traditions.
facts: The plate shows only the main shrine tower of the three towers, excluding the gate tower and the long-ridged fire tower; the main tower's entrance has an inset stone door frame and a relief of the dancing Shiva.

Official Khánh Hòa Province sources record that the tower group was built in the late 13th–early 14th century. The location is registered under the current Khánh Hòa Province, and the former name, Ninh Thuận Province, is kept for search.

name: Meridian Gate (Ngọ Môn) of the Huế Imperial City
sub: Complete gate platform and Five Phoenix Pavilion
yearNote: 1833 is the construction date of the Meridian Gate; the surviving timber pavilion, roofs and platform have undergone later repairs, and there are also records of modern repairs.
lede: The broad gate platform folds forward into wings at both sides, and above it the Five Phoenix Pavilion spreads out under roofs of differing heights. The Meridian Gate combines a masonry palace gate with a timber pavilion to form the front outline of the Huế Imperial City.
facts: The platform is U-shaped, with five passages in all: three on the front and two in the side wings; the five passages must not be drawn as five openings on the front.

Official tourism sources record its construction in 1833, with yellow tiles on the central roof and blue-green tiles on either side; the plate includes the complete platform and the Five Phoenix Pavilion.

name: San Agustin Church, Manila
sub: Surviving church facade and bell tower
yearNote: 1607 is the completion date of the surviving stone church, as distinct from the earlier wooden churches. The bell tower and later repairs have their own histories, and the present building as a whole is not dated as original fabric of a single year.
lede: Tiered orders of columns divide the doors and windows of the stone facade, a round window and a cross mark the triangular pediment, and the surviving bell tower adjoins it on the right. San Agustin Church preserves another architectural tradition of old Manila.
facts: The plate shows the surviving main facade and the single bell tower on the right; the low remnant of the lost left tower is kept and not reconstructed as symmetrical twin towers.

The National Museum of the Philippines records that the surviving stone church was completed in 1607; the original wooden church and later repairs are described separately, and the monastery as a whole is not drawn.

name: Sudeoksa Daeungjeon
sub: Single Daeungjeon hall and stone platform
era: Hall built 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
yearNote: Hall built in 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
lede: A gently sloping overhanging gable roof of tiles rests on the three-bay timber hall, with beam ends projecting tier by tier from the gable side. With its gray-brown timber and simple lattice doors, Sudeoksa Daeungjeon preserves the airy form of a Buddhist hall of the late Goryeo.
facts: The surviving Daeungjeon was built in 1308; the temple's founding and the hall's construction date are recorded separately.
Three bays wide and four bays deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof; the columns carry the eaves, and the beam frame on the gable side is an important part of identifying the structure.
The plate shows only the Daeungjeon and its stone platform, excluding the stone lantern in front and the temple's other buildings.

name: Buseoksa Muryangsujeon
era: Surviving Muryangsujeon rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
yearNote: The surviving Muryangsujeon was rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
lede: Long eaves extend along the five-bay hall, its timber columns slightly curved, and pale lattice doors line up beneath the deep eaves. Set high within Buseoksa, the Muryangsujeon is an important surviving timber Buddhist hall of the Goryeo period.
facts: The temple was founded in 676, and the surviving Muryangsujeon shown here is assigned to the Goryeo by its 1376 rebuilding date.
Five bays wide and three bays deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the columns swell at mid-height, and the lattice doors and stone platform are preserved in their present state.
The hall enshrines Amitabha Buddha; the plate takes the exterior of the hall, and the stone lantern in front is not included in this subject.

name: Dabotap of Bulguksa
sub: Complete Dabotap stone pagoda with stairways on four sides
era: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
yearNote: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
lede: Square stone pillars support a pagoda body whose tiers keep changing form, while balustrades and an octagonal canopy shift its scale in the upper part. Carved from granite into a complex outline close to timber construction, Dabotap is entirely different from the common multi-roofed stone pagodas.
facts: Korean authorities officially date Dabotap to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, the ordering uses an approximate value, and no precise completion year is claimed for the pagoda.

Square stone pillars and stairways on four sides below combine with octagonal elements above, and official sources explain that its number of stories is hard to count in the way used for an ordinary pavilion-style pagoda.
Following its present state, the single surviving stone lion is kept, the lost lions are not added back, and the neighboring Seokgatap is not drawn.

name: Changdeokgung Injeongjeon
era: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
yearNote: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
lede: Double flying eaves support a broad gray-tiled roof, and red columns and blue-green dancheong painting surround the five-bay hall. With its terrace, central stairway and tall, open interior, Injeongjeon forms the main hall of Changdeokgung where state ceremonies were held.
facts: The National Heritage Portal gives the date of the surviving building as the 4th year of King Sunjo of Joseon (1804), and the palace's founding year is not substituted for it.
Five bays wide and four bays deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the double eaves outside do not mean there are two separate floors inside.
The plate shows only Injeongjeon and its terrace; the side corridors, the rank stones in the courtyard and other palace buildings are not included.

name: Namdaemun of Kaesong
sub: Stone gate platform and postwar rebuilt gate tower
era: Inner-city gate first built 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
yearNote: The inner-city gate was first built in 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
lede: A single stone arch pierces the gate platform, and the open three-bay gate tower is covered by a broad tiled roof. Namdaemun of Kaesong layers the gate site of the Goryeo capital, the old stone platform and the timber gate tower restored after the war in a single place.
facts: The gate was built together with the inner city wall in 1391–1393; the surviving gate tower is a postwar reconstruction, and the timeline uses 1955.

The ICOMOS evaluation records that the gate tower was destroyed in 1950 and restored from 1954; the caption in the nomination file and the repair notes give 1955, and the dating note keeps both records.
The gate platform has a single arch, and the gate tower is three bays wide with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a great bell hanging inside; this entry does not include the small shrine nearby.

name: Pyongyang Pothong Gate
sub: Gate platform and double-eaved gate tower of Pothong Gate
era: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
yearNote: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
lede: A massive stone platform is pierced by a single arched gateway, and the double-eaved gate tower rises from its top. Pothong Gate preserves the form of the western city gate of old Pyongyang, its masonry platform and painted timber tower forming two clearly distinct upper and lower parts.
facts: Kim Il Sung University sources record that the surviving gate underwent major repairs in 1473, followed by further extensions; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not the exact date of the surviving timberwork.
The gate tower is three bays wide and three bays deep, with two tiers of eaves; the platform is built of granite, with a single semicircular arched gateway at the center.
The depicted subject is the surviving platform and gate tower; the extending city walls are not reconstructed, and the modern streetscape is not included.

name: Lecture Hall of Sungyang Academy
sub: Five-bay lecture hall of the academy
era: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
yearNote: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
lede: The five-bay lecture hall stands across the academy terrace, its open central wooden floor and end rooms forming a simple hall. Sungyang Academy places teaching and rites at the front and back, and the lecture hall is its space for study.
facts: The academy was established in 1573 and received a royal name in 1575, and the surviving lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the specific construction year of the timberwork is unclear, and about 1600 serves only for timeline placement.

The World Heritage nomination file records the lecture hall as five bays wide and three bays deep; the plan has an open three-bay central hall with rooms on either side, under a single-eaved overhanging gable roof.
The plate shows only the lecture hall, referring to nomination photographs, old photographs and plans; neither the three-door gate in front nor the shrine above is mistaken for the lecture hall.

name: Sonjuk Bridge, Kaesong
sub: Old stone beam bridge and 1780 stone balustrades
era: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
yearNote: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
lede: A short granite beam bridge spans a shallow stream, its deck enclosed by round-topped stone posts and rails. Sonjuk Bridge became a memorial site because Jeong Mong-ju was killed there, and the later balustrades also record its withdrawal from everyday traffic.
facts: The nomination file says the stone bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, and its exact construction year has not been confirmed; about 1100 is an ordering position, and 1392 is the year of the killing.
The bridge is 8.35 m long and 3.36 m wide, with stone piers carrying stone beams topped by stone slabs; it is not an arch bridge. The surviving stone balustrades on both sides were added in 1780.
Only the old Sonjuk Bridge and its later balustrades are drawn; the separate bridge built alongside for traffic, the stele pavilion and the inscribed steles are not part of the subject.

facts: Cultural Heritage Online dates the Karamon to 1651 and records it as a mukaikaramon gate one bay wide and one bay deep, with copper-tile roofing.

yearNote: The timeline follows the 1706 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
lede: Vermilion columns support the upper story and a broad tiled roof, and the central passage is flanked by two niches for guardian figures. The Rōmon of Nezu Shrine covers its two-story gate with a single large roof, in compact proportions.
facts: The Rōmon belongs to the building of Nezu Shrine completed in 1706; Cultural Heritage Online records it as a three-bay, single-passage two-story gate with an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof and pantile roofing.
The lower story has only a single central passage, with niches for zuishin guardian figures on either side; a balustrade runs around the outer edge of the upper story.

name: Asakusa Shrine
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1649 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
lede: On the east side of Sensō-ji, this shrine preserves early Edo shrine buildings. The low, broad worship hall spreads out in vermilion columns and gold ornament, on a scale quite different from the nearby main hall of Sensō-ji.
facts: The surviving shrine buildings were built and donated by Tokugawa Iemitsu in 1649 and have come through disasters and war.

The main sanctuary (honden), offering hall (heiden) and worship hall (haiden) form the core of the shrine, with the main sanctuary linked to the offering hall and worship hall by a connecting passage.
This plate shows only the front of the worship hall. Asakusa Shrine and Sensō-ji are separate entries, and their dates and personal records are kept separately.

name: Kiyomizu Kannon-dō of Kan'ei-ji
sub: Kannon Hall and the stage in front
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1631 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding. It was moved to its present site in 1694, and conservation repairs were completed in 1996.
lede: The vermilion Kannon Hall overlooks the slopes of Ueno, its wooden stage projecting toward Shinobazu Pond. It borrows the concept of Kiyomizu-dera in Kyoto, yet has survived through Tokyo's own history of construction and relocation.
facts: The Kannon Hall was built by Tenkai in 1631 and moved to its present site in 1694 for the construction of Kan'ei-ji's Konponchūdō.
The temple officially records conservation repairs to the cultural property from 1990 to 1996, restoring its appearance at the time of the Genroku-era relocation.
The plate shows the Kannon Hall and the stage in front, omitting the Moon Pine (Tsuki no Matsu) and the hillside scenery; the raised stage of Kiyomizu-dera in Kyoto is not applied to this hall.

yearNote: The timeline follows the 1697 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
lede: The copper-plate roof has oxidized to blue-green, and the broad curved roof covers a solid timber structure. The main hall of Gokoku-ji carries on the scale and craftsmanship of an Edo prayer temple of the Genroku period.
facts: Gokoku-ji was founded in 1681; the surviving Kannon Hall shown was completed in 1697, and the founding year of the temple cannot be substituted for the building's date.
Cultural Heritage Online records the main hall as seven bays wide and seven bays deep, with an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof, a three-bay kōhai (front canopy) and batten-seam copper-plate roofing.

name: Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji
sub: Single-story Zen Buddhist hall with mokoshi
yearNote: The timeline follows the 1407 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
lede: The great eaves of the main roof are raised high, with a low mokoshi skirt roof encircling the building below. With its compact square mass, the Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji preserves the form of a Muromachi-period Zen Buddhist hall in the Kantō region.
facts: Based on an ink inscription dated the 14th year of Ōei found during repairs, Cultural Heritage Online records the Jizō Hall's construction date as 1407.

The building is a Buddhist hall three bays square, single-story with a mokoshi, under an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof; the upper roof is covered with wood shingles and the mokoshi with copper plate. The two tiers of eaves do not mean two stories.
It stands in Higashimurayama, Tokyo; the plate shows only the Jizō Hall, not the other buildings of Shōfuku-ji.
